item.title: “Tourism and climate are intrinsically linked.” So why isn’t the travel industry talking more about the super El Niño?
item.description:
Source: Adventure
As El NiÃ±o looks set to peak in late 2026, weâre already witnessing disruptions to tourism. Regenerative tourism expert Susanna Kelly-Shankar puts it into perspective and explains how travelers can prepare for climate-related events. Right now, another once-in-a-lifetime El NiÃ±o is building. In Peru, it unleashed heavy rains, triggering flooding and restricting access to Machu Picchu. Indonesia is grappling with the opposite, as wildfires tear across vulnerable orangutan habitat. Higher temperatures, more droughts and floods are what this climate pattern is known for. While Super El NiÃ±os are rare, the few documented have driven global catastrophes, including the 1876-78 global famine that killed 50 million people. Events in the 1980s and 90s led to a 15 percent loss of coral reefs and a population collapse of the GalÃ¡pagos Island penguins. And yet, as major news outlets and the World Meteorological Organization sound the alarm of another outsized climate event, one multi-trillion-dollar industry remains relatively quiet. Tourism. So, it isnât particularly surprising that, as I scroll through social media, it seems as if travel is carrying on âbusiness as usualâ. And itâs not just social media; I have yet to see United Nations Tourism publish any El NiÃ±o-related content. Typically, the start of El NiÃ±o is signaled by slowing Pacific Ocean trade winds, a natural cycle that alters weather patterns. But this yearâs El NiÃ±o is anything but natural, shattering records as sea surface temperatures surge 5.4Â°F (3Â°C) above baseline [editorâs note: This is an accurate conversion, based on anomaly temperature fluctuations from National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/NOAA], well over the threshold for a very strong event. Experts predict it to be one of the most intense climate disruptions ever recordedâand it hasnât even peaked. A disconnect between environmental research and tourism isnât helping, with research on climate siloed from industry focus on visitor experience and expenditure. Whether the industry feels ready or not, it canât ignore the looming storm. In the air and on the ground, extreme heat, wildfires, and shifting jet streams can cause flight delays and destroy roads and rails. However, my graduate research on integrating nature-based solutions into tourism development taught me that tourism and climate are intrinsically linked forever locked in a cycle of change. As strong El NiÃ±os become more common, we need to break those silosâputting community knowledge and nature at the center of every decision. So while we witness one of the most volatile climate events of our lifetime unfolding, why might the industry remain deafeningly silent? One reason may be because travel is built on the promise of abundanceâunlimited resources, perfect seasons, and reliable transport. Big industry players may be hesitant to alter operations that impact their bottom line, based âonlyâ on predictions. Perhaps travelers too cling to vacations already on the books with a âcome hell or high waterâ mentality. Others, wary of giving in to fear-mongering, want to move forward cautiously. And tourism-reliant communities are understandably reluctant about warding off visitors. Whether the industry feels ready or not, it canât ignore the looming storm. In the air and on the ground, extreme heat, wildfires, and shifting jet streams can cause flight delays and destroy roads and rails. At our destinations, droughts and floods can exacerbate food shortages and drain local water supplies, driving up costs while creating tension between travelers and host communities over resources. All this can make planning challenging and calls for putting safety and community needs first. But how exactly do you prepare for climate unpredictability? At the core of regenerative tourismâan approach that challenges the status quo, where tourism and community become active collaborators to create thriving communities and natureâis a fundamental mindset shift: Decentering ourselves from the travel narrative. This means digging deep to acknowledge the privilege gap between travelers and communities to flip our perspective. What is decentering? Think of it like this. We can still enjoy our travels, but personal experience shouldnât come before anyoneâs well-being. For those who travel for pleasure, extreme weather is often an inconvenient hiccupâa canceled flight, an altered itinerary, or a closed cultural site. But for the communities who host us, those same torrential rains or severe droughts destroy homes, wipe out crops, and decimate public infrastructure. We also need to maintain realistic expectations. That could mean accepting that record heat may close tourist sites, ski resorts may have low snowpack, landslides may disrupt transit networks, and once-vibrant reefs may be bleached white. As El NiÃ±o strains global resources, we need to remember that tourism is resource-intensive. Travelers generate a lot of food waste, and hotel guests consume up to eight times more water than the average resident, with many resorts trucking in water during drought. Simple swaps help us prioritize community needs over personal comfort while cutting excessive food, water, and energy use. We can choose community homestays over water-heavy resorts, trade all-you-can-eat buffets for independent restaurants that support local farmers, and prioritize small-scale, community-led tours over resource-heavy motorized excursions. Traveling with a local guide keeps us attuned to on-the-ground realities. Another tenet of regenerative tourism is tailoring our actions to each community’s unique needs. Being a good guest starts with a simple search for âEl NiÃ±o impacts in [destination]â to uncover local priorities. If drought is expected, return to the basics: take shorter showers and turn off running water for an immediate effect. And when weather disruptions do happen, instead of succumbing to sensational fear-mongering, look for reliable on-the-ground sources like municipal notices, park services, or local tourism boards. We also need to maintain realistic expectations. That could mean accepting that record heat may close tourist sites, ski resorts may have low snowpack, landslides may disrupt transit networks, and once-vibrant reefs may be bleached white. Of course, there is also a risk to travelersâ personal safety. In a crisis, an unprepared traveler quickly becomes an added strain on local emergency infrastructure and first responders who may be needed elsewhere. To manage risk, have a plan B for your travels. Always take comprehensive travel and health insurance, make flexible bookings, and register your trip with your government. And of course, always heed local weather warnings and evacuation orders; this may even require returning home. As weâve seen in the aftermath of Nepalâs floods, being a responsible traveler during climate upheaval is recognizing that travel can serve as a lifeline or liability. In times of crisis, hotel beds and clean waterâall of which tourists require in abundanceâmay be critical to displaced residents and emergency responders. Before setting off, letâs ask ourselves: Will our presence aid economic recovery, or use up life-sustaining resources? Thereâs no blueprint for traveling during a Super El NiÃ±o. Navigating this balance requires adaptability and making informed choices about when to carry on, pivot, or even hit pause. We can shift timelines, like traveling during shoulder season to avoid extreme heat, or reroute itineraries to minimize risk from tropical storm seasons. And when travel is welcome, our capital becomes a tool for restoration. Rather than traditional offsets, consider directly donating 1 percent of your total trip costs to a community initiative that builds resilience against extreme weather, such as reef and mangrove restoration, to leave the places you visit a little better than when you arrived. Whatâs clear is that a Super El NiÃ±o is building, and it will disrupt not only our travels, but also the communities we love to visit. Our responsibility as travelers during El NiÃ±o is to understand our privilege and make choices that put communities first. Travelers hold immense power: Every choice about when, where, and how to travel carries far more weight than we realize. Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the worldâs largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Susanna Kelly-Shankar is a regenerative tourism expert with an MSc in biodiversity with research focused on nature-based solutions for tourism. She advocates for a more sustainable tourism industry by highlighting the intersection of tourism and the natural environment. Can't find what you're looking for? Try using these tags:

item.title: TSA pauses expansion of Gateside program that lets non-travelers through airport security
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
TSA pauses expansion of Gateside program that lets non-travelers through airport security The Transportation Security Administration rolled out a new program in September that allows TSA PreCheck members to travel through airport security without a ticket, harkening back to the days before 9/11, when people could greet or bid farewell to their traveling loved ones right at the gate. But now it looks like TSA plans to roll that program back — at least for now. The Gateside by TSA PreCheck program launched in September 2026 at 13 airports as part of a pilot program. It appeared to quietly expand to 300 U.S. airports several weeks ago. While TSA did not publicize the change or update its website to include the broader list of airports, its application page for gate passes offered users a choice from that wider selection, and passes were offered. Earlier this week, however, the expansion appears to have been retracted, with only the original 13 airports available through the TSA's application portal. A representative from the Norfolk Airport Authority in Virginia told local TV news station WAVY that the TSA had informed him that the program was on hold indefinitely, except for the original pilot airports. It's not clear why the expansion was pulled back. TSA did not immediately return TPG's request for comment or additional details. The TSA's Gateside website notes that the program "will roll out to more airports across the country in the coming months." The 13 airports that are still participating in Gateside are: - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) Several other U.S. airports offer their own version of a gate pass for non-travelers to proceed through security; however, non-passengers cannot use TSA PreCheck lanes and must go through the main security checkpoint instead. Those airports include: - Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ) - Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) - Kansas City International Airport (MCI) - Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) - Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) - Nashville International Airport (BNA) - Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) - San Antonio International Airport (SAT) - Tulsa International Airport (TUL) - John Wayne Airport (SNA) in California - Ontario International Airport (ONT) in California - Capital Region International Airport (LAN) in Michigan - Tri-Cities Airport (PSC) in Washington - San Francisco International Airport (SFO) - Orlando International Airport (MCO) - Shreveport Regional Airport (SHV) in Louisiana - Tampa International Airport (TPA) The pilot Gateside by TSA PreCheck program has been rolled back to the original 13 participating airports, down from an expanded list of some 300 airports that were allowing members of TSA PreCheck to get passes through airport security even when they weren't traveling. The program allows loved ones to accompany family members or friends to the gate even when they aren't flying themselves. It's a bit surprising that the expansion was pulled since the announcement garnered a lot of positive media attention for the government. The TSA hasn't said why the expansion was scrapped, but still says more airports will be added in the coming months. We'll see if that timeline sticks and will bring you updates as they come in. item.title: The Untold Oral History of the Melly, the Fleece Hoodie That Became an Outdoor Cult Classic
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
A November 2017 Melanzana team photo, featuring Melanzana co-founder Fritz Howard (back row, far right, wearing black beanie and sunglasses) and Ann Stanek, former advertising lead (middle row, far right, wearing black top and glasses) (Photo: Courtesy of Melanzana Blog) At a hardware store in Portland, Oregon, I spot it from across the garden center: the signature micro-grid fleece, sleeves a different color than the torso, drawcord hood. A few moments later, the man wearing the unmistakable hoodie pushes his shopping cart into the next aisle, apparently also scoping out landscaping rocks. As we pass each other, I catch his eye. “Nice Melly,” I quip. He smiles knowingly. “You from Colorado?” Anyone who owns a distinctive fleece from the brand Melanzana has undoubtedly had one of these encounters. The company, based in the former silver mining town of Leadville, Colorado, population 2,633, has inspired a peculiar kind of recognition among its devotees. Little did I know when I bought my own hoodie—blue torso, orange sleeves—in 2017 while living in Boulder, that I was joining an unofficial club of people drawn to simple mountain clothing made by hand. Since 1994, co-founder Fritz Howard has led Melanzana’s every move. As a lanky New England ski bum in his twenties, Howard and his childhood friend, Kevin “Kevco” Crochetiere, got their paws on some Polartec fleece remnants from an outlet in Lawrence, Massachusetts, and began sewing basic mountain garments for themselves and friends. Howard’s mom taught him to sew when he was a kid, and for the first two winters of the fledgling business, he lived in the woods outside town in a tipi he had sewn himself, keeping his expenses low. They initially called their small enterprise Eggplant because the silly, uncool vegetable evoked the antithesis of big outdoor brands. But a trademark conflict soon forced a change, and they settled on Melanzana, Italian for eggplant. Howard chose Leadville because, even back then, he wanted to live in a place without the ostentation of a ski resort. Friends of his say he never expected, or really even wanted, the recognition Melanzana has today. As someone who identifies as anti-corporate, Howard intended to make affordable and quality gear for friends and neighbors as a service to the community—not for personal gain or fame. As demand grew, though, the hobby accidentally evolved into a business, and three decades later, Howard’s hoodie has become a symbol of sorts, connecting its wearers while putting Leadville on the outdoor gear map. Outside reached out to Howard for this story, but, being a private person, he said he preferred to step back and let others who have played an important role in Melanzana’s success tell the story instead. Told through the voices of former employees, Leadville residents, devoted customers from around the world, and a moderator of the Melanzana subreddit, this is the untold narrative of how Melanzana became legendary in the outdoor industry, Colorado, and beyond. Melanzana’s first storefront was tiny and tucked between other small businesses in the 700 block of Harrison Avenue, Leadville’s main thoroughfare, across from a cluster of brick buildings including the old church and city clerk’s office. Mark “Smokey” Burgess (first retail employee, now the owner of the Leadville consignment store Community Threads): I was in between jobs, and Fritz approached me. He’s like, “Why don’t you come work for me?” I said, “I don’t think so; I don’t want to do retail.” He said, “I’ll let you live in my tipi.” I was like, “Let’s go look at it.” It was spring, so it was super snowy, and we post-holed to get to the tipi. I was like, “Sweet, I’ll do it.” Zach Neater (former employee, recently returned to Leadville after years away): Smokey and I would come in on Wednesdays. We always had our dogs, Charlie and Louie. Fritz had his gang of dogs, too. He was a skijoring racer and would be in the back surfing sled dog websites while we were cutting up fleece. It kind of felt like a little community clubhouse with everybody growing up together. Smokey: We would bust our ass to get product on the shelf. The weekend would come, people would buy it all, and then we’d be like, “Oh shit. We’ve got to make more.” It’s been the exact same business model since way back when. It’s really not that much different. Ann Stanek (hired to oversee advertising in 2004; now owns the artist collective Harper Rose Studios in Leadville): Smokey was working when I bought my first fleece. That’s when he sewed and did retail. I didn’t like the length of it and asked if there was any way he could just whack off three inches. He was like, “Sure, if you go get me a bagel and a coffee.” And I did. That’s how we do it in Leadville. Smokey: Melanzana’s saying was “Original, Functional, Soulful.” And it was. Everything we did was just Fritz and us doing it. If we needed a new cutting table, we went to the hardware store and bought two-by-fours and plywood, and we built it. The racks I built back in the late ’90s are still in use. Kendra Kurihara (bookkeeper from 2012 to 2016): I started coming to Leadville in 1993 to work for Outward Bound. Then I bought a house in 2001. I became friends with Fritz soon after that. We skied together a few times. I would go into the store, where Smokey’s store [Community Threads] is now, because I knew Smokey and Fritz, and I liked them and wanted to talk. I never bought anything because I was so poor and so cheap, and I think because I had pro deals with other companies to buy clothes. Smokey: I’m not gonna lie, back in the day [the product] wasn’t that awesome. I mean, it was the mid- to late-nineties. It was the very beginning, so it was a pretty rudimentary fit. I have one hanging up on the wall of my shop today. People try to buy it, and I’m like, “No, look at it; it’s like putting on a pizza box.” But back in the day, it was pretty innovative. All the locals, of course, bought them. Johnny Welsh (local bartender who bought his first fleece circa 1997): If you walked in the front door, there was a wooden receptacle about four feet high. The company had extra scraps in there. I took some home and made a flute case that I still have. I bought a hat, and it’s the exact colors of the scraps that I picked up. Smokey: We used to cut everything out by hand with a knife roller. Then Fritz was going to digitize all of his patterns. He rolled them up, took them on a plane to L.A.—I think it was L.A.—and that was the start of really getting into manufacturing. We built this big, long cutting table. He and I would roll out fleece, and he would print out his digitized patterns all nested in together. Then he cut them out with a stack cutter. That was big-time back then. Stanek: The sewers would sew the same colors for months. There was a cutter named James Healy. He was the first one to lay out a new color on the big table. At the top of his lungs as he was rolling out the new colors, he’d be like, “New color! New color!” Everybody would cheer. Kurihara: Everyone had a key. I think they could come in any time they wanted. I lived just down the street from the shop, so sometimes I’d turn onto my street and think, Oh the lights are on. Someone’s sewing, I guess. Stanek: We got to choose the music. It was a five- or six-CD player. There was a big CD book, and we’d toss in the music, whatever we wanted to listen to for the day. A lot of Grateful Dead, Willie Nelson, Burning Spear, and reggae. Neater: What I loved about it was we were part of that outdoor community before social media. Kurihara: I think Fritz did a really good job of avoiding cliquiness by making sure we had a diversity of people, be it age or background or lifestyle. We had 20-year-old hippie chicks and older retired people who were looking for different work towards the end of their careers. Stanek: There was a gal, Lane. She was a sewer, and she would make costumes for shows. That’s why she gravitated to Melanzana. She brought a super fun vibe. She brought a hula hoop in, and every so often, we’d take hula hoop breaks. Kurihara: I’ve actually only bought one Melanzana in my entire life. When we worked there, we had a 100 percent discount. I was like, “Maybe we should put some guardrails on this.” Fritz finally did. But you still got to spend, like, $800 a year. Early on, Melanzana made all kinds of outdoor apparel. The 1996 summer catalog lists river shorts, windshirts, microfiber jerseys, overmitts, T-shirts, and scrap caps. The Polartec Micro Grid hoodies that would become the brand’s signature product weren’t introduced until the early 2000s. Smokey: Here’s the story with the hoodies. There were four hippie girls sewing. They kept saying, “Fritz, you should make hoodies.” He’s like, no. We were just trying to keep up with demand. A couple of the sewing girls started making these pullover hoodies anyway, not even resembling what they are now. We made some for ourselves, too. We knew Fritz wasn’t happy about it. Then he saw it and decided that he would make some, basically the hoodie that it is today. They were so functional and so good. That’s when it all kind of shifted. (Around the same time, a woman in the community was also pestering Howard to make hoodies.) Kurihara: We just gradually brought more colors in. We would do eight colors in ten or twelve different combinations. We’d find a color that we liked—a random fabric, a T-shirt, a photo, a paint chip. We’d put it together and send it to the fabric mill, then they would send a sample back. I just didn’t trust that way of collecting colors, so I was like, “Let’s get a Pantone color swatch.” Smokey: [Fritz] was just constantly working with Polartec to get materials, experimenting, and refining his design skills. That’s when I was transitioning out. (Smokey left the company in the late 1990s to pursue other things, and went on to open the consignment shop Community Threads in one of Melanzana’s former spaces a block away.) Stanek: Fritz was so funny in where he was picky, and one of those things was how a garment was photographed for the website. You’d lay the shirt on the ground and flip one elbow up and one elbow down, kind of in the pocket, but you’d scrunch it up so it had a little bit of movement but not too much, but still the shape but not too much. Oh my god, I swear my tummy muscles are strong because I had to lean over the fleece, and it had to be just the right angle of the dangle. Kurihara: I was anxious all the time thinking we’re growing, we don’t have room, we need to expand, or we need to do something. And Fritz would be like, “We’re not there yet.” Stanek: Fritz is a great model for everybody to really just stand by what you have and don’t try and do too much; stick to your values. In 2008, Fritz bought the building at 716 Harrison Avenue, where it’s still located today. At first it was three separate addresses, but Melanzana gradually took over the entire 7,500 square feet. In 2011, he installed a rooftop solar system to power the building. Already popular locally, the brand grew faster as word of mouth and social media spread. Stanek: The last project I did with Fritz was the “Nice Melly” sticker. We were like, wouldn’t it be fun if we had these stickers people could grab after they get a Melly? Smokey: It’s just part of wearing your Melanzana. I was at Dead & Company’s 60th anniversary in Golden Gate Park [in 2025], and there was a guy just over there with the exact same color as me. We looked at each other and nodded like, right on, man. Stanek: I’ve even said to him, “This has to be so cool to look around and see all these people in your things.” He’s very proud and psyched, I think, in those kinds of situations. Smokey: It used to be a really popular gift for people’s crew and pacers for the [popular endurance race, the Leadville] 100. Adam Ducharme (tourism and economic development director of Lake County, which includes Leadville): What I notice is that people don’t just come to Melanzana to buy a fleece. They’re coming because they want to experience a place that feels real. Mariel Fulton (grew up in Colorado, bought her first fleece circa 2008): I first got mine in high school at a cross-country camp held at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville. On the last day, we always fast-hiked up Mount Elbert, and I forgot a jacket. Melanzana was not a popular thing then, and I’d never heard of it. But it was the only real place to grab a layer, so we walked or ran down from campus, grabbed an energy drink at Kum & Go, and I got myself an all-brown hoodie in the colorway “Cup of Joe.” Honestly, the store was pretty empty, and we could see folks sewing in the back. It became my most beloved piece of gear, and I wore it on every hike. I still have it! Evan Stout (artist from Colorado): I got my first Melly in late 2019 right after coming home to Colorado from living abroad in East Africa. While I was living abroad, I met folks who owned Mellys, and it felt like a miracle that someone on the other side of the world knew about this tiny brand. It was such a point of connection to home for me. Lauren Fagan (Melly collector): I got my first Melanzana in 2013 before they became a Colorado staple, back when you could walk into the store in Leadville any time of the day and try stuff on. I now have four hoodies, two dresses, and one half-zip. So many companies are making knock-offs now, but they just don’t compare. My OG Melly is still in excellent condition 13 years later. All of the stitching is intact even after hundreds of washes and adventures. Mellanzaniac (moderator of the Melanzana subreddit who spoke on the condition of anonymity): They don’t make the absolute best gear, they don’t make the absolute lightest gear, they don’t make the absolute most unique gear, but I like the fact that it is a quality piece of merchandise. I’m more impressed by the fact that they take care of their employees; they pay their employees a living wage, and they give them benefits. When demand exploded during the pandemic, Melanzana faced a problem many brands envy: more customers than it could serve. The company responded with purchase limits, online lotteries, and caps on store traffic. Some shoppers interpreted the restrictions as a scarcity tactic, but the truth was far less calculated—the tiny sewing operation simply couldn’t make enough hoodies to satisfy everyone who wanted one. In March 2024, Melanzana opened a second cut-and-sew facility in Alamosa, another small Colorado mountain town with a population of 9,871. The growing staff is helping the company return to online sales for the first time in six years. “As we continue to ramp up, we hope to carve away at the wait times in Leadville, and eventually bring more Mellys to all our people, on the web,” the company wrote. Today, nonlocals still need an appointment to visit the store. Stanek: It was awesome because you’re part of this big movement and you could see over the years the growth and the respect people had—but then there starts to be this tipping point where now friends of friends are saying you’ve got to get one of these. Pretty soon there are people who don’t even know why they want the Melanzana, but they want the Melanzana. Mellanzaniac: Even before the lottery, it was ridiculous to try to get a hold of one. You see a lot of people complain about the appointment system they use today and say they’re just manufacturing scarcity. And I’m like, “Clearly you were never in Leadville when there were 100 people in line at eight in the morning waiting for the doors to open so they could run in, grab everything off the shelves, and immediately post it on eBay.” Ducharme: I think there can be this perception that there’s sort of this gatekeeping, or trying to create a false sense of supply and demand scarcity, but I can assure you with every fiber of my being, Melanzana and Leadville-Twin Lakes are not that. We are just really invested in maintaining a sense of humanity that might even be from a bygone era. Mellanzaniac: It’s a piece of gear that is recognizable enough that if you see someone with it, you know what they’re wearing. It used to be that you knew they had gone to Leadville because that was the only way they could get it. Smokey: Melanzana used to do a local sale. They would take all their second-quality product, and twice a year, they would let all the locals come in and shop. During the COVID frenzy, they couldn’t really do that. I worked it out with Fritz, and he just brought boxes and boxes of seconds over. We had three H racks, and we had a top-secret Melanzana sale for the locals. I think I might still have the sign somewhere. It said, “Shhh! Melly sale.” That was more or less to take care of the locals. Stanek: We all get a little defensive, those of us who know and understand. People get so frustrated about the appointments, but it makes sense, actually. It’s all made by hand, and if there’s going to be something for people to shop, they’ve got to manage the inventory. Smokey: Here at Community Threads, we’re super protective of them. When people come in and say, “What’s up with that store? You’ve got to have an appointment. What a great marketing scheme.” We’re like, “Here’s the deal, man.” We will actually take the time to get the story straight. Kurihara: [Fritz] would always say that he never wanted all of this. But there’s nothing you can do when your product is hot. What he realized is that you don’t have any control over demand. We might be behind, or we might be ahead, but there’s no point in only listening to the market or the demand because they’ll turn at an instant and drop you like a hot potato. Or they’ll love you to death, and then they’ll hate you. They can be mercurial. So don’t listen to that—you’ve got to listen to yourself.

item.title: Healing waters: 10 of the best spa towns in Europe for a restorative autumn break
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
In 2021, Unesco designated 11 historic spa towns across Europe as one transnational world heritage site, recognising their “exceptional testimony to the European spa phenomenon, which gained its highest expression from around 1700 until the 1930s”. This was the original wellness tourism, and these grand health resorts include Bath in England and the town of Spa in Belgium, as well as the west Bohemia spa triangle of Karlovy Vary, Františkovy Lázně and Mariánské Lázně. Of that trio, Karlovy Vary is the most well known and within a day trip of Prague, but Mariánské Lázně is arguably the prettiest. The town offers three natural healing traditions: mineral springs, carbon dioxide springs known as Maria’s Gas, and therapeutic peloids (mud and clay). Czech nationals are still prescribed weeks-long spa stays to recover from surgery, severe illness or chronic conditions, but anyone can check into the Nové Lázně hotel (doubles from €234 B&B, including spa access), a canary yellow neo-renaissance confection built in 1896 that faces the central park. Its spa is a trip back in time: baths surrounded by marble columns and intricately decorated treatment cabins, including one built for King Edward VII, who visited nine times. Join tourists and locals drinking the waters from special porcelain cups while walking along the colonnades, and don’t forget to pair it with a spa wafer – large, thin, crispy confections with sweet fillings such as hazelnut or chocolate. It’s not all virtuous. Germany is home to about 350 designated spa towns, including three of the Unesco Great Spa Towns of Europe: celebrity favourite Baden-Baden, quiet riverside Bad Ems and elegant Bad Kissingen in Bavaria. The latter’s striking architecture is arguably the most interesting of the three, much of the central spa district having been rebuilt by star German architect Max Littmann in the early 20th century. This includes the grand fountain hall, with its stained-glass roof, where Brunnenfrauen (fountain women) dispense different mineral waters from bronze pipes, and the huge basilica-style Wandelhalle, where the town’s spa philharmonic orchestra performs several times a day. Music has always been part of the spa experience – the Staatsbad Philharmonie Kissingen holds the world record for the most concerts performed in one year (727!) – and the beautiful art nouveau-style Regentenbau houses one of the best concert halls in Europe. The modern KissSalis Therme (from €19 for two hours) on the southern edge of town is the main public bathhouse today, with indoor and outdoor thermal pools, mud treatments and various – clothing-free – saunas. At the more classical end of the spa spectrum, the Grand Hotel Kaiserhof Victoria (doubles from €209 B&B, including spa access) sits next door to the Wandelhalle on the town’s Kurgarten. The water used in the spa here is pumped up directly from the brine spring, while the inhalation room has a wooden graduation tower covered in knobbly salt deposits, which mimics the healing effects of mineral-rich sea air. Deep in the north of the Black Forest, this spa town offers ways of immersing in nature beyond soaking in waters from the thermal springs. Rising above the town, Sommerberg (meaning “summer mountain”) will get pulses racing. A funicular railway whizzes visitors to the top, the starting point for hiking and biking routes. For more heart-pumping views, the accessible Treetop Walk (€12.50) spirals above the dense pine trees to an observation tower 40 metres up, with a tunnel slide back down the middle for extra thrills, while the Wildline suspension bridge (€9.50) – with its 380-metre walkway – arches over the Enz valley for maximum views. Back in town, there are two thermal baths to dip into: the modern Vital Therme, where those with joint and back problems are prescribed movement therapy and spa treatments (€14 for three hours); and the historic Palais Thermal, where the pools are surrounded by marble pillars, statues of Venus and Moorish tiles (€21 for three hours). Mokni’s Palais Hotel is connected to the Palais Thermal building, meaning guests can pad over in their bathrobes (doubles from €183 B&B, including access to the spa). Local legend has it that, after many battles, the medieval lord Seigneur Hugues de Tessé freed his faithful warhorse Rapide in Normandy’s Andaines forest to live out the rest of its days in peace. Much to the nobleman’s surprise, the horse later returned to him stronger and full of life, then led his master to the warm, sulphurous waters of Bagnoles’ spring. Centuries later, a spa resort sprang up so the Parisian bourgeoisie could also tap into this fountain of youth, with belle époque villas laid out on the shores of a lake in the middle of the forest (today, it’s also handily less than an hour and a half from the ferry at Caen for British wellness seekers). That belle époque quartier was the vision of local politician Albert Christophle, whose former hunting lodge on the edge of the village is now the very lovely five-bedroom Château du Gué aux Biches (doubles from €195 B&B). This summer, its Danish owners, Klaus Bentin and Soren Rasmussen, added a new restaurant in the old kitchen, serving up smørrebrød (open sandwiches). The hotel has a partnership with the nearby spa at B’O Resort, meaning Klaus or Soren will line up your treatments, and there are bicycles to borrow so you can pedal a couple of kilometres over for that clay body wrap or hydromassage. The surrounding forest is crisscrossed with hiking, biking and trail running routes. In autumn, take things more meditatively by going mushroom foraging among the more than 1,700 varieties sprouting from the Andaines forest floor. This genteel town in the Hohe Tauern Alps was built on water; indeed, a roaring waterfall cascades right through the middle of it. The healing reputation of its radon-rich waters, which bubble up from the town’s thermal springs, saw grand hotels built in the 19th century to house the emperors and aristocrats, writers and thinkers (Sigmund Freud among them) who came to be cured of their ills. The fashion for “taking the waters” trickled away, but in recent years there’s been something of a revival, with a clutch of new hotels opening. The Cōmodo (doubles from €188 B&B) is one of them, a slick spot refashioned from a 1960s sanatorium. Bedrooms look out over the valley and mountains, as does the thermal water-filled indoor pool. There are several public fountains where you can still drink water straight from the source (warm, slightly salty and metallic tasting), but perhaps more palatable is to soak at the brutalist Felsentherme public bath complex with its numerous pools (€40 for a day pass). Just as warming – but with fewer health benefits – is a bowl of Kaspressknödelsuppe (beef broth with cheese-infused dumplings) at the cosy cabin of Schafflinger Alm (soups from €4.50, mains from €17) after a bracing hike through the forest or carving up the Schlossalm-Angertal-Stubnerkogel ski area, where the season kicks off in late November. Just before crossing the Colonnade Bridge to get to Piešťany’s Spa Island, there’s a statue of a man breaking his crutch, symbolic of the healing powers of the town’s thermal waters and sulphurous mud, harnessed on this enclave of wellness in the Váh River. The first simple wooden bathhouses were built on the island in 1778, but the opening of the Thermia Palace hotel and its Irma Balneotherapy House in 1912 turned it into a health resort. Further hotels and spas are dotted between the trees and become increasingly concrete and functional as you get further from the bridge. The Thermia Palace is still the fanciest option, with a raft of treatment programmes in the spa, from extensive diagnostics and lab tests to mud packs and pools (doubles from €210 half-board, including spa access). The blue-black goop is applied all over the body at a toasty 45C and left for about 10 minutes before being unceremoniously hosed off. Outside, the spa park also feels restorative, with lily ponds, fountains and free-roaming peacocks. In town, Elektrárňa Piešťany is a former power plant turned cultural centre that feels surprisingly vital, with film festivals and rock concerts, while the strikingly brutalist House of Arts hosts chamber orchestras and tango music trios. This town in eastern Slovenia is famed for Donat Mg, one of the world’s most magnesium-rich mineral waters, traditionally consumed for its digestive benefits. The company now sells millions of bottles of the stuff each year, but here at the source you can sip it for free from the fountains in the Pivnica Drinking Hall – although its salty, fizzy, metallic flavour is something of an acquired taste. Like other towns of its ilk, Rogaška attracted the great and the good of Europe in the 19th century, and its confection of architecture is testament to that. A short stroll away from the drinking hall, through immaculately clipped gardens, the butter-yellow Grand Hotel Rogaška is straight out of the town’s golden age (doubles from €198 half-board include spa access). Bedrooms are traditional, but the spa has all the bells and whistles, from carbon dioxide baths and mineral water inhalations to reflexology and magnetotherapy. Somewhat fittingly for a town famous for its drinking water, Rogaška is also known for its glassware – and visitors can tour the Rogaška crystal factory (€12) to see the glass-blowing in action before buying glasses for their Donat Mg from the on-site shop. The surrounding wooded hills are the place for autumn walks. In Emilia-Romagna’s so-called “food valley”, not far from Parma, this small spa town will help balance out some of that indulgence. Last year, the Italian thermal brand QC Spa of Wonders reopened the beautiful art deco-style Terme Berzieri, where the gilded interiors – all frescoes, mosaics, majolica and stucco – are as much of a draw as the salty spring waters, rich in iodine and bromide (five-hour spa sessions from €62). There’s the usual thermal attractions, as well as a sauna cinema and infinity rooftop pool, while treatments in wooden barrels nod to the area’s winemaking. Try some of those wines at the Cantina Il Poggio vineyard in the hills outside Salsomaggiore, which produces a range of styles including the local sparkling Malvasia di Candia Aromatica (tastings from €30). Continue the tastings with a visit to a parmigiano reggiano producer, such as Caseificio Ugolotti (tour and tasting €23), before picking up some ham from Parma’s famous La Prosciutteria. Stop for a roast pork sandwich at legendary panini place Pepèn, before feasting your eyes on the Pilotta Palace complex with the Galleria Nazionale, Palatine Library and Farnese theatre, while the opulent Teatro Regio hosts the annual Verdi festival in October. The organic agriturismo Case Zucchi, about a 10-minute drive from Salsomaggiore, makes a suitably foodie base, with bedrooms named after herbs and the breakfast table piled with fresh bread, eggs, ham, cheese and fruit each morning (doubles from £104 B&B). High in the Serra de Monchique mountains, surrounded by cork oak and eucalyptus forests, the whitewashed hill town of Monchique offers a slower-paced autumn escape than the nearby Algarve coast. Its cobbled streets are lined with craft shops, ceramic workshops and simple taverns serving chouriço (smoked sausage) with a small glass of medronho (fruit brandy). In a wooded valley below town, the spa village of Caldas de Monchique is little more than a handful of 19th-century buildings around a shaded square and park, where you can drink slightly warm spring water from the public fountain. Wallow in the alkaline waters a little longer at Caldas de Monchique Villa Termal Spa Resort (doubles from €84, thermal water circuit £17 for 90 minutes). The spa offers hydro rituals including a Vichy shower, massage and bath, or thermal water circuits around the pools, sauna and Turkish baths, before a dip in the outdoor pool. Afterwards, the 1692 restaurant, with its stained-glass windows, dishes up bacalhau à Monchique (salt cod stuffed with chouriço and ham). It’s not far from here to Fóia, the highest mountain in the Algarve at 902 metres. It’s worth the walk to the summit for the views, or hike on a further 2½ miles (4km) to the Barbelote waterfall, which cascades over a rocky cliff face in the wetter months. There’s a little run of spa towns in the north of Portugal near the Spanish border, a curative route through Pedras Salgadas, Carvalhelhos, Vidago, Carlão and Chaves. In Chaves, the waters are some of the hottest in Europe, coming out of the ground at a scorching 76C. The Romans built a large therapeutic bathing complex here, that was only rediscovered by accident in 2006 when work began on an underground car park. Now, the free Museu Termas Romanas de Chaves allows visitors to explore the pools and soaking baths, perfectly preserved thanks to an earthquake in the 4th century that sealed them for millennia. To take the waters today, head to the Aquae Salutem Thermal Complex (€30 for 90 minutes), a circuit of outdoor pools, saunas, steam and showers that opened in 2025. About half an hour down the road, the Pedras Salgadas Spa and Nature Park sits on the fringes of one of the other small spa towns. The owners have built 18 eco-houses and treehouses on stilts (doubles from £171 B&B, spa access additional £17 per room) among the pine trees at the source. Guests can do a spot of forest bathing before dipping into the spa – redesigned by one of Portugal’s most famous architects, Álvaro Siza – for a thermal water hydro-massage, or wander between the pink spring pavilions in the park. Pedras Salgadas is also a popular, naturally sparkling mineral water brand.

item.title: Spa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont Blanc
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
Mont Blanc is hiding behind the clouds, but the Aiguille du Midi spears the sky above a mountainside ablaze with russet, gold and tawny tones. The maples flare red; rowan trees are dusted with crimson berries. Our little group has trundled up to Mont Lachat station (altitude: 2,115 metres) on the Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs improbably steep slopes from the French alpine town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. Operational since 1909, the railway was once intended to reach the 4,809-metre summit of Mont Blanc, but war, glacial terrain and waning funds put an end to that ambition. But even from Mont Lachat, the view is a showstopper. On one side, the Bionnassay Glacier slips scenically down the slope, a buzzard soaring over the milky-green glacial lake at its base, while on the other the Chamonix valley basks in soft autumnal sunshine. Autumn is golden season in the Alps, when you can find quieter hiking trails, lower prices and air crisp enough to stir the senses without nipping your fingers. Once focused purely on winter sports, the region’s resorts have spent years building up their summer credentials to offer hiking and biking through flower-strewn meadows. Now they’re marketing their shoulder season, too, to meet a growing demand for off-peak escapes. The little spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, 50 minutes from Geneva and sandwiched between its glitzier neighbours Chamonix and Megève, is perfectly placed to take advantage of this trend. Unlike many resorts, the town of 5,800 doesn’t fall silent once the snow (or summer crowds) melts away, in large part thanks to its thermal waters, which were discovered at the beginning of the 19th century. A year-round gondola called Le Valléen now links the train station in the village of Le Fayet, farther down the slope where the thermal spa is located, to Saint-Gervais proper. Opened in late 2024, it means you can arrive by rail from London via Paris and reach the heart of the resort without needing a car. “If you go to Megève in the shoulder season there’s no one there,” says long-serving mayor Jean-Marc Peillex. “That’s not the case here. The secret is that instead of thinking about tourists, you think about the people who live here. Then the tourists will be happy too.” Saint-Gervais (850 metres) may lack Megève’s polish but it has its own quiet charm: a medieval fortified house, a 17th-century church with geometric stained glass windows, elegant belle époque buildings near the spa and a thriving market every Thursday. Several excellent restaurants stay open year round, and our hotel, the chocolate-box Coeur des Neiges, offers rooms at less than half the summer or winter rate, making it an ideal base for autumnal exploring. From here we take the Mont Blanc tramway one stop to Motivon, at 1,400 metres, then hike for an hour without seeing another soul; the only sound is the gentle clanging of cowbells. Our destination is the Distillerie Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc, one of Europe’s highest microdistilleries at 1,365m. It’s actually set in a converted donkey shed with windows framing pine forests and plunging valleys, shelves fashioned from old skis and two gleaming copper distillation stills. This is where Scotsman James Abbott, kilt and all, produces some 450 bottles a year of single malt whisky (in a Speyside style), along with vodka, the traditional herbal liqueur génépi and a superb mountain gin infused with ingredients such as blueberries and wild herbs from the nearby slopes. “The locals noticed that when I went to parties, I took whisky, not wine,” James laughs. “They said: ‘Why don’t you make your own – you drink enough of it.’” It turns out he does it rather well: the whisky sells for €95, the gin for €50, and both go down beautifully after a day in the mountain air before we hop back on the tramway. Although the tramway stops running from the end of September, there’s no shortage of scenic hiking trails fanning straight out from town which are accessible later in the year, plus a free, year-round bus service linking the villages that make up the commune of St-Gervais. We’re due to take it the next morning for a walk from Saint-Nicolas-de-Véroce, whose baroque church is resplendent with blue-and-gold interiors and frescoed ceilings, but a heavy rainstorm postpones our plans. That’s not a problem when just down the road (or a free cog lift ride down the mountainside) are Les Thermes de Saint-Gervais, which have been soothing weary bodies since 1806, when notary Joseph-Marie Gontard discovered the springs. The mineral-rich waters, packed with sulphur, magnesium, calcium and zinc, bubble up from underground at 39C, feeding a three‑hour wellness circuit. We drift between pools of different temperatures, move lazily from sauna to steam room, enjoy the rainforest spa and wallow outdoors as jets of water pummel our backs while the gondola glides silently overhead. Who cares about the rain? By the time we emerge, the storm has cleared, so we continue to Saint-Nicolas. From here, a steep two‑hour trail winds up to the Refuge du Mont-Joly, a century-old wooden inn that smells of woodsmoke and melting cheese. Normally there are sweeping views of Mont Blanc from the terrace, but today the peaks are shrouded in cloud. We might not be able to see the mountains but we can taste their produce, notably in the enormous portion of blueberry tart that follows a tartiflette big enough to satisfy a sumo wrestler. As I tuck in, snow begins to fall. By morning it will be gone, melted by the late-summer sun. But now it lies thick and soft outside, turning the world white, as if the Ice Queen from Narnia might step through the door at any moment. That’s autumn in the Alps for you. The trip was provided by the Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc tourist board. Doubles at the Coeur des Neiges from €108 room-only, or from €76 room-only at Plan B at Le Fayet. The Refuge du Mont-Joly is closed from the end of March to late May, and from November to mid-December. The Tramway du Mont Blanc now stops at the Nid d’Aigle lookout (2,380 metres), after the line was extended in July

item.title: A stay in Pakistan's unspoiled Ishkoman valley
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
A stay in Pakistan's remote Ishkoman Valley, where humans still consult fairies I took a 650km motorcycle ride to this traveller's hostel, where activities include lazing with sheep, enjoying Pakistani hospitality and visiting shamans who can learn your fate. I scramble up a scree-covered slope, trying to keep pace with a flock of woolly white sheep, each wobbly step triggering a mini landslide below us. Unfazed, the sheep charge on, navigating the precarious cliffside as if by memory and leading me like seasoned guides to an overlook. They halt abruptly and begin to graze. I catch my breath and look out across Northern Pakistan's Ishkoman Valley, framed by snow-capped peaks and cut through by pale glacial stream. Pale pink cherry blossom trees line the narrow switchbacks, descending to Coyote Den Ishkoman Hostel – my pastoral mountain retreat for this week, where I'm trekking high peaks and conferring with a female shaman who is said to speak with fairies. To reach the high-altitude Ishkoman Valley in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan region, I had planned a 650km (403 mile) journey from Islamabad, trading the capital's traffic and smog for open skies. Bordering Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor, Ishkoman is one of Pakistan's least-visited mountain regions. Travellers seeking quick access usually take a short (if notoriously unreliable) flight into Gilgit, followed by a four-to-five hour taxi ride. The overland bus journey can take more than 20 hours. But for savouring Pakistan's wildly diverse scenery, there's nothing like hitting the open road. I rented a 150cc phool patti motorcycle covered in technicoloured truck-art designs for the three-day mountain journey, navigating out of Islamabad's grid-like streets before speeding north on the Karakoram Highway. The Karakoram – the world's highest paved international roadway – follows the trail of the ancient Silk Road, soaring over the turquoise Indus River far below. From Besham City to Chilas and onward to the northern gateway of Gilgit, exposed cliffside highways revealed snow-capped jagged peaks behind each hairpin bend, including the dominating 8,126m (26,660ft) face of Nanga Parbat. After the brimming bazaars of Gahkuch, the road narrowed to a single ribbon of tarmac, following the undulating terrain into the remote reaches of Ishkoman Valley. For three days, I had stopped only to take photos, sleep at roadside guesthouses and share steaming cups of chai with uniformed officers at police checkpoints. Finally in Chatorkhand, I walked wearily through the wooden gates of Coyote Den. Since arriving, I've spent countless hours wandering the grounds, sheep in tow, and picking persimmons with Sana Marwat and Alex Reynolds, co-owners of the sprawling property – conceived as a budget-friendly "traveller's hostel" for wanderers and bikers. "Ishkoman is famous for its masonry," says Reynolds. "The wood used in our construction was all sourced from local pine and poplar trees, and the stones taken from nearby waterways." The result is a collection of stone cottages dispersed throughout a rose-filled garden. Panes of stained glass cap the windows, colourful local rugs adorn the walls and dinner is always served family-style in the mud-walled dining room. Though the key word here is relaxation, visitors can also trek from nearby Nalter back to Ishkoman Valley. "It's a three-to-four day, 45km (28 mile) traverse, including the 4,700m (15,420ft) Pakora Pass and a glacier crossing," Reynolds says. Plan your trip: How to get there: The fastest route is a domestic flight to Gilgit followed by a four-hour private taxi to Chatorkhand. For a more scenic journey, drive up the Karakoram Highway. The drive takes around 20 hours and should be broken into multiple days, with Besham and Chilas good stopping points. What to do: Fish for trout at The Mountain Resort Birgal Valley, hike to the Dain waterfall, trek across the Pakora Pass or take a Jeep or motorcycle to Hayol Meadows. Coyote Den can arrange visits to Rashida and sheep walks with local shepherds. Be safe: Carry your passport at all times for registration at roadside checkpoints. This very isolation is one of Ishkoman's key allures. "We chose to build Coyote Den in Ishkoman because it's one of the most untouched parts of the Northern Mountains," Reynolds explains. "The community here is also, as a whole, quite highly educated and therefore more open-minded and tolerant." Mountain life is also more pragmatic, with both women and men working outside the home on farms. A majority of the valley's population is Ismaili Muslim, a branch of Shia Islam that places particular emphasis on the mystical interpretations and rich inner meanings of the faith. Sipping sweet, homemade red wine, I relax into my floor cushion in the chid, a traditional Pakistani gathering room. The rapid beating of the dadang drum and soulful reverb of the rubab's strings fill the room as a handful of local men swirl in circles performing, not for my benefit, the Dani Hareep dance of the region. Without reliable Wi-Fi or television, I embrace the local way of winding down – an evening of laughter and exuberant traditional dance. Within this particular religious climate a woman known as Rashida, a female shaman who speaks with fortune-telling mountain fairies, is one of the community's most popular residents. Tomorrow, with the help of the Coyote Den crew, I will pay her a visit. The woman who speaks with mountain fairies The next morning, I pile into Marwat's dusty truck bed for the 20-min drive across the river and up the mountain to Rashida's home. Locals have been visiting her family for generations, but Marwat says hostel guests also love dropping by. In local Chitrali folklore, predating the spread of Islam in the region, peris (fairies) are incandescent, winged beings who exist between the human and divine worlds. Shamans were traditionally believed to communicate with them and seek their guidance. Although the tradition has declined sharply over the past century, with few practitioners believed to remain, the two belief systems continue to co-exist – at least the steady flow of devout Muslims filtering in and out of Rashida's home seems to see no contradictions in seeking advice from the mystical realm. Sitting at a small table in her mud-walled home, eyes fixed on a mirror pinned high on the otherwise bare wall, Rashida prepares to relay answers from the peris. By her own telling, she acts as an intermediary between the human and supernatural worlds. With Marwat and Coyote Den guide Hakim Ulluh translating, I pepper Rashida with my burning questions – painstakingly relayed through a telephone game of languages. "Ishkoman Valley alone has 10 spoken languages," Marwat explains. "Khowar or Chitrali is the most common here, and it's entirely different from Urdu, Pakistan's national language." From Khowar (Rashida) to Urdu (Ulluh) and Urdu to English (Marwat) and back again, we examine my future. Where will I end up when I finally stop bouncing from country to country? (New Zealand, apparently.) Should change my career? (No.) Will I divorce my beloved husband one day? (Thankfully, also no.) After four slow days of hammock lounging, riverside strolls with the sheep and sipping milky, mountain-style chai beneath the property's mulberry tree, Reynolds and I set out to explore the valley on foot. As we climb the loose cliffside towards the Dain waterfall, she extolls her love of Pakistan and explains how she has worked within the boundaries of tradition and religion to create a business that empowers women. "Half of the staff at Coyote Den are women, which is quite unusual in a region where women don't have [paid] jobs outside of the home," she explains. "We give them a flexible working schedule so they can go home in the middle of the day to take care of their kids' lunches, and we make sure they don't have to work at all after sunset, unless absolutely necessary." I step across the rushing, glacial-fed Ishkoman River on the narrow wooden plank bridge, the breadth of the valley sprawling out in front of me. I had come to Pakistan seeking adventure and instead found myself craving solitude. Somewhere in this remote valley on the ancient Silk Road, it came to me. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: The ghost town that almost became Aspen
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'A fortune of failures': The Colorado ghost town that almost became Aspen On a crisp June day, I wander among the empty log cabins in the ghost town of Ashcroft, 12 miles (19.3km) from Aspen at the base of Colorado's Elk Mountains. The only sounds are the rustling of aspen leaves, the gurgle of Castle Creek and the occasional whistle of a high-elevation warbler. In winter, save for the distant glide of cross-country skiers or the soft clop of snowshoes, the valley is nearly silent. It's hard to reconcile this quiet place with the booming mining town that once stood here – or with the ambitious plan, nearly 100 years ago, to transform it into a major European-style ski resort. "Ashcroft would have been Aspen," says Aspen Historical Society archivist Anna Lookabill. "I don't think Aspen would have happened had the Ashcroft plans come together." Before Aspen became a playground for the rich and famous, home to high-end boutiques and $25m mansions, the two towns were rivals – first for silver, then for skiing. In 1879, prospectors poured into Colorado's Roaring Fork Valley in search of silver, establishing camps at Independence and Aspen. By the following year, Ashcroft had become one of the region's hottest mining towns. "The ore was close to the surface in Ashcroft compared to Aspen," Lookabill says. "It had the potential to be a good investment early on. Aspen was slower to get going because the ore was a little deeper." Walking between Ashcroft's surviving log cabins, it's hard to reconcile the quiet with the town that once stood here. At its peak in 1882, more than 1,000 people lived here, with hotels, mercantile stores, a bowling alley, dance hall, 14 saloons and Pitkin County's first school. But the boom was short-lived. Within a few years, the population had collapsed to around 100, with many residents and businesses relocating to Aspen. By the 1930s, nearly all of Ashcroft's buildings were abandoned. But a group of business associates who had skied in Europe – Ted Ryan, T J Flynn and Olympic bobsled gold medallist Billy Fiske – saw something in the empty valley surrounded by towering peaks: the making of a ski resort. They formed the Highland Bavarian Corporation and brought in Swiss mountaineer André Roch to survey the surrounding peaks on touring skis. He chose Hayden Peak above Ashcroft as the centrepiece. "Mount Hayden was going to be the mountain with the ski area. Ashcroft would be the Bavarian village," Lookabill says. Ashcroft would have been Colorado's first major ski area – and, at the time, the world's highest. Plans included a tram from Ashcroft up Hayden Peak, dozens of ski runs and several chairlifts. Today, visitors can look up from the ghost town to where the ski area would have climbed above 13,000ft (3,962m) and the slopes would have taken skiers directly into town. Why go: For an atmospheric excursion from Aspen that combines ghost-town history with hiking, cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in the Elk Mountains. Best time: February for snow, or June for quieter trails. What to do: Join a snowshoe tour or rent cross-country skis and explore the 22 miles of groomed trails. In summer, explore the ghost town on foot. Where to stay: Experienced backcountry skiers can recreate Roch's stripped-back touring experience at the Markley Hut, reached via a 2.3-mile (3.7km) climb on skis, snowshoes or splitboard. Less rugged travellers can stay in downtown Aspen at The Gant or Limelight Hotel. The Highland Bavarian Corporation secured $650,000 in state and federal funding and development was about to begin. Then, World War Two cancelled the entire plan. "They had the ski area laid out, the tram laid out. Washington was allocating funds to build this ski area, because it was going to be the new tourism driver for the US. They had an order for steel to build the lifts and the tram," Lookabill says. "The US needed the steel to build tanks and fighter planes." While Ashcroft's plans stalled, skiing took hold down the valley. Roch had already begun teaching locals how to ski, launching The Roaring Fork Winter Sports Club (which eventually became today's prestigious Aspen Valley Ski and Snowboard Club), and leading touring groups around Mount Hayden. For easier access, he marked a run on Aspen Mountain – still called "Roch Run" – and Ryan oversaw the installation of the first lift: a "boat tow" built with old mine hoists, a second-hand motor and a pair of sleds. It marked the beginning of Aspen's transformation into a ski resort, and effectively ended Ashcroft's chances of becoming one. What Ashcroft was left with was the landscape itself. Today, rather than luxury lodges, visitors find a handful of preserved cabins surrounded by 22 miles (35km) of Nordic ski trails and snowshoe routes in winter, with horseback riding and hiking taking over in summer. Though Ashcroft is an easy drive from Aspen, there are no chairlifts or cable cars; in winter, human-powered travel is the only way to explore the pristine valley. Johnny Wilcox, whose father bought Ashcroft Ski Touring from Ryan in 1986, runs guided horseback tours and winter skiing and snowshoeing. His family also operates the gourmet Pine Creek Cookhouse. "The ultimate experience is to ski up here at night with a headlamp on," Wilcox says. "That brings you the closest to the mining and ski history, breaking trail through the snow with no chairlift to be seen." That absence is part of Ashcroft's appeal. While just down the road, Aspen buzzes with four ski resorts, fine dining and fashion boutiques, Ashcroft sits along Castle Creek, surrounded by pine forests, aspen groves and empty, treeless summits. "That's largely what makes this valley special," Wilcox says. "It's a step back in time. We don't have snow mobile tours. We have no Wi-Fi, no cell service. We are off the grid. In the winter, it's not easy to get here, so people who come really want to be here." Walking between the ghost town's surviving cabins – one a former dance hall, another a saloon – it is difficult to imagine an Aspen-sized town with thousands of visitors, a tram humming overhead and skiers skidding to a halt amid multi-million-dollar houses. "I always think of Ashcroft as a fortune of failures," Lookabill says. "It was a boomtown and it died off. There was potential of being a ski area, that ended up dying off. Now it's a touristy place, but a large, open, beautiful space. These booms, or fortunes that failed, ultimately preserved it." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Why don't Scandinavians say please?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Why is there no word for please in the Nordic languages? It has never been more important to be a polite and respectful traveller. But how do you ask nicely when there is no equivalent word for "please"? I'm in a Copenhagen bakery, standing in line for sugar-dusted slices of lemon cake, delicately plaited cardamom buns and golden-brown cinnamon swirls. When I reach the front of the queue, I'm ready to order in simple Danish. But then I hit a snag: in this country, there is no single word that works quite like the English "please". Like a lot of people, when I travel I learn the basics of hello, goodbye, yes, no, please and thank you. But that's just not possible in Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Icelandic or Finnish, where there is no catch-all word that works in quite the same way. So, what's going on? Are Nordic speakers simply more direct, or is politeness being expressed in ways outsiders may not immediately recognise? For travellers, understanding the difference can make everyday interactions much easier to navigate. The first thing to understand, says linguist Dr James Puchowski, a researcher at the Nynorsk Kultursentrum (The Norwegian Museum of Written Culture), is that looking for a direct translation of "please" may be the wrong place to start. Danes, for example, might ask for a pastry in a bakery using the words må jeg bede om – "may I ask for" – as a way to signal manners. In Sweden, a speaker might add tack (thank you) on to the request; while in Norway, politeness might be conveyed with an uplift to the end of the request and a smile. There are also words that translate as "please", including the Swedish snälla and Norwegian vennligst, but these tend to be used in more specific contexts – snälla often conveys pleading, while vennligst is more commonly used in formal requests or instructions. Neither functions quite like the everyday English "please". Danish language teacher Daniela Hummelgren says directness is part of the communication style. "Efficiency is valued here and communication is generally direct," she says. Being extra polite might be seen as annoying if it slows a process down. But are they being rude? Puchowski sees these differences as a reflection of societal structure. In Nordic countries, he explains, egalitarianism is prized and distinctions between people are less strongly marked in everyday speech. For example, more formal forms of address like Herr and Frue (Sir and Madam) have largely fallen out of everyday use – a reflection of how they see themselves as more equal and less defined by class. This egalitarian streak is often associated with Jante's Law, the Scandinavian idea that nobody should consider themselves more special or important than anyone else. In everyday interactions, Puchowski says, that can mean less emphasis on signalling status. Politeness may therefore rely less on a deferential word like "please", and more on phrasing, tone and context. Similar social norms extend across the region, including Finland, despite Finnish belonging to a separate language family from Danish, Swedish, Icelandic and Norwegian. "Language is more than words," Puchowski said. "It's also about how you present an idea." Hummelgren says visitors should take their cues from the people around them. "You need to calibrate the level of politeness of where you are," she said. "Observe the situations around you, so you can get accustomed to the level of what is polite and what is not." Even without speaking the language, travellers can pay attention to tone, body language and how people address service staff and strangers. In Sweden, one simple option is to add tack – "thank you" – to a request. Research into the Swedish tack links its use to equality and reciprocity, rather than deference. The same basic word is used across much of the region: tak in Danish and takk in Norwegian and Icelandic, while Finnish speakers use kiitos to say thanks. But visitors needn't worry too much about getting it wrong. Nobody will tut or give you a dark look if you order a coffee without saying "tak". In fact, Hummelgren says that being excessively polite can itself seem unusual – and even read as suspicious. "I've never heard of anyone sending a physical thank you card after a job interview or something similar," she said. "It would read as a bit over the top and perhaps like you are looking for favours." For travellers, the lesson is that politeness does not always depend on the same words or rituals. You may not hear "please" – but that doesn't mean politeness is missing. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: Connecticut's forgotten witch trial past
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Connecticut's forgotten witch trial past Decades before Salem, Connecticut was the centre of America's witch trials. A new statewide haunted history trail connects the towns and sites tied to this overlooked chapter of history. As I wander the tree-lined streets of Windsor, Connecticut's historical Town Green, I'm drawn to a circular patio of red Heritage Bricks – many of which feature inscribed personal tributes to local friends and family. I scan the inscriptions and spot a chilling outlier: "Alice 'Alse' Young: Witch Hanging Victim, May 26, 1647." Young was the first documented person to be executed for witchcraft in the American colonies. While Salem, Massachusetts is intrinsically linked with witch trials, the neighbouring state of Connecticut experienced its own wave of mass hysteria that predates the infamous Salem panic by more than four decades. Now, Young's memorial brick is a stop on Connecticut's new Haunted History Trail, a self-guided statewide route encompassing more than 130 locations – from ancient burial grounds to haunted homes to occult shops – associated with paranormal or tragic stories. Warning: This article contains mentions of hangings that some may find upsetting Boasting a nearly 400-year history, Connecticut is home to an unusual wealth of supernatural sites. But its true witchy past might be scarier than all its ghost stories combined. Occurring between 1647 and 1697, Connecticut's witch trials grew out of the Puritan witch-hunting culture early colonists brought over from England. Salem's witch trials began in 1692 and lasted only 15 months, but during Connecticut's own 50-year witch panic, at least 49 individuals were accused of entering into pacts with the devil or using supernatural powers to cause harm to others. Of those, 34 were indicted and at least 11 were hanged. The last suspected Connecticut witch – Mary Barnes – was executed in 1663 on Hartford's Gallows Hill, but trials continued to be held in the state until 1697. The final American colonial executions for witchcraft took place in Salem in 1692. That Salem held the final witch trial executions helps explain its enduring notoriety – immortalised in films from The Crucible to Hocus Pocus. But why do so few know about Connecticut's dark witch trial past? "We don't know what happened to all those records," says Beth Caruso, co-founder of local historical advocacy group, the Connecticut Witch Trial Exoneration Project. "It may be that when people started being ashamed of these trials, some of the powerful families destroyed [them]." Even as a lifelong Connecticut resident, I knew nothing about its role in the colonial witch trials. So, I set out to drive through one of the darkest chapters of my state's past. Dating to 1633, Windsor's historical centre is filled with red 17th- and 18th-Century gabled houses. It's easy to imagine Puritans in bonnets scurrying through the streets. The city was both Connecticut's first English settlement and Young's hometown when her execution ignited the nation's witch trials. As was often the case in witchcraft accusations, the suspected evidence was thin to the point of absurdity: Young and her daughter survived the 1647 influenza epidemic while four children living next door died. It was enough to see Young hanged in the Connecticut Colony's capital, Hartford. "Her case was pretty unjust, and she suffered," says Caruso. "On top of it, nobody even knows her story." I also find a Heritage Brick honouring another Windsor resident, Lydia Gilbert. Gilbert was tried and executed in 1654 after one of her boarders was accidentally killed during a militia training exercise by a fellow soldier, who was acquitted. It's uncertain why blame shifted to Gilbert. "[She] likely would not have been present on the green at the time of the shooting, as only men served in town militias," writes Caruso. "Supernatural speculations such as this would never hold up in any modern court." Nonetheless, Gilbert was condemned and, like Young, hanged in Hartford. Hartford soon became the epicentre of Connecticut's witch trials. The Hartford Witch Panic (1662-1663), a flurry of trials that concluded in four hangings, began when eight-year-old Elizabeth Kelly, delirious from fever, cried out that her neighbour, Judith Ayres, was choking her. Another woman, Ann Cole, was believed to be possessed by the devil. Executions were carried out at the Meeting House Square, located on the site of the current Old State House. Just a little further along the trail is Hartford's Ancient Burying Ground, where I see the graves of 14 of the men responsible. Established in 1640, the 1.3-acre plot is the city's only surviving 17th-Century landmark. As we strolled among the weather-worn headstones, Christine Jewell, Director of the Ancient Burying Ground's Association, told me about the magistrates and jurors buried here who cooperated in zealously sending people to their doom. Their engraved names are tricky to read, but I can't miss the life-sized statue of Reverend Samuel Stone near the cemetery's entrance. Hartford's co-founder, this Puritan minister was part of a tribunal investigating Connecticut's witchcraft charges. Jewell directed me to the monument of Samuel Wyllys. A prominent Connecticut magistrate, Wyllys was directly involved in investigating witchcraft accusations. His preserved collection of court witchcraft depositions was kept in his family for generations. "Part of what we know about the witchcraft trials is because of the Wyllys family," says Jewell. When to go: The Connecticut Haunted History Trail launched on 16 September 2026. The Halloween season sees atmospheric events including Ghosts of New Haven Tours and Downtown Mystic Ghost Tour, but the self-guided trail can be travelled year-round. Where to learn more: The Windsor Historical Society, which displays a photo of town clerk Matthew Grant's diary page citing Alse Young's hanging, or The Webb Deane Stevens Museum in Wethersfield. Spooky stays: The Griswold Inn in Essex, built in 1776, is widely reported to be haunted. The 1754 House in Woodbury is also believed to be home to several 17th- and 18th-Century ghosts. We also visited the tomb of James Richards, a magistrate involved in the 1665 trial of Elizabeth Seager, on trial for the third time. Her conviction was ultimately overturned by the acting Connecticut Governor John Winthrop Jr. A physician and alchemist, Winthrop often reviewed evidence in witch trial cases, intervening on Seager's behalf and saving Katherine Harrison from a death sentence in 1669. He then helped institute the "two-witness" rule and "rejection of spectral evidence" that effectively ended executions in the state. "They would ask him, 'Was this caused by witchcraft?' And he always said it was medical," said Caruso. "He was a voice of moderation at a time when there weren't a lot of voices of moderation." Before embarking on the trail, I knew nothing about Connecticut's role in the witch trials. But driving through the upscale coastal town of Fairfield – home to four spots on the Haunted History Trail – jogged a memory. While working at a Fairfield newspaper years ago, I'd heard the name Goody Knapp. In Puritan society, "Goody" was an abbreviation of "good wife" – a title for married women of lower status. "We know certain women of the town came to Goody Knapp and [asked] her, 'You are a witch and who else is a witch?'," said Walt Matis, programme and volunteer coordinator of the Fairfield Museum and History Center, the town's first stop on the trail. During Knapp's trial, it was intimated that she had "witches' marks" on her body. But she might not have been accused at all if not for another unfortunate Goody – Goody Bassett, a woman from the neighbouring town of Stratford. It is unclear why Bassett herself was being tried, but during her trial (and likely under torture) she intimated that there was another witch in Fairfield that "held her head full high", says Matis. Bassett was hanged in 1651; Knapp was hanged in 1653 in a field located in what is now Bridgeport. Visitors can find her memorial along the trail at Bridgeport's Burroughs Community Centre. In Fairfield, I also linger at Edward's Pond at the Fairfield Museum and History Center's Museum Commons, built on the town's 17th-Century Town Green. Now merely a divot, Edward's Pond was once used for ducking tests – where accused witches were bound and thrown into water. Floating meant guilt, sinking meant innocence. In 1692, accused and tried persons Elizabeth Clawson and Mercy Disbrow volunteered to be ducked. Both women floated but were eventually acquitted.
