In need of a pick-me-up after all that gloom, I drive to Stratford, with its charming mix of historic Colonial and coastal bungalow architecture, and duck into Goody Bassett's Ice Cream Shop. "If you're from Stratford, you already knew the name Goody Bassett, so it was a fun name for kids growing up, usually around Halloween," says owner Paul Joy. Joy also honours Bassett on his menu – Goody's Cauldron, a nine-scoop sundae ice-cream eating challenge. It is believed that Bassett was hanged in Stratford, though no official records exist. Local legends pinpoint the town's Meeting House, Gallow's Brook or the former Phelps Mansion as possible sites, says Joy. In the absence of concrete proof, a stone plaque on the trail dedicated to Bassett sits under a tree on Stratford's West Broad Green. Connecticut's connection to witchcraft lives on: 35 stops on the Haunted History Trail are witch and occult shops. I visit The Blackbird House in Wethersfield, a colonial inland port where several alleged witches were accused and hanged. I snoop through tarot decks, crystals and minerals before buying a black witches' hat. Justice may finally be near for Connecticut's accused witches. Caruso and Griego's 2017 petition to clear Young and Gilbert's names resulted in the passing of a unanimous resolution. "I think it was an important reckoning for [Windsor] to actually know what happened," said Caruso. Thanks to the project's efforts, First Church in Windsor, where the fervently anti-witchcraft pastor Reverend John Warham presided, also released an apology. The Connecticut Witch Trial Exoneration project also helps locals with genealogical research. "I kept getting emails and notes from so many descendants, saying 'Thank you for humanising my ancestor'," says Caruso. "It just seemed like the right thing to recognise these victims since we know the stories are so absurd in many cases." In 2023, Connecticut legislators passed a joint resolution exonerating all the state's victims. And now, the Connecticut Haunted History Trail is helping visitors – and locals like me – learn about the victims who were wrongly accused and forgotten, one stop at a time. "More and more people are finding out," says Caruso. "It's not that people don't care. It's just that people don't know."

item.title: Canada's bizarre mummified toe cocktail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
On my second night in Canada's northern Yukon Territory, a bartender at the Eldorado Hotel pulled out a pair of tongs, plucked a mummified toe from a silver tray, plunged it into a glass of alcohol and dropped it into my glass of Yukon Jack whisky with a plunk. "Whose toe is that?" I asked. "And which toe is it?" "Not really sure," he said, with a sly smile. "It's a gnarly one, though." The dehydrated, salt-preserved digit was black and shrivelled. In its heyday, it may have been a well-kept pinky. Or perhaps one of the less celebrated middle toes, finally getting their spotlight. Warning: This article contains images and descriptions that some may find upsetting. I was in Dawson City, a 2,300-person former gold mining hub located 330 miles (531km) from the nearest actual city, about to try the famous Sourtoe Cocktail. This two-ingredient drink (a shot of whisky and… a toe) has been a tradition here for more than 50 years. It just might be the world's most unusual libation. A laminated white flyer on the worn wooden table explained the "Sourtoe Rules", noting that my membership to the Sourtoe Cocktail Club would be voided if I chewed, sucked, bit or otherwise ingested the severed digit. It also exclaimed, in extra-large letters, that there was a $2,500 (£1,884) fine for swallowing it. I was happy to limit toe contact as much as humanly possible. Most patrons feel the same way. However, there have been accidental swallowings in the past, plus a notorious incident in 2013 where a man downed the toe on purpose and was reportedly run out of town for unsportsmanlike conduct. "Are you ready to join the club?" the bartender, who identified himself as the official "Toe Captain", asked me. It was too late to back out now. I nodded. He then recited the official "Sourtoe chant", adding to the romance of it all: "You can drink it fast, you can drink it slow, but your lips must touch this gnarly toe!" And with that, I dutifully took my shot of whisky through clenched teeth as someone's former toe kicked me in the mouth. Before Dawson City was famous for its toe-garnished cocktail, it was famous for its gold. When the mineral was discovered nearby in 1896, it became the epicentre of the international Klondike Gold Rush. Within two years, tens of thousands of people descended into the area in search of fortune. The town grew from a network of prospector tents to include saloons, hotels and restaurants – many of which still stand today. But when gold was struck elsewhere a few years later, the prospectors moved on and the town's population plummeted, leaving the few remaining hardy residents to eke out a living in Dawson City's harsh landscape, 60 miles (96km) from the Alaska border. : The Sourtoe's origins go back to US Prohibition (1920 – 1933), when two rumrunner brothers, Louie and Otto Linken, got stranded in a blizzard while smuggling booze across the border to Alaska via dogsled in the 1920s. Louie stepped into icy water and soon suffered frostbite. According to legend, they journeyed on, but when it became clear Louie needed an amputation, Otto took out an axe and hacked off his brother's toe in their remote cabin. The brothers kept the toe in a jar of alcohol for posterity. In the early 1970s, Dawson resident Dick Stevenson (locally known as Captain Dick) found the jar while cleaning out the brothers' abandoned cabin, and for unknown reasons, decided it would make for a great cocktail garnish. Thus, the Sourtoe Cocktail was born in 1973. As the story goes, Captain Dick thought it would be fun to let people become honorary "sourdoughs" (Gold Rush slang for locals) by drinking the Sourtoe. Initially, he dared some friends and saloon patrons to try it. Dawson City's isolated location and history of colourful, rough-and-tumble characters played into the legend of the Sourtoe nicely. Word soon spread, and before long, visitors started sidling up to the bar to taste the toe-flavoured tipple. Today, the Sourtoe has become something of a must-do for visitors who make the long journey to experience Dawson City's Gold Rush history and rugged frontier culture, and some 140,000 people have downed the daunting drink. All automatically become members of the Sourtoe Cocktail Club, and their names are proudly written in a hefty ledger book post-sip. Terry Lee has served as the main Toe Captain – the bartender tasked with serving the mummified toe to patrons and presiding over the ceremony – for 13 years. During the busy summer season, he works five days a week, making 75 to 100 Sourtoes a night during his four-hour shift. The Sourtoe is served between May and September at the Sourdough Saloon (in the Downtown Hotel), then the rest of the year at the Eldorado Hotel's Sluice Box Lounge. "It's considered somewhat of a rite of passage. A lot of the locals have done it," said Lee. Since Captain Dick (the original Toe Captain) passed away in 2019, several other people have been trained as Toe Captains, but Lee is the modern face of the toe. Lee first tried a Sourtoe in 1980 with Captain Dick and immediately fell in love with the history. A few months into his Toe Captain tenure, a customer accidentally swallowed Louie's original frostbitten toe, so Lee was one of the last people to drink with the original appendage. Over the years, the catalog of toes has grown from one to around 25, which are used in rotation today. The toes arrive in a variety of ways. Captain Stevens donated all 10 of his toes when he died in 2019. A British athlete who suffered frostbite in the Yukon Arctic Ultra marathon donated three of his digits in 2018. An untold number of people have willed their toes to the Downtown Hotel (including the tourist who swallowed one, in an effort to make amends). Sometimes, toes show up in the post unannounced. Like much of Dawson City, the Sourdough Saloon looks like it's straight out of the Gold Rush era, with its wooden tables, red wallpaper and swinging doors. The Sluice Box Lounge has a similar vibe, with velvet swivel barrel bar stools emblazoned with the hotel's name. The town still has no traffic lights or crosswalks. Many of the buildings have been standing since the 1890s. Colourful false-front facades dot the streets advertising businesses like the Diamond Tooth Gerties Gambling Hall, The Dawson City General Store and Bonanza Market. In summer months, there's nearly 24 hours of light. In winter, the Yukon River freezes over and part of it becomes an official government-maintained ice bridge. "Because the weather and the environment are so extreme here, it attracts people that are extreme in other ways. You get a lot a big characters," said Tara Kehoe, the exhibit curator at the Dawson City Museum. "Dawson is a weird intersection of people who love living in nature and are artistically inclined, so you get a lot of people with big, strange ideas because of that." This toe-garnished cocktail is the kind of offbeat creativity Dawson City is now known for. The town has also hosted annual events like the Great Klondike International Outhouse Race, a town-wide Easter egg fight on the frozen river and a spring carnival called Thaw Di Gras. "The Sourtoe has become a weird sort of bragging right. Everyone here loves it, even if they haven't tried it. If you have friends coming to town, you have to take them to at least watch other people drinking it," said Kehoe. She added: "The Sourtoe is so odd that it really sticks in your mind. Even when I've travelled overseas, when I tell people I'm from Dawson City there's always a person or two who says, 'Wait, isn't there a drink with a human toe?'". In a weird way, the cocktail has become a community bonding experience – and the toe's grip on tourists is only getting stronger. In June this year, The Sourdough Saloon set a new record, serving 156 toes in a single night, the crowds joining in on the iconic chant. You can drink it fast, you can drink it slow… Having now done it, I'd suggest drinking it fast.

item.title: A rare stay with Mongolia's reindeer herders
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Beyond the end of the road: A four-hour horse ride to stay with Mongolia's reindeer herders Deep in Mongolia's taiga, reaching the Tsaatan takes multiple days by road, 4x4 and horse – but the reward is two nights immersed in one of the country's most remote communities I duck as a pine branch whips over my head. The stocky horse beneath me pushes through a shallow stream, scrambles up the rock and crests the embankment. Tightening my grip on the saddle, we follow Zaya Oldov, our guide, across northern Mongolia's taiga awash in golden hour light. The silence breaks as hundreds of reindeer begin melting out of the forest around us. Soon, we're immersed in a sea of antlers and soft footfalls as the herds come home. Beyond them, a dozen conical ortz, reminiscent of North American teepees, sit along the far tree line, grey smoke snaking from their roofs. A wave of relief washes over me. After three days of travel, we've finally reached the Tsaatan camp. Around 80 Dukha families, commonly known as the Tsaatan, live in a restricted border region near Russia, in one of Mongolia's most isolated landscapes. Unlike the country's traditional steppe pastoralists who move ger-to-ger only a few times per year, the tiny reindeer-herding community traverses harsh, uninhabited landscapes six to 40 times a year in search of fresh mountain moss and suitable weather for their herds. Oldov is Tsaatan by marriage and Mongolian American by birth. Before she arrived in the taiga more than two decades ago, tourism here was rare. But today, thanks to her work developing the TCVC (Tsaatan Community and Visitors Center), visitors can stay with local families while supporting their livelihoods. Travellers sleep in an ortz, share tea and meals with them and learn about daily life with the reindeer herds. The only way to book is via WhatsApp with Oldov. Three friends and I had organised two nights with the community while we were road tripping through Mongolia. That horseback ride was only the last stage of a much longer journey to reach the Tsaatan. From Ulaanbataar, we hired a car and drove 630km (391 miles) north to Mürün, the regional gateway to the taiga, following a paved road through Mongolia's open grasslands. There, we collected the permits required to enter the restricted border region before continuing towards the "town" of Tsagaannuur. The next leg took us two days off-road, across deep river crossings, swampy traverses, mountainous climbs and a nearly entirely map-less route. By the time we reached a wooden homestay near Tsagaannuur's deep-blue lake, we had been on the road for 22 hours. Oldov arrived early the next morning to meet us, several small horses in tow. "They aren't the easiest horses to ride," she warned, "they tend to spook at anything white in the grass." As a relatively inexperienced rider, I braced myself for the four-hour trot. Raw, rugged and completely undeveloped, the landscape oscillated from wild coniferous forest to grassy hills cut by streams and waterlogged wetlands. Our horses picked their way across the changing terrain, saddlebags bulging with supplies, until we finally arrived at our destination. Stepping inside our ortz, four narrow wooden bed frames lined the walls around a small charred black fireplace with a round chimney. There is no electricity, running water or decoration beyond what can be packed and moved with the camp. "The wintertime temperatures plummet to -58C [-72F]," said Oldov. "During those months, we construct shorter, smaller ortz to better retain the heat." Fortunately, it was August. The peak season to visit the Tsaatan, for obvious reasons. Plan your trip: Accommodation: Visitors sleep in a traditional ortz within the Tsaatan community. Conditions are basic, with no running water or electricity. Meals, bedding and all other necessities are provided. Booking: Contact Zaya Oldov on WhatsApp at +976 9977 0480 to arrange the stay, transport and permits. Fees go directly to the local community. Prices vary by group size and season; expect to pay around $200 (£151) per person for two nights. How to get here: Most travellers fly from Ulaanbaatar to Mürün, then arrange a 4x4 transfer to Tsagaannuur through Oldov. From Tsagaannuur, the final leg is by horseback and varies depending on the community’s seasonal camp location. How long to stay: Minimum three days/two nights, though longer stays can be arranged. Permits: The camp is in a restricted border region near Russia, so visitors need permits, which can be arranged in Mürün with assistance from the TCVC. The camp had moved here only weeks earlier, its 17 ortz and possessions transported on reindeer backs. This summer location meant our final leg by horse took around four hours; at other times of year, it can take eight to 12 hours. The herd was never far away from camp. Reindeer are central to life in the Tsaatan community. Each family's herd provides milk for their dairy-rich diet of cheese, yoghurt, cream, butter and the salty tea that's ubiquitous as water out here. Reindeer are rarely slaughtered for meat, so that night's dinner was sheep. Without refrigeration, the organ meat is always eaten first. That evening we ate boiled sheep liver, kidneys, intestines and stomach, alongside warm, freshly made fry bread. "Tomorrow, you'll get to meet the community," Oldov told us. "And the rest of the day is yours." In the morning I was woken by the rhythmic hollow-clicking of reindeer ankles, a sound that helps keep the herd together when visibility is nil during passing Siberian blizzards. The camp was already awash with activity. Men chopped the firewood they had dragged by horse from forests miles away while the women filled silver buckets with milk from bridled reindeer carefully selected from the hundreds sleeping within the trees. Although still traditional, life in the taiga is changing. Restrictions on hunting, alongside the effects of climate change, have increased the community's reliance on cash income. Oldov said that tourism now provides one source of that income, allowing local families to host visitors while remaining with their herds. Later that day, Oldov took us from ortz to ortz, introducing us to families and showing us how daily life in the camp works. We dropped off essential goods we had brought as part-payment for our stay: flour, salt, black tea and AA batteries. At each home, we were offered generous cups of reindeer milk tea. In one ortz, an elderly woman pulled a bulky pink plastic clock from the pocket of her deel, a traditional robe, and fiddled with the batteries. It hadn't worked for weeks. We adjusted the contacts and the clock blinked back to life before we used our smartphones to reset the time. In a place where almost everything must be carried between seasonal camps, even a plastic clock earns its spot by running for months on two batteries. In another home, strips of meat hung drying in the warmth of the fire, alongside deerskin bags filled with juniper and other plants gathered from the surrounding forest. A local medicine woman explained, through Oldov, how different herbs are used in traditional remedies, from Siberian pine for colds to bergenia crassifolia (bear pine) for stomach problems. For spiritual or psychological ailments, she said, people turn to the shaman. Our final visit was with the community's shaman, who plays a spiritual role within Tsaatan life. Inside her ortz, she showed us an elaborate ceremonial headdress passed down through generations, decorated with ribbons, dried eagle feet and strips of animal hide. Juniper smoke hung in the air as we offered our final donation: a bottle of Russian vodka, the spirit she said is used in rituals and duties for the community. On our last night, I stepped outside my ortz in the frigid chill, my camera pointed towards the Milky Way erupting across the sky, unbroken by artificial light. A reindeer wandered into the frame as I pressed my shutter. After two nights in camp, leaving felt abrupt, especially after the long days it took to get here. As we rode back towards Tsagaannuur, Oldov seemed to understand my reluctance to return to civilisation. More than two decades ago, she arrived here herself – and never left. "It was this profound sense of peace that has kept me here," she said.

item.title: The US coast that wouldn't let African culture die
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
The American coast that refused to let African culture die Along the US's South-eastern coast, Gullah Geechee communities preserve a distinct culture and language rooted in West Africa that is spoken nowhere else on Earth. It's low tide at Fish Haul Beach, a marshy stretch on Hilton Head Island's northern fringe. Fish Haul was the first beach I ever visited as a child, and now I have brought my 18-month-old son. My wife and I watch him stumble and slosh through the shallow water of South Carolina's Port Royal Sound. Just as I didn't realise it on my own first visit, my son has no idea that the sand and salt marshes under his feet are where the first self-governed town of free Black people in the United States was built. Known as Mitchelville, it was created by formerly enslaved people of West and Central African heritage who spoke a language found nowhere else in the world: Gullah. These people, who came to be known as the Gullah Geechee, eventually established a series of free settlements and communities on the isolated sea and barrier islands across the south-eastern US, developing their own distinct culture while preserving many of their indigenous African traditions. On 12 October 2026, this roughly 500-mile (804km) strip known as the Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor will celebrate the 20th anniversary of when the United States Congress designated it a National Heritage Area. Along this scenic coastal stretch, spanning from North Carolina to southern Florida, Gullah Geechee culture lives on through its unique language, musical traditions and beliefs, offering travellers a window into the many ways African culture directly shaped the US. Gullah Geechee culture has its roots in the late 17th and 18th Century, when African peoples were increasingly brought to English colonies in what is now the United States and enslaved on plantations. Planters in the Carolina Lowcountry along the Eastern seaboard sought out people from Central African countries and West Africa's Rice Coast, exploiting their agricultural knowledge to cultivate rice, indigo and Sea Island cotton in the coastal wetlands and islands. The working conditions were brutal, but that same geographical isolation helped the enslaved and their descendants retain – and adapt – African cultural practices. Traditional West and Central African one-pot cooking techniques combined with local seafood, vegetables, grains and meats gave rise to Gullah Geechee cuisine. Lowcountry red rice, which combines rice, tomatoes, spices, smoked pork and sausage, is often compared to jollof rice, a one-pot rice stew cooked with tomatoes, spices and meat strongly associated with the Senegambia region of West Africa. West African coiled basketry traditions were likewise adapted to the Lowcountry, using readily available sweetgrass, bulrush, palmetto and pine. The "ring shout" – a Gullah Geechee ritual where participants form a circle, then move counterclockwise in a rhythmic pattern while stomping their feet, clapping their hands and singing in "call and response" – recalled West African musical and spiritual practices. A need to communicate with slave owners and Africans who spoke other languages led to the development of Gullah. Colonial English is Gullah's main lexical source but African-derived words, like oona (you all) and nyam (eat) survive in Gullah speech: cooter (turtle) is believed to be related to the Bambara and Malinke kuta, while goober (peanut) is generally traced to nguba in Kimbundu and Kikongo. The origin of the name Gullah Geechee itself is hazy. "Gullah may derive from Angola or from the Gola people of West Africa. Geechee may come from the Kissi people or Geechee from Georgia's Ogeechee River," said Luana Graves Sellars, cultural preservationist and founder of heritage organisation Lowcountry Gullah. During the Civil War, many formerly enslaved people from the Sea Islands aided Union troops as scouts, labourers and soldiers. After Union forces captured Port Royal Sound and Hilton Head Island in 1861, hundreds of freedom seekers sought refuge behind Union lines. In 1862, General Ormsby Mitchel initiated the construction of a freedman's town on the north-eastern part of the island, on the former Fish Haul Plantation. Named in his honour, it developed into a self-governed town. After the Civil War, the withdrawal of Union forces and the loss of wartime employment contributed to the town's decline. By the early 1880s Mitchelville had largely been abandoned, and the Great Sea Island Hurricane of 1893 devastated what remained. Meanwhile, Gullah Geechee people across the Sea Islands built free lives. Plan your trip: When to go: Every third week of October (17 October in 2026), the Gullah Food Festival at the Gullah Museum of Hilton Head Island features food, storytelling, music and history. In honour of the Corridor's 20th-anniversary year, the 3rd Annual Gullah Convening follows on 19 December. Each February, Hilton Head hosts a month-long Gullah Celebration. What to do: Book a Gullah Heritage Trail Tour, a bus tour led by Native Islanders or a sweetgrass basket workshop at Coastal Discovery Museum. Where to eat: In Bluffton, visit Ma Daisy's Front Porch, a Gullah cultural complex and restaurant. Where to stay: Da Gullah Geechee Pavilion offers rentals on ancestral land in historic Jonesville, on the Northern edge of Hilton Head. Today, about one million people in the US claim Gullah Geechee heritage, including singer Darius Rucker and former First Lady Michelle Obama. I am not one of them – I am a Black father raising a Black son in the American South. My parents brought me to Fish Haul because they wanted me to see a place where African culture survived both the Middle Passage and the passage of time; where Black life preserves a more visible continuity with Africa than the one I inherited in Alabama. And now, on our three-day visit to the Gullah Geechee Corridor, that understanding would pass through from me to my son. We timed our visit to Hilton Head for Juneteenth, when the island comes alive with days of celebrations. The day after visiting Fish Haul Beach, we headed to Bluffton – a historic river town dating to 1825. Leaving Hilton Head's luxury resort and golf club traffic for the Lowcountry mainland, we were unconsciously retracing the steps of Gullah Geechee families when they settled in this area after Mitchelville was abandoned. As we drove through Old Town Bluffton, we saw moss-draped oaks, clapboard cottages and broad porches raised on brick piers above the May River. My wife, who often wraps her hair in scarves printed with traditional West African patterns, was pleased to see that we were surrounded by Black women wearing those same textiles. As we approached Martin Family Park, rhythmic beats halted us in our tracks. My son pointed towards the sound. There was a small group gathered around five or six people who were clapping and stomping to a rhythm. One voice called. The others answered. A ring shout. An unfamiliar melody in a familiar cadence struck something deep in me. Their songs sounded like an old Black hymn, like those I grew up hearing in church in Alabama. Now they felt like echoes across an ocean and time. First, my son stomped, clapped and mimicked the sounds. I'm typically reserved, but soon my wife and I were swaying, too. "[A ring shout] has that effect," Sellars later told me. "There are celebratory ring shouts. Religious ring shouts – ring shouts only for grown folks. But they all capture your attention and almost beg you to participate." Open invitations to participate are just one of the ways visitors can experience Gullah Geechee culture in Bluffton. I saw locals hauling sweetgrass baskets on their shoulders, and caught Gullah words passing between neighbours – brief snatches of oona and gwine (going to). For Sellars, language is only one form of expression. "Understanding the Gullah Geechee language is about understanding that everything we do speaks," she said. Even the food – today, it remains a comfort that spans generations. Dishes like shrimp and grits, purloo (one-pot rice and seafood stew) and gumbo (thick stew with okra, shrimp and sausage) are ever-present at Gullah Geechee homes, and Gullah Geechee restaurants dot the cities of the Corridor. Back, in Hilton Head, I ventured to Ruby Lee's, a cosy spot with exposed-brick walls lined with Gullah Geechee art, and ordered Hoppin' John: a dish made of rice and black-eyed peas. The first taste reminded me of the jollof I'd tried at a Nigerian friend’s house. Hoppin' John was less spicy, but smoky and well-seasoned, like the rice and peas my mother makes. The distance between Africa and home closed in a bite. "For us, food represents a way of living," said Alex Brown, a fifth-generation Gullah resident and Hilton Head councilman. "Our historic culture of bartering is what produces these dishes. [Someone] may have some okra. Someone, rice. Someone else, shrimp. But together, suddenly we have okra gumbo." Later that day, we drove to Historic Mitchelville Freedom Park. Herons flew above a weathered praise-house replica, while we passed ghostly abandoned homes before paying respects at placards honouring Harriet Tubman's role in emancipating more than 700 Gullah Geechee slaves. For Brown, Gullah Geechee culture is essential to America's founding. "Our people are an important part of America's story," he said. "The story of American democracy cannot be told in full without mentioning Gullah sites like Mitchelville. Folks know Williamsburg. Folks know Jamestown. They have got to get to know Mitchelville." Though the Corridor designation has helped preserve and connect Gullah Geechee sites, displacement, ancestral land loss and climate change continue to shadow Gullah Geechee communities today. "Cemeteries where our founders rest are being disturbed, land straits once connecting islands are impassable," Sellars said. The Gullah Geechee Cultural Heritage Corridor Commission warns that heirs' property owners also face pressure from developers. "Our ancestors here not only founded a freetown but built a fort, Fort Howell, to defend that freedom," Brown said. "Black soldiers helped construct it in 1864. It was built with our hands and stationed by our bodies. This land is important to us." While the Corridor's land may be under threat, its percussive, enlivening language still moves up and down the coast, connecting Black people to African diasporic traditions and American democracy. My son will not remember standing at Fish Haul Beach. But one day, I hope he understands why I brought him.

item.title: What the rise in museum heists means for visitors
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'Every museum in the world is stressing': How brazen art heists are affecting visitors A spate of brazen thefts has rocked European museums. Now, some institutions are rethinking what's worth displaying. Visitors stepping into the Louvre's Galerie d'Apollon today will come face to face with more than 60m (198ft) of painted ceilings and dazzling sculptures. What they won't find, however, are the iconic treasures that once glittered inside its display cases. The gallery reopened in July 2026, nine months after thieves made off with France's crown jewels in one of the most audacious museum robberies in recent memory. The surviving gemstones have since been moved elsewhere while the Louvre determines how to display them more securely. The Louvre heist is just one example of how a recent string of museum thefts across Europe is changing what travellers can actually see in these beloved institutions. On 27 August, thieves broke into the Museum of Villena in south-eastern Spain. In just four minutes, they made off with an extraordinary collection of Bronze Age bowls, bottles, bracelets and other objects that included nearly 10kg (22lb) of gold. Less than two weeks later, burglars entered the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera and took four paintings – two were abandoned in nearby gardens as the thieves fled, while two others remain missing. In July, thieves posing as ordinary visitors stole the 2,500-year-old gold torque of Vix from a museum in Burgundy. According to Europol, such incidents have risen sharply and are becoming increasingly brazen. As one museum security expert in Belgium told the BBC: "Every museum in the world is stressing right now." Jean-Yves Goriou, head of the EU Organised Crime Unit at Europol, says information shared by member states shows "a clear and steep increase in the number of museum robbery cases since around 2022/2023". Some have also become more forceful: thieves have used sledgehammers and axes to smash display cases, explosives to blow through museum entrances and firearms to intimidate staff and visitors; in other cases, museum employees have been assaulted or restrained. Experts say the fact that many museums are publicly accessible makes them increasingly vulnerable to theft. "Museums are most likely doing what they can, given budget constraints and the fact that they are – by design – open to the public," Goriou says. For generations, that openness has allowed almost anyone to stand within a few feet of an Egyptian sarcophagus or a Renaissance painting. But as museums seek to better protect their most prized pieces, it's changing the visitor experience. Travellers to the Louvre who find the Galerie d'Apollon without its jewels still have tens of thousands of other objects to see. But for a smaller museum, losing one object can make a dramatic difference for would-be visitors. The so-called "Treasure of Villena" that was stolen in August wasn't simply one collection among many in the city's museum. It was inextricably linked with Villena itself: dozens of pieces of Bronze Age gold, silver, amber and iron hidden inside a vessel for roughly three millennia before an archaeologist brought them back into the light in 1963. Likewise, the Vix torque was the defining object of the Musée du Pays Châtillonnais in Burgundy. The 480g (1lb) gold necklace was discovered in the burial chamber of a Celtic woman who died around 500BC, a rare physical connection to the craftspeople of Iron Age Europe. Two faithful gold reproductions of the torque already existed when thieves stole the original from its display case. One copy had even travelled to an exhibition elsewhere in France because the museum would not loan the real necklace. Replicas have long been used by museums when originals are too fragile, valuable or difficult to travel, and the recent spate of thefts has encouraged some to consider this practice more widely. This summer, Dominique Garcia, president of France's National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research, suggested this approach when she issued a national security plan. Yet, France's new 33-point museum-security plan instead calls for particularly vulnerable originals to be temporarily taken off view until they can be displayed more safely. Some museums are already making that choice. After a 2024 armed robbery at the Musée du Hiéron in Burgundy, director Maud Siron stopped displaying the museum's most valuable works rather than risk losing them altogether. Paris' Musée Cognacq-Jay subsequently dropped a valuable pair of earrings from a planned exhibition, while the nearby Musée Carnavalet substituted a drawing and rhinestone brooch for a high-value jewel in a 2026 show. While museums all aren't automatically filling all their cases with copies overnight, visitors are finding more stand-ins and, in some cases, an empty space where a treasure used to be. According to Guy Turton, director of global audience strategy agency MHM, which works with galleries around the world, authenticity remains a powerful pull for museums. As he said, seeing the original piece can create "the feeling that another human made, used or encountered the same object, sometimes centuries ago" – a connection he says can influence the number of people willing to visit and pay an entrance fee. The Bayeux Tapestry is an especially timely example. With its permanent home in France undergoing renovation, its rare loan to the British Museum has drawn huge demand: the first batch of tickets sold out within a day, and visitors have queued down Great Russell Street to see the nearly 1,000-year-old embroidery in person. For visitors, that debate matters because seeing a copy is not necessarily the same experience as seeing the object itself. "If visitors expect an original and discover a replica without explanation, it can feel like a reduction in value," Turton says. "If the museum is transparent about why a replica is being used and what it enables them to experience, it can add value." Ellie King, director of museum consultancy Crown Cultures and a researcher of visitor experience, suspects many people would accept a museum displaying a replica if they understood that the original object was being safeguarded to protect it from theft. "For visitors, it may be the story that an object presents which is more important – especially if that story feels highly relevant and connected to the visitor," she says. For marquee museum treasures that remain on display, the most immediate change in light of the recent string of thefts may be physical: more distance between the visitor and the object. Turton says that distance can matter almost as much as whether it is original. "In observational research, we consistently see that visitors engage more deeply when they can approach an object, examine its detail and see it from different angles," he says. "Greater distance and more prominent barriers can weaken that connection, particularly if they make the experience feel remote or institutional." Some of those protections are already standard practice. Under the UK's Government Indemnity Scheme, portable valuables such as gold, silver and jewellery should be kept in locked, alarmed cases, while certain objects must be separated from visitors by at least one metre. If a museum cannot provide enough staff to properly supervise a gallery containing indemnified works, the guidelines allow for that space to be closed. Recent thefts are also bringing greater scrutiny to objects on loan to other museums. James Ferrer, a fine art and museums expert at global insurance broker Lockton, says insurers and cultural bodies are paying particularly close attention to security around high-profile loans, although he stresses that the goal is still to help museums meet those requirements rather than prevent objects from travelling. "We are there to help facilitate loans, not to present a barrier to stop loans from taking place," he says. Visitors may also find thicker glass or more staff in a room. None automatically makes the experience worse. Turton points to the Rijksmuseum's live restoration of Rembrandt's The Night Watch. The painting sits behind glass, but visitors can watch artisanal work that would normally happen out of sight, turning the barrier itself into part of the experience. "If security creates greater physical distance, museums need to work harder through interpretation, transparency and experience design to preserve the sense of connection," Turton says. As the uptick in museum thefts continues, visitors are likely to encounter different responses in different places. So long as the reasons for the viewing restrictions are clearly explained, Turton says audiences tend to understand the need to balance access, conservation and security. The challenge for museums is preserving both sides of that bargain: protecting objects that may have survived for centuries while keeping them accessible enough that people still want to travel to stand in front of them.

item.title: The Viking king who gave Bluetooth its name
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'The PR guys hated the name': The 1,000-year-old story behind Bluetooth A pair of ancient runestones in Jelling tell the story of the Viking king who shaped Denmark – and inspired the name Bluetooth. If you've ever wirelessly connected your phone to your headphones or laptop, you're probably already familiar with the name Bluetooth. But while the technology is modern, the story behind the name stretches back more than 1,000 years to a Viking king whose legacy can still be seen in Jelling, a small Danish town about 250km (155 miles) west of Copenhagen. Here, two ancient runestones tell the story of his reign – and offer the first clue to how his unusual nickname became attached to one of the world's most widely used technologies. The king was Harald Gormsson, who ruled Denmark in the 10th Century. His nickname was Bluetooth – Blátǫnn in Old Norse – first documented 150 years after his death and believed to be a nod to a "blue" or rotted tooth. One of Harald's most consequential achievements was Denmark's conversion to Christianity, thought to have taken place around 965. The larger of Jelling's two runestones, commissioned by Harald, declares that he "won himself all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian" and bears one of the earliest depictions of Christ in Scandinavia. Until then, much of northern Europe was divided into smaller territories ruled by chieftains. Christianity gave Harald a way to consolidate power, strengthen Denmark's ties with Christian Europe and help unify the emerging state. "It is the nation building of Denmark after 200 years of the Viking age, where the Northerners had a pretty steep learning curve," said Adam Bak, curator at the Kongernes Jelling Experience Center and Museum. "They get well-versed in different forms of politics in Europe, of what Christianity can do for them, and the centralisation of power in a state." Harald's story is written into the landscape at Jelling. His father, Gorm, commissioned the smaller and older of the town's two runestones in memory of his wife, Thyra. It is believed to contain the first written use of the name "Denmark" within the country. "We call it Denmark's birth certificate," said Anne Havgaard Mikkelsen, a resident of nearby Vejle. Jelling, then, is its birthplace. Though it has only 4,000 residents today, it was the seat of power in Harald Bluetooth's time. Originally a pagan burial site, Jelling became a place where pagan and Christian traditions overlapped during Harald's reign. Today, white posts mark the palisade that once enclosed the Jelling monuments, while hundreds of markers trace the outline of a vast ship-shaped layout, possibly dedicated to Thyra. Two burial mounds and a Christian church complete a landscape that Bak says is less about "bold Viking warriors and Thor and Odin" than about "politics and transition, the change from something older to something new". In 1994, the Jelling mounds, runic stones and church became Denmark's first Unesco World Heritage site. At nearby Kongernes Jelling visitor centre, interactive exhibits trace the transition between Viking beliefs and Christianity, while the two runestones – Denmark's baptismal stone and birth certificate – stand protected behind glass. More than 1,000 years later, Harald's reputation as a unifier would give his name an unexpected second life. In the late 1990s, engineers from companies including Toshiba, IBM, Nokia, Intel, and Ericsson were developing a new technology that could connect devices across different brands. They needed a codename. Jim Kardach, an American Intel engineer, was collaborating with Swedish engineers when the conversation turned to Vikings. Intrigued, he immersed himself in a book about the history (which is on display at Kongernes Jelling) and became fascinated with the king who united Denmark and Norway, just like this new technology might unite different devices. The code name leaked before the official press release was written, and the rest is tech history. "The PR guys hated the name because they associated 'Bluetooth' with bad tooth hygiene," said Bak. "They were very concerned about it and had all kinds of different names that were better at explaining what the product was, but were way more boring. Bluetooth blew up because it was so distinct a name." Its rune-inspired logo also helped its staying power. The ubiquitous symbol combines the Norse rune for "H" and "B" in honour of Harald Bluetooth. On the 25th anniversary of the technology in 2023, Kardach and other founders travelled to Kongernes Jelling to lightheartedly "apologise" for using Harald's name without permission. The museum in turn accepted the apology and gave them permission keep using it for the next 1,000 years. "Harald loved showing off," said Bak. "I think he would be very happy to know that billions of people say his name on a daily basis today."

item.title: The Amex Platinum isn't just for you: How to maximize its benefits for your family
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The Amex Platinum isn't just for you: How to maximize its benefits for your family Having a family makes just about everything more expensive. Trust me, I've spent years raising four kids, and I've learned a thing or two about making every dollar — and every credit card perk — count. The American Express Platinum Card® might have a reputation as a card for business travelers and luxury jet-setters, but it's surprisingly family-friendly, too. From airport lounge access and hotel perks to everyday savings, here's how to make the Amex Platinum work for your whole family. Maximize the Amex Platinum for family travel Get the whole family into airport lounges I'm actually writing this article from an airport lounge at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), where I'm riding out a long layover with my kids. Having a place to spread out, grab some food and give everyone a little breathing room (including me!) makes traveling together a whole lot easier. But getting the whole family into a lounge? That's another story. The Amex Platinum provides access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection, which includes Centurion Lounges, and Priority Pass lounges. At Centurion Lounges, cardmembers pay $50 per adult guest or $30 for children ages 2 to 17. Spending $75,000 in eligible purchases in a calendar year unlocks complimentary access for up to two guests, but that's a steep threshold. Here's a better strategy: Before paying Centurion Lounge guest fees, check for a participating Priority Pass lounge. Amex Platinum cardmembers can bring up to two guests at no additional charge, without meeting a spending requirement. Enrollment is required, and individual lounges may restrict guest access. For larger families, adding another Platinum cardmember for $195 annually (see rates and fees) could also be worthwhile. Two adults with eligible Platinum Cards and separate Priority Pass enrollments, for example, could bring four kids into a participating lounge without paying guest fees. Some of our most memorable family hotel stays have happened thanks to the Amex Platinum. On a trip to Porto, Portugal, we paid very little out of pocket and even scored a suite upgrade that gave us enough room to stay together without being too close for comfort. The Platinum offers up to $600 in annual hotel statement credits, split into two up to $300 credits (one from January through June and another from July through December), for eligible prepaid Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection bookings made through American Express Travel®. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay. Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with perks like daily breakfast for two, a $100 property credit toward eligible charges and guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout. That property credit is great for covering a meal, while late checkout is especially useful when you're traveling with kids. Of course, these properties can be pricey, so compare rates and room occupancy limits before booking. Breeze through airport security with the family The Amex Platinum can also make getting through airport security with your family a little (and sometimes a lot) easier. For starters, it offers up to $219 in statement credits per calendar year toward a Clear+ membership (subject to auto-renewal; enrollment required). Children 17 and under can accompany a member through Clear+ lanes at no additional charge. You'll also receive a $120 statement credit for Global Entry or up to $85 in statement credits for TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with your Platinum. Even better, eligible additional Platinum and Companion Platinum cardmembers receive their own application fee credits — another useful perk for families. Keep in mind that Clear+, TSA PreCheck and Global Entry are separate programs. Clear+ expedites identity verification, TSA PreCheck speeds up security screening and Global Entry expedites U.S. reentry while also including TSA PreCheck benefits. Save on travel extras and protect your family trips There's an up to $200 annual airline incidental fee credit, which can cover eligible charges like checked baggage fees and in-flight refreshments on your selected qualifying airline. That's especially handy when you're paying for multiple travelers. Enrollment is required, and airfare itself isn't covered. The card also offers valuable travel protections, including trip delay insurance**, trip cancellation and interruption insurance**, and baggage insurance***. Depending on the benefit, coverage can extend to eligible family members, potentially helping reimburse expenses if something goes wrong on your trip. Coverage depends on how you pay for your trip and the circumstances involved, so always review the terms first. **Eligibility and benefit levels vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. ***Eligibility and benefit levels vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Make the Amex Platinum work for your family at home, too With an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), the Amex Platinum isn't exactly cheap. And while getting some extra value out of your family vacations is great, occasional travel perks alone probably aren't enough to justify that price tag for many. But some of the Platinum's most useful benefits are for everyday expenses. Save on groceries, takeout and family meals The Amex Platinum offers up to $12.95 in monthly statement credits, plus applicable taxes, toward a Walmart+ monthly membership (enrollment required, subject to auto-renewal; Plus Ups excluded). That membership includes complimentary grocery delivery on eligible orders of at least $35, complimentary shipping on eligible purchases and other perks. Of all the Platinum's everyday benefits, this is probably the one I find most useful. Whether I'm stocking up on groceries, ordering last-minute school supplies or simply avoiding another trip to the store, it's a fantastic timesaver. The card also offers several credits that can help with family meals and transportation: - Up to $200 annually in Uber Cash for eligible U.S. rides and Uber Eats orders (up to $15 monthly, plus an extra up to $20 in December), after you add your Platinum to your Uber account and use an eligible American Express card for payment. - Up to $120 in annual statement credits toward an eligible auto-renewing Uber One membership. - Up to $400 in annual Resy credits, distributed as up to $100 in quarterly statement credits at qualifying U.S. restaurants. Enrollment is required for the Resy benefit, no reservation is required. These benefits can be valuable if they fit your family's existing habits. Just remember that the credits have separate enrollment requirements and restrictions, and they're not worth much if you have to change your spending habits to use them. The Amex Platinum offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment credits, broken down into up to $25 monthly statement credits. Enrollment is required. Eligible services include Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+, Peacock, YouTube Premium and more. You can split the credit across multiple subscriptions, which is especially handy when everyone in the family has different favorites. This can be an easy win for families already paying for streaming services. However, the credit only covers select providers, so it won't be much help if your favorites aren't on the list. Unused monthly credits don't roll over. Help your kids build credit as authorized users One of my favorite credit card strategies has nothing to do with points or travel. It's adding my kids as authorized users to help them get a head start on building credit. I've done this with my own kids, and my oldest recently headed off to college with excellent credit. Amex allows children as young as 13 to be added as additional cardmembers, and you don't have to pay the $195 annual fee for an additional Amex Platinum. Instead, you can add a no-annual-fee Companion Platinum Card (see rates and fees). American Express generally reports eligible additional cardmember account activity to credit bureaus once they turn 18, which may help them begin establishing credit history. However, the primary cardmember remains responsible for purchases made by additional cardmembers, so it's important to establish spending expectations before adding your children. As a bonus, purchases made by additional cardmembers earn Membership Rewards points for your account. Amex occasionally offers targeted bonus points for adding authorized users who meet spending requirements, so check your account before adding someone. Know when the Amex Platinum isn't the best fit for your family For all its surprisingly family-friendly perks, the Amex Platinum isn't the right fit for everyone. The $895 annual fee is a lot to justify, especially if you're not regularly using the card's benefits. It's also not a particularly strong card for everyday family spending. While you'll earn 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through Amex Travel (on up to $500,000 in purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent) and 5 points per dollar spent on eligible prepaid hotels booked through Amex Travel, most other eligible purchases earn just 1 point per dollar spent. If groceries, gas and dining make up a big chunk of your household budget, pairing the Platinum with a card that rewards those purchases more generously could make sense. The real question is how much value your family will get from benefits you'd use anyway. How much value could a family get from the Amex Platinum each year? Here's what a hypothetical family taking one or two vacations a year might save by using a handful of the Amex Platinum's everyday credits (some of which requre enrollment). In this example, the family uses one $300 hotel credit toward an eligible vacation booking, receives $20 per month in digital entertainment credits, uses the $15 in Uber Cash six times and takes advantage of two $100 quarterly Resy credits. The family also receives a full year of Walmart+ membership credits. Altogether, the family receives $985 in statement credits, Uber Cash and membership benefits, exceeding the card's $895 annual fee by $90. That's before considering airport lounge visits, hotel upgrades or other travel perks. Those benefits could make the Platinum even more valuable for families who travel regularly or maximize more benefits. The welcome offer can also take some of the sting out of the annual fee, especially in your first year. New applicants can find out if they're eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer. That's worth up to $3,500, according to TPG's October 2026 valuations, which put Membership Rewards points at 2 cents apiece. That's a substantial boost toward your next family vacation, provided you can meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases. Your family's numbers might look completely different, though. A $300 hotel credit isn't worth $300 in savings if you spend hundreds more than you otherwise would have on the room. The best way to decide whether the Platinum belongs in your wallet is to look at the benefits you'll actually use, not just their advertised value. The Amex Platinum might not be the first card that comes to mind for families, but it has a surprising amount to offer beyond luxury travel perks. Between airport lounge access, hotel benefits, everyday statement credits and opportunities to help your kids build credit, there are plenty of ways to spread the value across your household. Still, an $895 annual fee is a big commitment. The key is finding benefits that fit your family's existing habits rather than spending extra just to use a credit. If you can do that, the Platinum could earn its place in your family's wallet. To learn more about the card, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

item.title: United Explorer Card review: Premium perks without a premium fee
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
I've said again and again during my time as a (see rates and fees) cardholder that it's one of my favorite credit cards. For travelers who fly with United a few times a year, perks like a free checked bag, priority boarding and United Club passes can help justify the card's $150 annual fee ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year). That said, cobranded cards are generally not meant for wide audiences, and the United Explorer is no exception. If you rarely fly with United, don't transit through airports with United Clubs or consider yourself a member of the carry-on-only club, it will be difficult to justify this card's place in your wallet. *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. The is a step up from the no-annual-fee (see rates and fees). It can be a great first airline credit card for travelers who want United-specific benefits without paying a premium annual fee. Key United Explorer benefits include: - Free first checked bag: You'll receive this perk for you and one companion when you pay with your United Explorer. - Priority boarding: You'll be able to board in Group 2 of 6, ahead of general boarding. - United Club passes: Each cardholder year, you'll receive two United Club passes. These passes can be used when you fly any Star Alliance airline, not just United. With this card, you'll earn United MileagePlus miles, which can be redeemed for a wide variety of options. Two of the best include using your miles for United flights and redeeming them to cover your annual fee. Where I see the offering the strongest value for the widest audience is in its United-related perks. Airlines across the board have been increasing baggage fees due to higher fuel costs, making this card's free checked-bag perk more valuable than ever. Your first checked bag each way costs $50 with United (or $45 if you prepay). That means you'll offset this card's annual fee as long as you check a bag with United at least three times each year. Priority boarding may not have a monetary value, but it can be a huge help when your flight is full, and there's a risk of your carry-on getting gate-checked. I also really appreciate the two United Club passes that come every cardholder year with the United Explorer. You don't need to fly with United to use one; I was able to get into a United Club while flying with Air Canada, for example. United Club passes are $59 each, so the two annual passes can provide meaningful value if you use them. If you're on your way to United elite status, the United Explorer earns 1 Premier qualifying point (PQP) for every $20 spent (up to 1,000 PQPs each year). Unlike higher-tier United cards, however, it doesn't offer a lump sum of PQPs at the start of each year. Personally, I don't view this card as being the best aid for achieving elite status. The biggest reason I tout the Explorer as often as I do is because of how easy it is to get meaningful value from it without needing to use merchant credits that may not fit your spending habits. The card also offers several statement credits, though their usefulness will depend on your spending habits. Some of these, such as the up to $100 annual JSX credit and up to $10 monthly Instacart credit (activation required; through Dec. 31, 2027), may be too niche for most cardholders to get meaningful use out of. The up to $60 annual ride-hailing credit (yearly opt-in required) is nice, but it's broken down into small $5 monthly increments. With ride-hailing prices soaring due to high gas prices, this credit may feel more like a negligible discount than a proper credit card perk. That said, this credit will likely be the easiest for cardholders to maximize. As mentioned earlier, the earns United MileagePlus miles. As a cardholder, you'll earn at the following rates: - At least 6 miles per dollar spent on basic economy fares and at least 9 miles per dollar spent on standard fares (earning rate may be higher if you have status with United) - 3 miles per dollar spent on all other United purchases - 2 miles per dollar spent on hotels booked directly and dining - 1 mile per dollar spent on all other purchases Your miles can be redeemed for lots of options, including gift cards, statement credits through Chase Pay Yourself Back and to book experiences. These redemption options often don't offer the best value for your miles, so your best bet is to use them to book flights or to pay for your card's annual fee. Miles can be redeemed for flights on United or with one of its partner airlines, such as Air Canada or Lufthansa. TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens recently redeemed 28,200 United miles for two nonstop, one-way economy flights from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to Lihue Airport (LIH) in Hawaii. Flights were around $550 each, making this a great domestic redemption. If you redeem your miles to pay for your card's annual fee, you'll receive a value of 1.5 cents per mile. That's higher than TPG's October 2026 valuation of United miles at 1.2 cents per mile. Cobranded cards are intended for a fairly specific audience, which means they won't be right for everyone. The may not be for you if: - You rarely fly United or other eligible airlines - You rarely transit through an airport with a United Club - You already have extensive lounge access through other cards - You're chasing status with United, since this card limits your PQP earning to 1,000 PQPs each year United fans who don't have an appetite for a higher annual fee card should be able to get a lot out of the United Explorer, but it's still important to make sure you can properly justify its $150 annual fee (after the first cardholder year). The $350-per-year (see rates and fees) is the next step up from the . It offers substantially more perks, including an annual 10,000-mile flight discount, your first two checked bags free (versus just one), and a 1,000 PQP head start each year. You'll still earn PQPs at the same rate — 1 PQP for every $20 spent — but you'll be able to earn up to 18,000 PQPs in a year (versus just 1,000 PQPs). It's worth noting that, despite its annual fee, the United Quest doesn't offer any kind of United Club lounge access. If you already have extensive lounge access from other cards, that may not matter much to you. Otherwise, it's worth giving some thought. I think the United Quest and United Explorer are both compelling options. The decision between these cards largely comes down to which benefits you value most. The Explorer has a lower annual fee and two United Club passes, while the Quest offers additional checked-bag benefits and a stronger path toward United elite status. I'm very happy with my United Explorer, whereas Stephanie is an outspoken fan of her United Quest. Is the United Explorer worth it? The is worth it for most United fans, as long as you fly more than once a year with the airline. It's very easy to recoup this card's $150 annual fee ($0 introductory annual fee for the first year), as long as you check a bag when you fly and can make use of two visits to a United Club. Even in years when your flights aren't taking you on board United jets, this card comes with statement credits to help justify its cost. Unless you want more extensive benefits, a better path to elite status or aren't willing to pay an annual fee, the United Explorer is worth seriously considering. If you rarely fly United or don't use these benefits, a more flexible travel rewards card may be a better fit. Currently, new cardholders can earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: - Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Earn an additional 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening. According to TPG's valuations, these 80,000 miles are worth $960 (including the points from adding an authorized user). This offer matches the highest we've seen in the card's history (so long as you add an authorized user), making now a great time to apply. Other cards to consider if you don't want the United Explorer If the United Explorer doesn't feel like the right fit for you, consider these other cards instead: - If you want a no-annual-fee United card: The has no annual fee, but comes with fairly limited benefits. However, you'll still earn bonus miles on United flights and receive an inflight discount for eligible purchases. To learn more, check out our full review of the United Gateway. - If you want unlimited United Club access: The (see rates and fees) provides a basic United Club membership, with a value of at least $750 each year. If you're able to maximize this perk, that will easily justify this card's $695 annual fee. To learn more, check out our full review of the United Club card. - If you want a more flexible travel card: The (see rates and fees) earns Ultimate Rewards points, which can be transferred to any of Chase's 14 airline and hotel partners, including United. To learn more, check out our full review of the Sapphire Preferred. For additional options, check out our picks for the best United cards and best travel cards. The will remain in my wallet for the foreseeable future, thanks to how easy it is for me to get solid value from it each year. It doesn't require me to juggle multiple statement credits to justify it, nor does it require me to be exclusively loyal to United. Whether you have zero cobranded airline cards or five, I recommend you give the United Explorer proper consideration. For regular United flyers who want meaningful perks without paying for a premium airline card, the United Explorer hits a sweet spot.

item.title: Rove adds JetBlue TrueBlue as a 1:1 transfer partner
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Rove adds JetBlue TrueBlue as a 1:1 transfer partner Rove has been quickly adding transfer partners that are familiar to U.S. travelers, including Air Canada Aeroplan in May and Frontier Miles in July. Now, Rove has added another 1:1 transfer partner that U.S. travelers know: JetBlue TrueBlue. JetBlue TrueBlue is Rove's 22nd transfer partner. To celebrate, Rove is giving users a 20% bonus on eligible transfers to JetBlue TrueBlue until 11:59 p.m. EST on Nov. 14. That means that for every 10,000 Rove miles you transfer, you'll get 12,000 TrueBlue points. You can redeem JetBlue points for flights operated by JetBlue. These awards tend to track paid rates, but you can sometimes find JetBlue Mint awards on long-haul domestic routes for under 32,000 points each way. Plus, JetBlue prices some economy awards under 4,000 points each way. Just keep in mind that the rates you see are usually basic rates with no free seat selection option and fees to change or cancel — you'll need to redeem more points to get standard or flex rates. You can also redeem JetBlue points for flights operated by JetBlue's partners, which include Qatar Airways, United Airlines, Condor, Icelandair and Etihad Airways. For example, you can book a one-way flight on Icelandair from New York to Iceland for as little as 12,700 JetBlue points and $102 in taxes and fees. And you could fly Qatar Airways business class one-way from Chicago to Doha for as little as 83,000 JetBlue points plus $8 in taxes and fees. You'll see JetBlue TrueBlue redemption options when searching for flights directly through Rove, as it displays both directly booked paid flight options and transfer partner award options for its partners in the search results. Based on TPG's October 2026 valuations, JetBlue points are worth 1.35 cents each. That's similar to the value you'll often get when redeeming Rove miles for paid flights through its travel portal, and direct bookings through Rove can earn airline points or miles. However, the 20% transfer bonus may make transferring to JetBlue more appealing, especially if you find a particularly valuable award. Most JetBlue TrueBlue award flights can be canceled before departure without a fee, although some fare types (such as base fares) have cancellation penalties. Plus, JetBlue TrueBlue points don't expire. So, if you transfer Rove miles to JetBlue for an award that you subsequently cancel, you can generally get your points back into your TrueBlue account and save them for another redemption. However, Rove transfers are irreversible, so make sure you confirm award pricing and availability for the fare class you plan to book before transferring miles. Adding JetBlue TrueBlue as a 1:1 transfer partner gives Rove members another way to redeem miles for flights within the U.S. and abroad. The limited-time 20% transfer bonus makes this new partnership especially appealing, but be sure to compare redemption rates and confirm award availability before transferring Rove miles.

item.title: Breeze adds four 4 cities in 16-route expansion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Breeze adds four 4 cities in 16-route expansion Breeze, the fast-growing budget airline, is expanding. The airline said on Wednesday that it will add four new cities to its route network, while also announcing 16 new routes between the new cities and between existing ones. The airline will start flying from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS); Buffalo Niagara International Airport (BUF) in New York; Arnold Palmer Regional Airport (LBE) in Latrobe, Pennsylvania; and Las Americas International Airport (SDQ) in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic. The first flight from Boston is set to begin May 4. Service from Buffalo begins in late June, while Latrobe's first flight starts in February, and Santo Domingo flights begin in June. The new routes, other than those from the new cities, are largely based out of Myrtle Beach International Airport (MYR) in South Carolina, from which Breeze already flies to 15 cities on year-round and seasonal bases, according to data provided by Cirium. With the new MYR flights, Breeze will be the largest airline at the airport in both the number of destinations and the total number of seats, by the end of 2027, the airline said. "Every route we add to our network starts with the same question," David Neeleman, Breeze's founder and CEO, said in a statement. "Where can Breeze's direct service bring travelers a convenience they don't already enjoy today?" He added: "These new routes and destinations now bring Breeze's high-value, low-cost service to 95 cities, making affordable travel to great destinations more convenient than ever." Including the new cities, the new nonstop routes announced Wednesday are as follows: Breeze offers introductory fares for each route. Those promotional fares vary by route, ranging from $49 one-way (BUF-RDU) to $149 one-way (SDQ-TPA). Those promo fares are only available for certain dates, depending on when the routes are scheduled to start, so you may need to search a few dates to find one. The airline also announced several new "BreezeThru" routes, which allow passengers to fly a route with one stop, but no change of airplane. Those include: All flights are on Breeze's relatively new fleet of Airbus A220-300s, which feature Wi-Fi and the airline's "Ascent" first-class seating. Breeze uses a point-to-point model that focuses on nonstop flights between underserved cities or on routes with no direct competition. The airline started flying in 2021 while still under the haze of coronavirus pandemic-era restrictions, but managed to quickly grow its presence to 95 cities with more than 300 routes, becoming profitable in 2025. Initially, Breeze flew short flights of less than two hours using a fleet of Embraer jets leased from Azul, before building a fleet of brand-new A220s. In 2025, the airline launched a revamped rewards program, Breezy Rewards, which offers travelers points on every flight and features elite status tiers with benefits for frequent flyers.

item.title: Citi ThankYou Rewards transfer partners: Redeem your points with airlines and hotels
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Citi ThankYou Rewards transfer partners: Redeem your points with airlines and hotels With over 20 transfer partners, Citi ThankYou Rewards provides plenty of options for travelers to redeem their ThankYou points. Whether you have a Citi card or are considering stepping into the ThankYou Rewards program, it's important to understand where your points can go. Transferring points to airline and hotel partners is often one of the best ways to maximize Citi ThankYou Rewards, but the value you receive depends on which card you hold and how you redeem your points. Here's everything you need to know about Citi's 22 transfer partners. Here is a list of Citi's transfer partners and their transfer ratios (Virgin Atlantic and Virgin Red are separate transfer partners, but are listed together): Occasionally, a transfer bonus may be offered, in which you can score a higher ratio when transferring your ThankYou Rewards points. You can earn transferable Citi ThankYou Rewards points with some Citi credit cards, including: - Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (see rates and fees): Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening. - Citi Strata Premier® Card (see rates and fees): Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. - Citi Strata℠ Card (see rates and fees): Earn 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases within the first three months of account opening. Keep in mind, not all ThankYou points have the same value. To transfer Citi ThankYou points at the highest ratio, you must hold a premium Citi ThankYou card such as the Citi Strata Elite, Citi Prestige® Card (no longer available to applications) or the Citi Strata Premier. However, if you hold both a no-annual-fee Citi card and a premium Citi card, you can combine your ThankYou points into a single account and then transfer them to partners at a 1:1 ratio. The information for the Citi Prestige cards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. For more information about which cards can transfer rewards to Citi's partners, check out this guide. How to transfer Citi ThankYou Rewards points To transfer your Citi ThankYou points, follow these steps: - Visit ThankYou.com and sign in. - Click 'Travel' at the top navigation bar and select 'Points transfer.' - Ensure the name on your loyalty account matches the name on your Citi card. - You must transfer in increments of 1,000 ThankYou points, but cannot transfer more than 500,000 points in one transaction. Although transfers to most partners are instant, some can take more time. Citi states that a transfer can take up to 14 days to process. If you notice a transfer is taking longer than expected, I suggest being proactive and contacting that loyalty program's customer service sooner rather than later. I didn't do this earlier this year and it cost me. Before transferring points, confirm your desired award is available and compare the required miles and taxes and fees. Transfers are generally irreversible, so it's best to have a specific redemption in mind before moving your points. What are the best Citi ThankYou Rewards transfer partners? Not all transfer partners are alike, and although Citi ThankYou points can transfer to 21 travel partners, some are better than others. Ideally, the best partner for you is based on which airlines you fly often and to which destinations you fly. That said, here's a rundown of some of our favorite Citi ThankYou transfer partners. American Airlines AAdvantage is one of Citi's most compelling transfer partners, particularly for travelers looking to book domestic flights or award travel on American's Oneworld partners, such as Alaska Airlines and Japan Airlines. Citi is currently the only credit card issuer that offers transfers to AAdvantage, making this partnership especially valuable for fans of the program. I enjoy using my AAdvantage miles for domestic flights, since AAdvantage commonly offers the most affordable redemptions among popular award programs that I have access to. For example, I recently redeemed AAdvantage miles for two separate one-way flights so my mom could visit me in early 2027. The first, from Frederick Douglass Greater Rochester International Airport (ROC) to Portland International Airport (PDX), cost me 8,500 miles plus $11.20 in taxes and fees. The return trip was for 8,500 miles plus $5.60 in taxes and fees. In total, this saved my mom almost $585, meaning I received roughly 3.4 cents per mile for the entire booking. That's more than double TPG's October 2026 valuation of AAdvantage miles at 1.45 cents per mile. Keep in mind that AAdvantage uses dynamic award pricing, so redemption rates can vary depending on your route and travel dates. Book flights to Europe on Air France-KLM Flying Blue Air France-KLM Flying Blue has long been a favorite here at TPG, since you can often find solid award deals on flights to Europe through this program. For example, TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens recently redeemed 18,750 Flying Blue miles plus $33 in taxes and fees for a one-way flight from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG). The cash price for this flight was $675.50, netting her 3.4 cents per mile in value. That's far above TPG's October 2026 valuations of Flying Blue miles at 1.4 cents per mile. We recommend checking out Flying Blue's monthly Promo Rewards to possibly lock in an even lower award flight price. Fly from the US to Italy or Greece on Emirates Skywards Emirates Skywards is the most straightforward way to book business-class or first-class award tickets on the ever-popular and opulent carrier. A fun and unique way to fly the carrier is through its fifth-freedom routes between the U.S. and Europe. For example, you could fly between John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Milan Malpensa Airport (MXP) or Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and Athens International Airport (ATH) at the following rates: Note that to redeem miles for Emirates first-class, you must hold Skywards Silver status or higher. However, we have a handy hack on how to book a premium seat on this airline without status. Also keep in mind that Citi points transfer to Emirates at a 1:0.8 ratio with eligible premium Citi cards, so you'll need more ThankYou points than the number of Skywards miles required for an award. Qatar Airways Privilege Club is most well-known for its Qsuite business-class product. Privilege Club releases more space to its own program than it does to partner loyalty programs, so it may be worth using your ThankYou points for Qatar flights. Qatar Qsuite business-class seats typically start at 70,000 Avios one-way, such as for routes from the U.S. to Doha. Since the program uses Avios as its loyalty currency, you can combine your Avios across other programs that use the same currency. Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer is one of the best ways to book Singapore Airlines first-class. If you're flying on the carrier's Airbus A380, you'll be in for a treat as the first-class suite offers maximal privacy — and if booking two seats, you can combine them to give you and your travel partner even more space. At the saver level, you can book a first-class suite for as little as 32,000 KrisFlyer miles when flying to Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei or up to 209,500 miles when flying to the U.S. West Coast from Africa, the Middle East and Turkey. Notably, the KrisFlyer program allows you to waitlist if an award isn't available. Singapore Airlines still uses an award chart, unlike many airline loyalty programs.
