That can allow you to more easily plan for certain redemptions. If premium cabin rates seem high and you're looking for a deal, the monthly KrisFlyer Spontaneous Escapes program offers value. Virgin Atlantic Flying Club has been a favorite of award travelers, and although the program uses dynamic pricing for Virgin Atlantic-operated flights, there are opportunities to fly between the U.S. and London for cheap in Upper Class. For example, you can fly in business class on Virgin Atlantic from the East Coast to London for as few as 35,000 miles one-way or 41,000 miles from the West Coast. If you want to fly to Europe for as few as several thousand miles, you can get to London from the East Coast for as few as 6,000 miles. As with Air France-KLM Flying Blue, you can expect to pay hefty taxes and fees on most Virgin Atlantic redemptions. For example, a typical business-class flight between the East Coast and London will run you over $600 in taxes and fees. Economy is somewhat cheaper, at roughly $150 per award ticket. Still, this is quite a bit higher than other award programs. These taxes and fees will reduce the overall value of your redemption. What are Citi ThankYou points worth? According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Citi points are worth 1.9 cents each. Transferring your points to an airline or hotel partner will give you the best value and the chance of maximizing the value of your Citi points far beyond 1.9 cents each. You can book travel through Citi's own travel portal — but at most, you'll only earn 1 cent per point, so it's not the greatest option for maximizing points. There are additional ways to redeem points, such as purchasing gift cards, shopping with points and cash back; however, these will not get you the best value. I recommend avoiding them if you want to maximize your points. TPG senior editor for loyalty programs, Christine Gallipeau, recently transferred 230,000 Citi ThankYou points to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer to contribute to a round-trip business-class flight between John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) and Siem Reap–Angkor International Airport (SAI). If Christine paid cash for this round-trip, she would've paid $10,443.73. Considering the total cost of her award booking was 344,000 miles, she received roughly 3 cents per mile in value. According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, that's more than double what KrisFlyer miles are typically worth at 1.3 cents per mile. Knowing how to use your Citi ThankYou Rewards is important if you want to get maximum value from them. Citi offers a range of great transfer partners, but the ones that appeal the most to you will depend on your travel plans and which airlines and hotels you book with most often. Whenever you're ready to transfer your ThankYou points, use this guide to help you determine which partner will offer you the most value. Pay close attention to transfer ratios and bonuses, since they can make a difference worth thousands or even tens of thousands of points. And since transfers are generally irreversible, it's best to have a specific redemption in mind before moving your ThankYou points. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: World of Hyatt is finally making it easier to transfer points between members
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
World of Hyatt is finally making it easier to transfer points between members Huge news for Hyatt loyalists: starting tomorrow, Oct. 15, World of Hyatt members will be able to digitally transfer points to another member directly on Hyatt.com. For now, specific details about how the digital transfer process will work are scant, but it will certainly make the process more efficient, from what we understand. Historically, transferring World of Hyatt points between members has been a pain point. You think it'd be as simple as pulling out your phone, opening the World of Hyatt app and tapping a few buttons. But alas, the process actually requires filling out a PDF form online and emailing (or mailing) it directly to Hyatt for processing. Many considered the process slow and inefficient, especially when booking hotel stays on the go, trying to lock in a great points deal or simply traveling as a group or a family. "Since we often travel as a family and book award trips together, being able to easily move Hyatt points between accounts — whether mine, my husband's or even my parents' — will make things so much simpler than having to print out and upload a form circa a bygone, paper-based era," said Summer Hull, TPG's senior director of content. While we know for sure digital points transfers will roll out, it's unclear if other changes are coming. Currently, World of Hyatt members can transfer points for free, and no family affiliation is required, but transfers are limited to one transfer per member every 30 days. "An electronic transfer process is a long time coming to Hyatt, which has trailed some of the other major hotel programs, including Marriott Bonvoy and Hilton Honors," said Eric Rosen, TPG's director of travel content, before sharing other changes he'd like to see. "I hope that some of the other current limitations on transfers of Hyatt points between accounts will also be updated. For instance, while it's free to transfer points between World of Hyatt accounts, members can only transfer or receive points once every 30 days, which is a significant limitation. Hopefully, these transfers will continue to be free without per-transaction or annual caps on the number of points you can transfer, too. It's been a big year of change for the World of Hyatt program. In May, a new award chart went live, expanding it to five award rates (Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper and Top) from the previous five. The hotel loyalty program also launched a new partnership with Air Canada. And at the beginning of October, certain Chase credit cardholders who could transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt saw their transfer ratio shift from 1:1 to 4:3. Stay tuned for more details about the new World of Hyatt digital transfer system as more information becomes available.

item.title: Which Princess Alaska cruisetour is right for you? A complete guide to all your options
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Which Princess Alaska cruisetour is right for you? A complete guide to all your options Is an Alaska cruisetour with Princess right for you? If you've landed on this page, you're probably trying to figure that out, and you're likely a bit overwhelmed. Princess cruisetours to Alaska pair a seven-night cruise along Alaska's southeastern coast with at least a few days of overland touring in the state's interior. However, factors like the length of the trip, the places you'll visit and the things you'll see can vary greatly depending on which itinerary you pick. Princess is, quite simply, the leader in cruisetours in Alaska — in all sorts of ways. They offer more Alaska cruisetours itineraries and carry more cruisetour passengers than any other company. They also notably offer a whopping 28 Alaska cruisetour itineraries, each a little different. That's far more than any other cruise company. So if you're considering booking an Alaska cruisetour with Princess, here's everything you need to know first. What is an Alaska cruisetour with Princess? Let's start with the basics. A cruisetour combines a cruise along Alaska's coast with a multiday overland tour of the state's rugged interior. It is both a cruise and a land tour of Alaska — hence the name. Princess cruisetours combine a seven-day cruise along Alaska's southeastern coast, which Princess calls Voyages of the Glaciers, with three to 10 days of overland touring. The resulting cruisetours thus range in length from 10 to 17 days. A cruisetour isn't the only way to experience Alaska by ship. You can also sign up for a cruise-only trip to the state, and many cruise-loving vacationers interested in seeing Alaska do just that. All the major cruise lines operating in Alaska, including Princess, offer cruise-only sailings, and as someone who has covered Alaska cruises for many years, I can say they are wonderful trips. Still, for reasons I will explain below, a cruisetour is arguably the best way to get a broad Alaska experience in a single trip. Why choose a Princess cruisetour to Alaska? Cruise-and-land-tour combinations are available in many destinations around the world, but nowhere is it as big a phenomenon as in Alaska. This is because Alaska is a destination that, perhaps more than any other, is best experienced by a combination of ship and land travel. One of the two most famous places to visit in the state, Glacier Bay National Park and Preserve*, is best seen by ship; the other, Denali National Park and Preserve, is best explored by land. Only on an Alaska cruisetour can you easily see both of these iconic destinations in a single trip. A cruisetour can also get you to all or most of Alaska's best-known towns — Juneau, Skagway, Ketchikan, Anchorage and Fairbanks, to name a few — in a single easy-to-arrange trip. That's almost impossible to do any other way, including by renting a car and driving yourself. At least one of these towns, Juneau, isn't accessible by road. The others are spread out and sometimes difficult to visit independently. That's the general argument for choosing a cruisetour for your Alaska vacation. The argument for choosing a Princess cruisetour, specifically, is that no other company offers as much choice in cruisetour itineraries or as wide an array of exclusive or semi-exclusive elements as Princess. Princess is, quite simply, the leader in cruisetours in Alaska — in all sorts of ways. Princess offers more Alaska cruisetours itineraries and carries more cruisetour passengers than any other company. More importantly, Princess has been operating cruises and cruisetours in Alaska longer than almost any other company — nearly 60 years. That deep history has enabled Princess to build an unmatched array of exclusive company-owned infrastructure across the state, along with relationships with travel suppliers that deliver a truly seamless travel experience on land and at sea. In Alaska, Princess functions as a full-service travel company that owns some of the best land accommodations and operates its own transportation services, in addition to offering the largest array of cruise itineraries. This includes: - Five custom-built Princess lodges in key Alaska destinations - A fleet of luxury glass-domed Princess rail cars that provide direct-to-the-wilderness service - A fleet of luxury Princess Tours motorcoaches Princess, through its parent company Carnival Corporation, also owns part of the White Pass and Yukon Route railroad in Skagway, as well as part of the town's historic port and retail operations. Princess also arranges day tours out of its five lodges. This includes everything from flightseeing tours and whitewater rafting outings to guided hikes, fishing trips and a visit to the Kennecott Copper Mine. Princess is also one of only a handful of cruise companies with permits to enter Glacier Bay National Park*, allowing you to see the majesty of the park's glaciers up close from the deck of your ship. Every Princess cruisetour in Alaska includes a visit to Glacier Bay National Park*, which is not something most other cruise brands can say. What's included in a Princess cruisetour to Alaska? Booking a Princess cruisetour to Alaska means you're signing up for a vacation in which Princess will arrange almost every aspect of your trip, both on land and at sea. For starters, there is the cruise itself. Every Princess cruisetour in Alaska includes a seven-night, one-way sailing between Vancouver and Whittier, Alaska. Princess cruisetours also include accommodations (often at Princess-owned lodges) during the land portion of the trip and transportation around the state, either on Princess Tours motorcoaches or Princess-owned rail cars. Princess can also arrange your flights to and from the trip (for an extra charge) and airport transfers. Travelers on Princess trains in Alaska also receive included transfers to and from the rail depot and your Princess-arranged lodging. The five lodges that Princess owns in Alaska play a big role in the land portion of most Princess cruisetours, serving not just as lodging for the night but as a base for exploring some of the state's best-known attractions. They are: - Mount McKinley Princess Wilderness Lodge® - Copper River Princess Wilderness Lodge® The first two lodges are at iconic Denali National Park. Denali Princess Wilderness Lodge sits a mile from the park's entrance, which is notably closer to the park than any other lodging and is often billed as the most comfortable place to stay in the vicinity of the park. It features an expansive deck overlooking the Nenana River with views into the park. The Kenai Princess Wilderness Lodge is on Alaska's scenic Kenai Peninsula, known as an adventure playground for its world-class fishing and outdoor activities like hiking, rafting and kayaking. The Copper River Princess Wilderness Lodge sits at the junction of two rivers just outside of Wrangell–St. Elias National Park — the largest national park in the U.S. It offers spectacular mountain views. Among the things not included in some Princess cruisetours are meals during the land portion of the trip. Excursions while visiting ports on the cruise portion of the trip are not included in cruisetour fares. Excursions on the land portion of the trips, including while staying at Princess lodges, are included in some cruisetours but not all (more on that below). Where do Princess Alaska cruisetours begin? All Princess cruisetours begin in one of three places: Anchorage, Alaska; Fairbanks, Alaska; or Vancouver, British Columbia. Cruisetours that begin in Anchorage or Fairbanks start with the overland touring portion, followed by the cruise. Cruisetours that begin in Vancouver begin with the cruise portion, followed by the overland touring. In both cases, the cruise portion will be a one-way, seven-night sailing between Whittier, Alaska — a small port town about 50 miles southeast of Anchorage — and Vancouver. That means that when booking your flights, you'll need an "open jaw" ticket that brings you into Alaska at the start and home from Vancouver — or vice versa. Note that you can book your own air for these trips (many TPG readers like to use points and miles) or let Princess book flights for you through its Princess EZair service. You may have read that Princess operates cruises to Alaska out of five ports: Seattle, Whittier, Vancouver, San Francisco and Los Angeles. This is true, but Princess cruisetours are only available in conjunction with cruises out of Whittier and Vancouver. This is because sailings out of Seattle, San Francisco and Los Angeles are round-trip itineraries not designed to connect with overland touring. In both 2027 and 2028, Princess will operate eight ships in Alaska, but only four of those ships will sail the one-way route between Whittier and Vancouver used for cruisetours. In both years, the four ships sailing the one-way route are Discovery Princess, Crown Princess, Coral Princess and Island Princess. Princess calls these one-way sailings between Whittier and Vancouver Voyage of the Glaciers sailings. In addition to being one of the main elements of every cruisetour, you can book them as stand-alone, cruise-only sailings. When choosing a cruisetour, pay attention to which ship operates your specific departure, as each vessel is a little different. Among the four vessels, Coral Princess and Island Princess are the oldest and smallest (at 91,627 gross tons), and they are best suited to cruisers seeking a more intimate Alaska cruise experience. Each carries around 2,000 passengers. Crown Princess is about 20% larger than Coral Princess and Island Princess at 113,561 gross tons, with more onboard venues and a higher passenger count of around 3,000. It is part of the line's Grand Class of vessels, which is one of my favorite ship classes. It is a class of ships that is large enough to have many onboard venues and amenities, but not so large as to be overwhelming. Discovery Princess is the newest and largest (at 145,000 gross tons) of the four vessels on the Voyage of the Glaciers route and has many more onboard venues. If you're a fan of big new cruise ships, it's probably the choice for you. What are the itinerary choices for a Princess Alaska cruisetour? As noted above, Princess offers a huge range of cruisetour options in Alaska — 28 in all. Choosing the right one, however, isn't as complicated as that number might suggest. Depending on how long you want to stay in Alaska and what sort of experience you're after, you can narrow down the choices pretty quickly. Princess breaks down its 28 Alaska cruisetour itineraries into three broad categories that vary in length and tour inclusions: - Denali Essentials trips (10-12 days) - Denali Explorer trips (10-15 days) - Denali Escorted trips (12-17 days) At the core of the offerings are the Denali Explorer trips, the most popular choice, which offer a broad overview of Alaska's biggest attractions. Like all Princess cruisetours, the Denali Explorer trips include a seven-night voyage between Vancouver and Whittier. These cruises always include two days of glacier viewing at two of Alaska's three most famous places for seeing glaciers: Glacier Bay National Park, Hubbard Glacier and College Fjord. They also include stops at three of the most popular cruise destinations in the state: Juneau, Ketchikan, and either Skagway or Icy Strait Point. On top of that, you will get: - Three to eight nights of overland travel - Exclusive Princess rail service to or from Denali National Park - An included Natural History Tour in Denali National Park - A Sternwheeler Riverboat Cruise & Gold Dredge 8 tour in Fairbanks (if applicable) For these Denali Explorer trips, a visit to Denali National Park is central to the land portion of the experience. But some of the longer ones also include a visit to Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and/or Kenai Fjords National Park (where you'll stay at Princess lodges). If you're seeking a cruise to Alaska plus a visit to Denali and maybe a bit more, these are the tours for you. The Denali Escorted trips follow a similar structure to the Denali Explorer trips but are significantly more full-service. On Denali Explorer tours, meals are not included during the land portion, and no tour director accompanies the group. On the land portion of the Denali Escorted trips, by contrast, most meals are included, and you are escorted by a tour director. If you're the type of traveler who likes full-service tours where every detail, including meals, is arranged by the tour company, and you want a tour director, the Denali Escorted trips are the right choice for you. For travelers on the opposite side of the spectrum and prefer to be more on their own when vacationing, the Denali Essentials itineraries are the trips specifically designed for you. The land portion of Denali Essentials trips includes all the basic arrangements — your lodging and transportation between places — but no pre-scheduled tours, meals or the services of a tour director. The Denali Essentials trips are also among the shorter Alaska cruisetours Princess offers and focus on Denali National Park for their land portions. In addition to all of the above, Princess also offers hotel stays in Anchorage or Vancouver that you can add to the start or end of your trip. Known as Cruise Plus Hotel Packages, they include a hotel stay and a transfer to or from your ship or the airport. Many of the cruisetours include stays at two of the five Princess lodges in the Denali area. Sometimes, stays in three or even four lodges are included. For travelers who really want to do it all, the most epic of the 28 tours available is a 17-night fully escorted Denali Escorted tour that includes two nights at each of the five lodges. When does Princess offer Alaska cruisetours The Alaska cruisetour season runs from May to September. For 2027, Princess cruisetours run from May 8 to Sept. 8. For the 2028 season, the start dates for the first and last Princess cruisetours are also May 8 and Sept. 8. What do Princess cruisetours cost? The cost of a Princess cruisetour to Alaska varies widely depending on the type of tour you choose and its length, as well as the type of cabin you want on the cruise portion of the trip. The 10-day Denali Explorer cruisetours include a seven-night cruise and three nights of overland touring focused on Denali National Park. The longer and more inclusive 17-day Denali Escorted tours are at the high end. Generally, Denali Explorer cruisetours cost less per day than Denali Escorted tours because they have fewer inclusions. The Denali Essentials tours typically cost even less. Whichever tour you choose, planning ahead is the best way to get a good deal. Booking early gives you the widest selection of dates and cabins, and the lowest-priced options tend to sell out first. Keep in mind that, as is standard for cruises, all pricing is based on double occupancy. That means you will only get the prices listed above if two people are traveling together in the same room, each paying the stated fare. A cruisetour is one of the best ways to experience Alaska broadly, and no other company offers as wide a range of cruisetours or as many exclusive options as Princess. The longest-running and largest operator of cruises to Alaska by passenger volume, Princess has developed an unrivaled network of company-owned lodges and its own transportation infrastructure, including motorcoaches and rail cars, enables a seamless vacation experience for all of its passengers. Visit princess.com to book your next cruise or cruisetour to Alaska. *Princess Cruises is an authorized concessioner of Glacier Bay National Park. Some departure dates for Alaska cruisetours as well as specific cabin types for the cruise portion of such trips, can sell out months in advance, so it pays to begin the booking process early. For the best selection of cabins, itineraries and pricing, TPG recommends booking Princess cruisetours six to 12 months in advance. The season for Alaska cruisetours is very short, lasting from May to September, so those are the only months when you can do a Princess cruisetour in Alaska. Among these months, June and July offer the longest daylight hours (with up to 18 hours of sunlight for sightseeing), while July and August are the peak months for viewing whales and bears. May and September, which are the "shoulder season" months at the start and end of the Alaska cruise season, are often less crowded in Alaskan ports and can also bring somewhat lower fares. You are not required to book flights through Princess and can book your own flights to and from the starting and ending points for any Princess cruisetour. If booking independently, make sure to adhere to Princess's recommended arrival and departure times. At TPG, we always recommend that travelers fly to any cruise or cruisetour a day before the scheduled start of the trip so that they don't miss the trip in the event of a flight delay. Terms & restrictions apply. See rates & fees.

item.title: Delta One gets a boozy upgrade with $200 wines, luxe dining and new suites on the way
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Delta One gets a boozy upgrade with $200 wines, luxe dining and new suites on the way Two years ago, Delta Air Lines raised the bar on what airport luxury could look like in America when it cut the ribbon on its first-ever Delta One Lounge in New York. There was a luxurious check-in lounge, a bona fide spa — and true, high-end restaurant-quality food. And fine dining has been a staple as the carrier has expanded its business-class outpost to five locations across four hubs. Now Delta is hoping to up its food and drink game in the sky. The airline on Wednesday announced an overhaul to the menus it'll offer in its flagship Delta One cabin, going forward. On the way to its tray tables: Wagyu beef burgers, Hong Kong-style sea bass and braised lamb. Flight attendants will serve up $200 bottles of Silver Oak Cabernet Sauvignon out of Napa, and pop bottles of premium Kentucky bourbon from Blanton's. And that's before pouring Champagne Taittinger over sorbet scoops at dessert. It's part of a larger refresh to the so-called "soft product" in Delta's premium cabins. That service upgrade, executives say, is meant to sync the on-board experience with the one big-spending passengers now find in its most exclusive lounges. "We're basically ensuring there's consistency on board the airplane," Ranjan Goswami, chief marketing and product officer, told TPG at an event in New York previewing new amenities and eats. "If you're going to start your trip as you go to Italy, or on an African safari, or to go around Tokyo, you want to start that experience at Delta One." Delta will begin rolling out its revamped Delta One service on Nov. 2 on some key long-haul routes out of Los Angeles — including flights to Auckland, New Zealand, and Brisbane, Australia. The changes include an updated menu with new dishes like a seasonal risotto. Plus, expanded cocktail and mocktail offerings that will eventually include pours of expensive Sake on the airline's routes to and from Tokyo's Haneda Airport (HND). Beyond the menu, Delta is also debuting fresh linens, tableware and glassware to bring a new feel to the dining experience in its top cabins. And, the airline's amenity kits from Italian fashion house Missoni will include specialty socks from the popular retailer Bombas adorned with the carrier's longtime "Fly Delta Jets" moniker. All told, Goswami ranks these changes to the carrier's on-board offerings among some of the biggest "premium" investments in Delta's history — from the debut of "Business Elite" class in 1998 to the private suites that are a staple at the front of its planes today. "It's about the suite meets a brand-new food and beverage experience, meets a new sleep experience, all converging together," he said. Oh — and speaking of suites? New ones are coming. Earlier this year, Delta announced a next-generation Delta One suites product, which is expected to debut next year on its fleet of new Airbus A350-1000 aircraft. After sharing images of the new seats in April, we got our first "in-real-life" look at the product during this week's showcase in New York City. As TPG first reported in April, these latest Delta One digs come with longer beds and built-in mattress pads. Plus, they feature Delta's largest entertainment screen to date — and, of course, the sliding privacy doors the carrier was the first in the U.S. to pioneer a decade ago. Expect these seats to feature on long-haul routes to Asia and the Middle East, executives said this past spring. That's notable as Delta sets its sights on significant growth across the Pacific Ocean in the coming years. This push by Delta to boost its front cabin comes at an especially time competitive time for airlines — especially for customers willing to splurge on an high-end seat. Earlier this year, United Airlines made big waves when it rolled out its next-gen Polaris business-class product. It included extra-luxe Polaris Studios in the front and bulkhead rows — large suites that United has paired with splashy amenities of its own like a pairing of caviar and Champagne Laurent-Perrier Cuvee Rose. To date, Delta has not announced an extra-elevated business-class product to compete directly with United's new "studio" suites ("We're always looking at new ideas" was all Goswami had to offer.) But it's safe to say the push by carriers to woo big-spending customers to their planes — and ultimately their loyalty programs and credit card portfolios — has no end in sight. Across the industry, that arms race is already leading to fancier clubs, more premium seats and faster inflight Wi-Fi. Increasingly, it's also playing out in the form of higher-end food and pours of expensive booze. After debuting its updated Delta One "soft product" on those initial routes to Australia and New Zealand next month, the carrier plans to expand the offerings across its network. Passengers will start to see the updates up front on certain domestic Delta One flights in February. Then, it'll roll out globally in March. The carrier also plans to bring some of the new touches to its domestic first-class cabin earlier next year. On top of the new products and menus, Delta also plans to start giving customers more time to place pre-orders for their on-board meals. Today, passengers must submit their choices at least a day before their flight. Going forward, pre-ordering will be open until 18 hours before departure. Related reading:

item.title: The New Sense and Sensibility Film Takes Us to Bucolic Devon and Dorset
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Sense and Sensibility filmed? Jane Austenâs Sense and Sensibility is a tale of contrasts. Sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood have wildly different approaches to love, family and happiness, with reserved and practical Elinor falling for the understatedly charming Edward Ferrars, while the more impulsive Marianne becomes swept up in her feelings for the charismatic but impish John Willoughby. As romance gives way to heartbreak, misunderstandings and difficult choices, the sisters may not always see eye to eye. But if differing opinions are a theme throughout the film, things were more aligned behind the scenes: one thing the cast and crew could all agree on was thatâDartmoor is always a good idea.â âWe just fell in love with the West Country, Devon and Dorset,â says location manager Ian Hutchinson, of his time working on set. âIt was a lovely time making a beautiful movie.â Itâs a fitting sentiment for a film in which landscape plays such an important role. Austenâs story follows the Dashwood sisters after they are forced to leave their family home in Sussex when their fatherâs death leaves them and their mother in a precarious financial position. After moving to a more modest home in Devon, the sisters find themselves navigating the very different expectations of love and marriage in Regency society â with the grand country houses, windswept moors and historic landscapes around them providing a sumptuous backdrop to their changing fortunes. The result is predictably lush. Viewers are swept through the country estates of Dorset to the wilds of Dartmoor, before heading into Regency London and out to the palaces of Buckinghamshire. Englandâs winding lanes, rain-soaked woodlands, imposing stately homes and windswept landscapes almost become characters in their own right. Below, Ian talks about the places that made it onto the screen, his painstaking search for the perfect properties, and the surprising challenges of filming Austenâs world in our own. Kingston Maurward House and Parnham Park, Dorset The Dashwoodsâ vast and beloved Norland Park, which they lose following their fatherâs death, is set in Sussex in the book. For the film, however, the team used two separate sites in Dorset to recreate the romantic magic. The interior and exterior architecture of Kingston Maurward House provided the main backdrop for the grand home; its characterful 16th-century interiors and expansive grounds fit so well with the brief that it was an obvious starting point. But it didnât have everything the production was looking forânamely, that all-important lake at the back of the garden where the sisters often gathered. Nearby Parnham Park provided that missing piece, with its quaint wooden bridge and glassy lake completing the Dashwoodsâ idyllic estate. Ian wasnât especially sentimental about this park but, after they started filming, he was pleased when he quickly realised: âThis is not just a body of water, this is a sea of wildlife!â It allowed them to really exaggerate the scenes filmed there, enhancing them considerably from what was originally conceived. âWe were always hungry for more,â he says. The fun really began when the team moved to Dartmoor to film the Barton Cottage scenes, the considerably more modest home the Dashwood women are forced to relocate to after their bereavement. It wasnât easy to find the right place. The production team searched through around 50 remote properties across the region to find one that felt suitably isolated, in a process that started three months before production even began. âA lot of properties in the area have had a lot of money spent on them to modernise them,â says Ian. âWe were like, âHow do we bring that look down?â" They eventually settled on a completely derelict stone shell, devoid even of doors and windows, deep within the national park near Plymouth. Its insides were full of rubble so, to make it work, the crew built a custom two-storey stage set inside the ruined walls; a decision that allowed director Georgia Oakley to film characters seamlessly as they moved between the homeâs tight interiors and out to Devonâs wilds without need to cut the scene. âWe built a false floor to create an upper ground, created the stairs, and built a box within a box,â says Ian. âIt created that massive contrast between Barton and Norland.â It wasnât without its challenges. For one, there was the batsâ nest to contend with, which required a bat specialist who had to spend three nights in the property to gauge how many bats flew in and out. If any were near the filming area, they wouldn't have been able to shoot. âBats are very protected!â says Ian. âWe had to do a whole ecological survey of the area. A lot of conservationists said, "No, you shouldn't be filming there," but we put measures into place â which takes time and is quite costlyâand once we convinced everyone we wouldn't disturb anything, we were given a permit.â The remote location presented some logistical hurdles, too. âOne moment weâd have glorious blue sunshine, and the next we could have driving rain with thunder and lightning,â says Ian. âThen we had mud to deal with, and we were 40 to 50 minutes away from any civilisation in Plymouth. Getting the lunches, even, was a challenge.â Dartmoorâs famous tourist spot Haytor, with its sea of unusual jagged, rustic rock faces, also served as the backdrop for one of the filmâs key travelling montages. The team brought a horse and carriage to rumble along its steep granite tracks at dawn. "Not many people get to film there, and not many get to go there at dawn,â says Ian. âStanding there at four in the morning with the first light in the sky... I did stand there and think, 'This is why I love my job.'" Knebworth House and Broughton Castle, Hertfordshire and Oxfordshire In one of the filmâs pivotal points, Marianne famously takes a walk in the rain in the surrounds of Cleveland HouseÂ â after which she falls gravely ill. The mood of the film darkens, and the interiors follow suit. The team paired the iconic Gothic exterior of Knebworth House in Hertfordshire with the interiors of Broughton Castle, near Banbury, to represent this sad twist in the tale, ensuring the ominous feel was retained both inside and out. âIn that time period there were lots of different architectural styles. Knebworth has a very Gothic exterior, but feels different insideâthereâs lots of wood panelling, which makes it feel like a different era,â says Ian. âWhereas inside Broughton, the interiors very much feel like a Gothic castle.â To evoke the tight, claustrophobic atmosphere of Georgian London without relying on modern set builds, the team looked for period locations in and around the capital that have been altered minimally since they were built. National Trust property Rainham Hall in Havering doubled for the interiors of Mrs Jenningsâ house at Portman Squareâan especially good fit as its historic rooms are literally now preserved as a museum. âWe wanted real locations with genuine age,â says Ian. âWe didnât want people to question on screen whether itâs a build or not. We wanted it to feel real.â For the street scenes and exteriors, the crew filmed at Lincolnâs Inn in Holborn. This part of London retains a great variety of period features without many additional modern elements. It meant they didnât need to build anything artificial in a studio. âThere was the odd electrical line going from building to building, a satellite dish, and road markings that we had to paint out, but it was nice to use a part of London that was still real old London,â says Ian. âAll the way through the film, in terms of locations, we strived not to recreate anything, but to try and take what was already there and make it fit our world.â The decadent, Italianate architecture of West Wycombe Park provided the right visual shorthand for the immense wealth and rigid social standing of the Ferrars family. Again, the historic Palladian house required virtually no set dressing from the art department. âWe knew that was the look we wanted to go for because itâs a contrast to everything else in the film,â says Ian. âVisually, it raises the class with beautiful Italian curtains and wallpaper; it sets a clear contrast. We were very much about contrast throughout the film â using locations to tell the story of the charactersâ different levels of wealth and lifestyle through the properties they lived in.â Sometimes, the simplest shot can prove the hardest to pull off, proven here by the search for a specific hero image requested by the director: a carriage reflected perfectly in a body of water as it travels across the grounds. âBelieve it or not, that was hard to find," says Ian. "If the bridge is too high and the water is too low, you never get the full reflection.â The team finally found it after a five-month search in the estate grounds of Blenheim Palace in Woodstock. It took the entire duration of the film to locate. The result was worth the effortâthe scene is one of the loveliest in the film. âIt was probably only about three hours of waiting for the right light to shoot when we eventually found the right bridge,â says Ian. âI kept looking while carrying on with all the other important stuff. We found it right at the end, and it was one of the last things we shot.â A version of this story originally appeared on CondÃ© Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: The Best Airports in the World for Art, According to the “Oscars of the Aviation Industry”
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Our annual Readers' Choice Awards winners have been announced! We loved poring over the results to find out whatâs sticking with readers and spinning the data into a snapshot of the current moment in travel. Ahead: your manual for planning that next adventure. View the complete list of Readersâ Choice Award winners here. Walt Whitman was certainly not thinking of an airport when he wrote, âI know of nothing else but miracles,â but just as the poet finds wonder in everything from sharing a meal with friends to watching machinery at work, might he also have celebrated the unexpected beauty we sometimes find in the modern-day hellscape of an airport? If a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars, the art inside an airport that reminds us of our humanity and distracts us from our fatigue is an object worthy of praise. But until itâs taken up in verse, other forms of recognition will have to do, such as a dedicated category in Skytraxâs World Airline Awards. Industry insiders call the honors, âthe Oscars of the aviation industry,â and its 2026 winners for âWorldâs Best Art in the Airportâ are sure to get the discourse flowing. AV geek or average flyer, we can all be the judge of which ones swept, got snubbed, and deserve a layover in. To reveal a little of our own hand, these also happen to be some of our favorite airports. And according to our Readersâ Choice Awards, they are some of yours, too. With no further ado, these are the winners for âWorldâs Best Art in the Airport,â in ranked order. 1. The Houston Airport System - George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) and William P. Hobby Airport (HOU) For the fourth year running, first place is this Texas-based twofer. Comprised of George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) and William P. Hobby Airport (HOU), the Houston Airport System and its arts program are sterling examples of the old adage that everything is bigger, and evidently better, in the Lone Star State. Case in point, take IAHâs handblown glass centerpiece, Coastal Prairie Fiori, by artist Dale Chihuly. The intricate, snaking sculpture is comprised of 537 individual elements suspended from the rafters. Or, should you find yourself at HOU, you canât miss the David Adickesâ We Love Houston sculpture, the towering photo-op moment stands at 16.5 feet tall. In addition to the visual arts, the Houston Airports Public Art Program also includes artist residencies and their âHarmony in the Airâ performances that brings in over 120 live musicians to fill the air across both airportsâ terminals. 2. Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) Changi is an airport that is no stranger to superlatives. Having snatched âWorldâs Best Airportâ at the Skytrax World Airport Awards 14 times, it is literally the institutionâs most awarded airport. As a massive 1.46 million-square-foot shopping complex complete with gold bar-vending machines and the iconic Jewel Rain Vortex, Changi is a destination onto itself. And its stunning art program is a synecdoche for the Singaporean airport as a whole, with a major theme in the curation being the marriage of nature with technology and culture. Thereâs Terminal 1âs Kinetic Rain sculpture, a dancing wave of 1,216 copper-plated droplets that rises and falls with perfect synchronicity, as well as Terminal 3âs affecting Coming Home statues created by artist Han Meilin which greets visitors at the South Arrival Immigration Hall. Both pieces are part of the airport's permanent collection. While Changi invites its denizens to embrace its maximalism, thereâs nothing wrong with stopping to smell the sculpted roses. 3. Denver International Airport (DEN) Many have come to love the Denver Airport for all its weirdness, and so too has this red-headed stepchild of the airport community learned to wear its oddities with moxy. When Denver broke ground on the construction of its new airport some four decades ago, the city strung something of an albatross around its neck as the megaproject proved to be difficult to birth. Through its difficulties, inquiring minds began to wonder: Why is it so big? So expensive? What were they actually building out there? The resulting speculationâMasonic alien headquarters, New World Order safe house after releasing a global depopulation virusâbecame one of the most iconic conspiracy theories in Internet history. These, um, freethinkers were unintentionally encouraged by what eventually became the airport's art program. Namely, a giant blue mustang with glowing red eyes along the entrance road, affectionately known as Blucifer, murals by Leo Tanguma depicting, among other things, a gas-masked soldier terrorizing refugees with a sword, a time capsule donated by local Freemasons, and cast-iron talking gargoyles that haunt the baggage claim. The airport has leaned in, with posters over construction sites that say things like âThanks for being patient. The lizard people keep stealing our tools.â DEN might also be the only airport in America with a sense of humor. ââWe don't think of it as a problem at all because it doesn't present a problem,â says Marco Toscano, Director of Customer Experience. âIt's just a fun story to have.â Adapted from Charlie Sosnick, contributing writer. 4. Vancouver International Airport (YVR) Itâs impossible to sum up the entirety of a peopleâs arts and culture in one space, but Vancouver International Airportâs art collection provides an impressive preview of British Columbiaâs rich histories and traditions. Starting with the Musequeam Welcome Area, find a tribute to the Coast Salish Indigenous peoples. The installation is comprised of Susan Pointâs Welcome Figures; her Spindle Whorl depicting the act of flight, which is also the largest in the world; and the piece Out of the Silence, a series of hand-dyed, hand-spun woolen blankets that honors the Coast Salish womenâs identities as weavers. Throughout the airport, passersby take in the diverse mosaic of First Nations art represented throughout the terminals, from Haida spirituality at the âSupernatural Worldâ installation to annals of Inuit life from the Lorne Balshine Collection. YVR takes pride in its art collection, which offers âthe first and last impression of British Columbiaâ that many visitors will encounter. Thanks to its thoughtful curation, the collection ensures travelers are off to a strong start. 5. Kempegowda International Airport Bengaluru (BLR) At Kempegowda International Airport, Terminal 2 houses its own art museum showcasing 103 artists and 314 artworks. Blossoming with beauty, both natural and manmade, this arm of the airport is affectionately known as the âTerminal in a Garden.â The exhibits embody Karnatakan spirit, with Naurasaâthe nine aesthetic forms that comprise the foundation of classical Indian art derived from the Sanskrit text the Natya Shastraâguiding the airportâs approach to art. The collection pays homage to local materials like terracotta; incorporates biophilic design that keeps our connection to nature close; as well as honors ancient architectural traditions in a way that feels seamless and elegant as it frames the conveniences of modern-day. Say hi to Nandi, a fiberglass sculpture by artist Gopinath Subbanna which honors the namesake sacred bull said to shepherd auspicious passages, and stop by the Museum of Art and Photography (MAP) which provides a crash course on masterpieces of Indian art throughout the ages. 6. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) As the crucible of the Dutch Golden Age, itâs only right that Amsterdam is home to one of the best airport art programs in the world. Even the most spartan features of the airport get a splash of creativity. Check the time at the viral video installation Real Time Schiphol Clock from artist Maarten Baas in Lounge 2. The unconventional clock is really a 12-hour looped video of Baas, silhouetted and seemingly inside the translucent clock face, manually painting the ticking by of minutes. Keep looking up as you move to Lounge 4, where youâll find M.C. Escherâs sprawling 48-foot-long Metamorphosis mural. Should you have a layover long enough to be boredom-inducing but not quite forgiving enough to take a jaunt out into the city, you can still visit visit the Rijksmuseum, which runs a free 24-hour extension at the airport. How often is it that you get to come face-to face with the 17th-century masters while waiting for Starbucks to open? 7. San Diego International Airport (SAN) If you ever want to behold something beautiful in San Diego, just look outside. Itâs hard to beat the seaside cliffs, the gentle Pacific, and the breezy Mediterranean-esque climes âAmericaâs Finest Cityâ lays claim to, but the art in this airport is so convincing it might persuade you to spend another moment or two indoors. In 2025, the lauded program debuted five exhibits alongside the new Terminal 1. The new kids on the block include the 21-foot-tall jellyfish sculpture RISE that sits outside the terminal entrance, Amy Ellingsonâs A Day in the Sun which utilizes hundreds of thousands of shimmering mosaic tiles to evoke sunrise and sunset, the Torrey Pines hanging sculpture by Nova Jiang, Erwin Redlâs dazzling light installation Vessel of Light that pulses along music, and the parking plazaâs Migrations sculptures by Walter Hood. 8. Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) With 70 pieces in its permanent collection, Chicago OâHare is far from owning the largest catalogue in this list, but each of its artworks packs a punch. Michael Haydenâs Skyâs the Limit light sculpture has become practically synonymous with the Chicago airport as the glowing tunnel that ushers its passengers from the stress of a long travel day into Windy City magic. Should you find yourself traveling with little ones, they can find their creativity reflected in Youth in the Loop, an imaginative mural painted by groups of teen apprentice artists. While not a piece of manmade art, visitors to OâHare would be remiss to not marvel up at Ernestine, the four-story tall fiberglass Brachiosaurus skeleton who overlooks Terminal 1, Concourse B, because youâre never too old admire a dinosaur. 9. San Francisco International Airport (SFO) Playing word association with the Bay Area is bound to conjure aspirational qualities, whether you think first of its tech-forward reputation or its midcentury literary past. As SFO is the gateway to NorCal's gateway city, it's only fitting that this reader-favorite airport is a microcosm of all things San Francisco. The arts program here is the product of a dream-team collaboration between theÂ SFO Museum and the San Francisco Arts Commission who bring in the best of local talent and court world-class artists to the collection. In 1999, the SFO Museum earned the singular distinction of being the first airport museum to be accredited by the American Alliance of MuseumsÂ (AAM), and it still remains the only airport in the world to have done so. You can find everything from video art to figurative drawing displays here, but the most accessible pieces remain the works of public art such as Charles Sowersâ interactive Butterfly Wall or Janet Echelmanâs Every Beating Second, which looks as if it might take flight from where it hangs in Terminal 2. 10. Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport Mumbai (BOM) Mumbaiâs Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International AirportÂ takes the cake for the airport art program with the largest collection on this list. The airportâs museum, the Artbeat of New India, has over 7,000 artifacts and art pieces in its arsenal, and itâs no exaggeration to say you could spend all day perusing it all. The program takes advantage of showcasing its expansive bounty, with inventive displays of all the ways in which these artifacts traverse borders of time and space. Thereâs Thresholds of India, which stars 6,000 historical artifacts like Nagaland wooden totems, Kerala masks, and Gujarati architectural motifs to name just a few. As youâre coming and going, youâll see Layered Narratives, a series of 29 murals illustrating Mumbaiâs evolution as a metropolis. Even as you rush through the halls to make your hotel check-in, youâll be compelled to stop and take in Baggage Acclaimed, a testament to the countryâs varied craftsman and textile traditions.

item.title: How to Escape Productivity Culture When It Follows You Outside
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
A few months ago, I was hiking with a friend when I tripped and pulled my hamstring. We both had our own alpine climbing goals that summer, and I’d been looking at our morning hike as a training opportunity. I didn’t want to hold either of us back. I assured him that I’d be able to hobble along at our same brisk pace and, when that became impossible, told him that he should leave me behind. He refused both. Instead, he sat down beside me on the trail. “You know,” he said. “I think I spend too much time doing in nature, and not enough time being in nature.” The brisk pace—and therefore the training gains—could wait. It shouldn’t have felt revolutionary, but it did. And it made me realize just how much I’d let my own obsession with productivity bleed into my recreational life. I am a person who lives in fear of my own idleness. Every spare scrap of my time is scheduled, tracked, color-coded, and accounted for. The other day, my partner glanced over my shoulder at my phone and asked if I was playing Candy Crush. “No,” I said, holding up the screen to show him the tightly packed colored squares. “That’s just this week’s Google calendar.” On the one hand, I know that my constant busyness comes from a deep-seated need for control. Fill my schedule with social plans, and I’ll never be lonely. Control my time, and maybe I’ll feel like I’m controlling my life. On the other hand, I do genuinely like doing stuff. When I lie on my deathbed, I want to feel fully wrung out, like I gave my all to this whole business of life and left no shred of time on the table. No trail unexplored. No mountain unclimbed. Some folks would call that approach very industrious, or very American. Others would call it toxic productivity. Toxic productivity is a fairly modern term that encompasses both the desperate need to be productive at all costs—and the guilt that sets in after a day without measurable output. It can look like working long hours at the office. It can also look like assigning checklists and training goals to your hobbies to make them feel “productive,” or trying to monetize them so they feel justified. Initially, I bristled at the idea of “doing in nature” as a binary to “being in nature.” Couldn’t I have both? Couldn’t I like being outdoors and give mountain sports my all? Wasn’t doing the opposite a waste of time? Sitting beside someone who was perfectly happy to listen to the birds and watch the wind flutter through the ponderosa pines, I suddenly wasn’t so sure. I’d spent hundreds of hours pushing myself through pain and chasing an imagined future self instead of dwelling in the present. Maybe that also counted as wasted time. Instead of letting the outdoors be an escape, I’d turned it into yet another arena for excellence. I hadn’t even made it back to the trailhead, and I was already mentally recalculating the mileage and gain I’d have to do later in the week to make up for our lost training time. He, meanwhile, had nowhere to be but right there. Maybe some people can push their pace and fully absorb their surroundings at the same time. I don’t know if I can. As long as I’m thinking about my time, my heart rate zone, or my pitch count, a significant fraction of my mind is elsewhere. Partial presence in nature is better than no presence in nature. But I realized that to get a full reset, I needed to make time to stop chasing, sit in the dirt, and simply be still. In Western societies, the relentless chase of self-improvement is usually celebrated. But research indicates that active pursuit of anything can actually make you less happy. That includes the pursuit of happiness itself. A 2018 study from a pair of researchers at the University of Toronto and Rutgers University revealed that people who pursue happiness tend to do so because they believe time is running out, and that happiness is a destination that they must reach before it’s too late. Worse, the act of chasing happiness can actually put you in that kind of scarcity mindset, even if you aren’t already. That’s the irony of setting goals, especially around wellness. The authors of the 2018 paper write that “trying to be happier often leads people to monitor not only happy thoughts but also unhappy thoughts at the same time, and the ironic salience of this negativity makes them feel unhappier.” In other words: fixating on a thing—whether it’s your health, your fitness, or your climbing grade—means you’re naturally focusing on your moments of failure as well as your moments of success. The result is often more dissatisfaction than you would have experienced had you just let yourself enjoy the thing without goals attached. In the 2018 study, researchers found that participants were more likely to identify as happy if they viewed happiness as a state of gratitude as opposed to a thing to obtain. Let’s, for a moment, pretend I believe in the premise that I won’t be happier if I win that race, slash that mile time, or notch that climbing grade. Won’t I be unhappy if I do the opposite? If I sit around being idle? If I skip that lunch run or give up on that climb? Or if, God forbid, I take a whole day—or week, or month—off my sport and watch my fitness hit rock bottom? Whether you’re ready to hear this or not, all that counts as rest. A friend of mine, Madeleine Dore, once compiled her own thoughts about hustle culture and productivity guilt in a book refreshingly titled I Didn’t Do the Thing Today. In it, she describes human creativity like a sponge. Sometimes, you’re in an absorb phase. Sometimes you’re in a squeeze phase. During a squeeze, you can produce and produce and produce, but after a while, you’re completely wrung out. At that point, the only way to refill is to let yourself lie fallow. That doesn’t mean monetizing your hobby or poring over data to optimize your training. It means sitting in the dirt. Reading a book. Sleeping. Ambling. Watching the clouds go by. The secret to a fulfilling and creative life isn’t in the squeeze; it’s in the absorb. Do that, and you’ll start to feel your brain sponge refill. You’ll begin to appreciate the pure, intrinsic joy of moving your body outdoors just for its own damn sake. And you’ll finally learn to revel in who you are right now—not in the fictional person you’re still trying to become. Here’s how I’m attempting to lean into being in nature. These might work for you too: Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: The Only Backpack You Need for Flights, Day Hikes, and Weekends Away
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy I own a lot of backpacks. It’s an occupational hazard. I have racks of them in my garage, all hanging in anticipation of their specific use case. Long, multi-day hikes through the backcountry? I have a pack for that. Quick mountain bike spins around local trails? I have a backpack for that (a hip pack, actually). But the perfect travel backpack, the carry-all that can be my trusty companion for planes, trains, and automobiles, has eluded me. Until Matador Equipment made the Adventure Pack, a 24-liter backpack designed specifically for modern adventure travel. I’ve carried this pack on trips for the last four months, and I’ve decided it’s the best travel backpack I’ve ever owned. + Two ways to access the main compartment How much do I love thee? Let me count the ways. First, let’s talk about size. At 24 liters, it’s big enough to serve as the only bag I need on overnight trips where I don’t need a lot of gear. You can stuff a lot of layers, underwear, and camera equipment into this thing. But it’s small enough to fit into any overhead bin, even on the tiny jets that leave from my small-city airport. Matador makes a larger Global Travel backpack that can fit everything you’ll need for a multi-day trip, but it’s too big for some overhead bins. The Adventure Pack hits the sweet spot. It’s also small enough to use as a day pack for side missions while you’re on the road. I’ve ditched my clothes in the cabin or hotel room and stuffed the pack with camera gear, a couple of layers, and snacks for day hikes and rides. I even took it on a boat while fishing the Yellowstone River. The size makes it super versatile. Second, Matador got a lot of the obvious things right. For instance, the pack has two expandable water bottle pockets. A lot of backpacks only have one, and some have none. Can you imagine? Before the Matador came into my life, I was using a Thule backpack that was great in so many different ways, but it only has one water bottle pocket. With two expandable sleeves working as holsters, I can load one with a reusable bottle and the other with a sandwich for the plane, so I don’t have to buy those expensive snack boxes in the air. There’s also a large top pocket for miscellaneous items, the little things you don’t want in your pockets but need access to all the time, like gum or headphones. Again, some backpacks, like a Yeti pack I used often in the past, skimp on this catch-all pocket, but Matador makes sure it’s large enough. And I love the robustly padded laptop sleeve with a false bottom, so I can throw this bag around and not worry about my money maker crumbling under pressure. Matador didn’t stop with the obvious details. They incorporated a handful of smart features that come in handy on the road, like two ways to access the main compartment: a top-loading zipper and a large clamshell zipper that lets you pack the main body like a suitcase. The clamshell zipper also gives you quick access to the middle of the main compartment, so you can organize your gear to grab a book or extra layer on the fly without digging through the whole bag. For the extra-cautious traveler, there’s an RFID-blocking, hidden “Smuggler’s Pocket” in the center of the back panel. Unless you know it’s there, you’ll never find it. There’s even a tiny location-tracker pocket for your AirTag if you’re worried about someone stealing your kit. Personally, I like the three burly grab handles that let me snatch the pack from the overhead bin when I’m rushing off the plane to catch a connecting flight. A passthrough sleeve on the back panel lets you attach the bag to a roller bag handle so you don’t have to wear it all the time. It’s also a comfy carry thanks to the well-padded shoulder harness and back panel. I’ve had long days lugging this fully loaded pack through the airport, or running through it, and it never creates hot spots or pressure points. Gear protection is a priority for me because I travel with a computer and a couple of cameras, so the recycled waterproof nylon and sealing zippers are really important. It’s not a full dry bag, and you’re not going to use it as a flotation device in case of a water landing, but it will keep your gear dry in a rainstorm—I know from experience. The only thing I don’t love is the shock cord webbing on the outside panel, which feels a little flimsy. It’s fine if you want to stuff a rain shell or fleece into it, but it’s not robust enough to handle something like a bike or ski helmet. I’m always traveling with helmets, so this is an issue for me. But that’s a minor complaint that’s specific to the Goldilocks way I travel. Most people wouldn’t think it’s an issue. And at $199, it’s not the cheapest pack in the travel category. But considering the waterproof materials which have kept my expensive computer and camera equipment dry in recent months, I personally think the extra expense is justified. I’ve used this backpack on almost every trip I’ve made in the last four months. Most of that travel has been by plane, and I think it’s the perfect carry-on backpack for frequent flyers, especially if you want a sporty carry that can handle hikes when you’re away from home. It’s too big for an everyday-carry work backpack, unless you want it to double as a work bag/gym bag so you can get a workout in on your way home from the office. For me, it’s my go-to “go” bag. I have another trip in a week that will have me in multiple airports and living out of a van as I travel through Utah. The Matador Adventure Pack will be my trusty companion throughout.

item.title: National Parks Are Offering Free Off-Road Wheelchairs. It’s a Game Changer for Families Like Mine.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
My family of five had just taken our first few steps onto the Bear Lake Trailhead at Rocky Mountain National Park, and we were already immersed in nature, the evergreen trees looming overhead, the lake glistening in the background. I breathed in the crisp air and, for the next few minutes, we followed the wide, flat trail surrounded by mountains. About 20 minutes into our hike, the trail became steeper, and we couldn’t continue forward without going up a few steps. My middle son is disabled and uses a wheelchair, so usually, when a trail becomes bumpy or more rugged, we turn back. This time, my husband secured his footing, stepped forward, and pulled my son, who was seated in a Cascade Tandem Hiking Cart, or off-road adaptive cart, up the steps. Adrenaline rushed through me as the hiker carried my son deeper into the woods, the rest of my family picking up the pace behind them. We soon came across another set of steps and navigated them more easily. Another half-mile later, we stopped to explore a brook glimmering in the sun, and I looked out at the mountain peaks, feeling a new sense of accomplishment and hope. A few weeks before our trip, my husband and I considered purchasing a Cascade Cart to bring with us on vacation. When we contacted their customer service department, I was excited to learn that a local charity, Avery’s Light, had recently donated two Cascade Carts to Estes Park Mountain Shop, located about ten minutes from Rocky Mountain National Park, and that we could borrow one at no cost. I reached out to the mountain shop, confirmed the hiker was available, and reserved our park entry time on Recreation.gov. On the morning of our first day at the park, Rio Roman, an employee at the Estes Park Mountain Shop, spent almost an hour showing us how to assemble, use and disassemble the hiker. He also mapped out the best trails to take it on, including the popular Bear Lake Trail, making our trip more enjoyable and memorable than ever. “For us, it’s about more than equipment; it’s about ensuring that nature belongs to everyone,” says Roman, who has a daughter with disabilities and enjoys using the Cascade Cart with her. In addition to the two hikers, the mountain shop also has six GRIT Freedom all-terrain wheelchairs, two backpacks from We Carry Kevan, and one XL bike/stroller combo from WIKE, which comes with a complimentary electric bike rental to pull the trailer, available for rent. The availability of track chairs, backpacks, hikers, and other equipment that helps people with disabilities enjoy national parks is a growing trend. As of this fall, all five Utah national parks offer all-terrain wheelchairs. And across the U.S., nearly 30 National Park Service sites now offer mobility devices to visitors through park-operated lending programs or partnerships with other organizations. For example, Indiana Dunes National Park has an adaptive program with free assistive equipment, including two Freedom Trax, a motorized off-road attachment for manual wheelchairs, a Zoom chair, and a Hippocampe Blue Blazer off-road wheelchair. Great Smoky Mountains National Park in Tennessee launched its first adaptive program in 2023 with three adaptive hikes, an adaptive bike program, and a GRIT chair. The park also partners with Catalyst Sports and Friends of the Smokies to add a Cascade Tandem Hiking Cart, a Rough Rider Aurora, and a Black Diamond TrailRider to its offerings, which can be used on approximately 14 miles of trails throughout the park. They also offer ranger‑led programs using adaptive equipment. Bryce Canyon National Park recently acquired two Extreme Motus Off-Road Wheelchairs. The chairs are available on a first-come, first-served basis and can be borrowed by visiting the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center. And, in 2026, Zion National Park launched a program making an all‑terrain wheelchair available for public use on a first-come, first-served basis, made possible through a grant received by the park’s official philanthropic partner, Zion Forever Project. Visitors can find additional information, including a list of recommended trails online and at the park visitor center. “This program underscores the park’s commitment to reducing barriers and enhancing opportunities for all visitors to explore their national parks,” said Jeff Bradybaugh, Zion National Park Superintendent. The National Park Service is also working to implement the EXPLORE Act, which was signed into law in 2025 year, and will expand access to public lands and promote opportunities for individuals with disabilities to participate in outdoor recreation. For example, the act emphasizes providing clear and accurate trail information on park websites so visitors who use mobility devices can better understand trail conditions and accessibility. For families like mine, who love nature, want to explore, and have a family member with a disability, this new trend is a game changer. I can’t wait to check more national parks off our bucket list and enjoy the outdoors without feeling held back.

item.title: Who Is the Ghost Woman on Idaho’s River of No Return?
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
In honor of spooky season, Outside editors are sharing their backcountry encounters while hiking, camping, or otherwise enjoying the outdoors. In the summer of 2026, whitewater rafters on Idaho’s Main Salmon River kept reporting sightings of an unexplained “ghost woman dressed in white.” Associate editor Madison Dapcevich has spent weeks rowing the so-called River of No Return. She sat down with a fellow river-runner and local historian to find out if this modern mystery is, indeed, a haunting spirit of one of the river’s pioneer women. On a cold, drizzly day in July 2026, Nate Lewand and his fleet of whitewater rafters passed by Black Canyon, an obsidian-colored gorge on the Main Salmon River in Idaho. As they rounded the bend, they spotted a woman standing on a narrow sandy beach far too small to hold a tent. She wore clean linen clothing, military-style boots, and carried a burled walking stick. Despite being right at the water’s edge in the rain, the woman was bone dry. She had no gear—no ropes, no backpacks, and no raft. “She was just standing there,” Lewand told Outside. “We hollered to see if she was okay and slowed down a bit. She didn’t respond, so we yelled some more. She just stuck her hand up as if to wave, but she didn’t.” No trail runs along this stretch of the canyon, and the surrounding walls are sheer granite cliffs. I know these areas well, having rowed the Salmon River myself. The canyon is a special place with deeply rooted history that you can feel with every passing oar stroke. “We looked at a topographic map of how she got down there, and there’s no easy route,” Lewand said. “She would have had to rappel or be an amazing climber or floated in without any gear—or she just existed in this place.” Lewand, 36, an experienced river runner from Park City, Utah, has spent eight years on the water. This was his fourth trip down the Main Salmon, an iconic 80-mile whitewater corridor cutting through Idaho’s Salmon-Challis National Forest. His group wasn’t the only one to encounter the mystery figure. Between mid-July and early August, multiple river runners took to social media and local forums claiming they saw a “ghost woman dressed in white.” One group reported hearing haunting wails echoing off the canyon walls at night; others said they saw a figure standing silently, high on a ridge above the rapids. Lewand noted that at least five other groups told him they also saw the woman at several remote locations along the river, including areas called Black Canyon, Lower Corey Bar, and Yellow Pine. “We were trying to stay positive, so our crew started calling her Mother Nature, hoping for good graces on the rest of the trip,” Lewand said. “People have gone out intentionally looking for her since, but no one seems able to find her again.” Whether the figure was a disoriented hiker or something paranormal, her appearance gave rise to a new moniker along the riverbanks: the Salmon Siren. Tales of ghostly women along waterways are as old as wilderness travel itself. In Mexico and the American Southwest, stories persist of La Llorona, the weeping woman doomed to wander riverbanks searching for her lost children. In Ireland, the Banshee (bean sí) wails near waterways to warn of impending death. Scotland has the Bean Nigh, a river spirit seen washing the bloodstained clothes of those about to meet their fate. Across Europe, similar archetypes appear: France’s Dame Blanche, Germany’s Weisse Frau, and the Dutch Witte Wieven, who drift through river mists and ancient ruins. They are almost always women, clad in white, forever tethered to the places where they suffered immense loss. It feels fitting that this classic folklore would find a home along the banks of the Main Salmon River—famously nicknamed The River of No Return. Early explorers, miners, and homesteaders dubbed the Main Fork of the Salmon the “River of No Return.” In the 19th and early 20th centuries, travelers built heavy wooden boats to float supplies down the river’s roaring rapids and deep gorge—which reaches depths greater than the Grand Canyon. The swift currents, intense rapids, and treacherous drops made returning upstream nearly impossible. The river remains a testament to the Wild West. The Salmon is the longest undammed system in the Lower 48, flowing from the heart of the Frank Church-River of No Return Wilderness—a 2.3-million-acre roadless area and the largest protected wilderness in the continental United States. That ruggedness still draws river runners like me. There’s no cell service, and hiking in or out is excruciatingly difficult. I’ve rowed the 80-mile stretch three times, facing torrential hail and big waves. Along the south-facing banks of the river is an arid, high-elevation desert. The other, north-facing aspects are lush and green, with hot springs and bubbling brooks. Sweeping white-sand beaches and fruit orchards are scattered throughout the corridor. “It’s almost like you travel from planet to planet throughout the days of working down the river in the middle of a nowhere canyon in Idaho,” Lewand said. I couldn’t help but wonder: Could the sightings be connected to the women who lived, worked, and died along these rugged banks? Kathy Deinhardt Hill, a historian at the Central Idaho Historical Museum in McCall and author of Spirits of Salmon, analyzed the several tragic tales of women whose lives were intertwined with the river. Deinhart told me of several pioneering women who lived along the river, from 1853 to 1998. We spoke about the different women’s live, and I asked her who she believed could be the so-called Salmon Siren. She said she believes the Salmon Siren is the lingering spirit of Rose Cook, a frontierswoman featured in Deinhardt’s book. Born in Salem, Oregon, in 1862, Rose Cook moved to Elk City, Idaho, after her first husband died and began working as a schoolteacher. There, she met Warren Cook; Deinhardt says she was 40 and he was 27. Shortly after at Mile 148 on the Salmon River. Scottish immigrant and prospector William Campbell founded the ferry in 1898, but disappeared in a winter snowstorm in 1902 and was presumed dead. “In the spring of 1905, Rose became pregnant,” Deinhardt said. “In October, she fell ill, most likely from a stroke.” Jim Moore, a man who lived across the river, came to help, along with another couple, Eugene and his wife, Ella Churchill, who served as midwife. “Even with their help, Rose was unable to deliver the baby,” Deinhardt said. The baby was stillborn, and shortly after, Rose died on October 12, 1905. Two days later, she and the child were buried on the hill above the meadow at Campbells Ferry. “People from up and down the river, as well as Elk City and Dixie, Idaho, made their way to the river to pay their respects,” Deinhardt said. “Later, Warren never spoke of the matter and eventually left the river. He moved to McCall, remarried, and worked as a forest ranger.” Deep in the Frank Church–River of No Return Wilderness lies Rose’s grave. Her 1905 tragedy reveals the brutal realities of life on the Salmon River at the turn of the century. Another woman pioneer of the Salmon River, Emma Zaunmiller, also died in a horse accident at Campbell’s Ferry in 1938. Married to Gene Churchill, Ella Prescott worked on a ranch along the Salmon River from the early 1900s until her husband died in a boating accident in 1915, according to Deinhardt On September 18, Churchill was running a supply boat when it became stuck on a rock near Yellow Pine Bar. When the men tried to dislodge the boat, the current swept Churchill into the river. “At this point, the current was so swift that it submerged him, and he let loose of the line. About 200 feet below the line, his head appeared for an instant above the water, a whirlpool drew him under again, and he sunk to rise no more,” according to a 1915 article in the Grangeville Globe. His body was found about 25 days later downriver, and he was buried with a wooden headstone that’s no longer there. One year later, Ella married Clarence Prescott. That same year, she filed a homestead claim on the ranch. Prescott helped Ella with the ranch, but he was in poor health and, according to Deinhardt, died in 1920. At the time, the federal government granted homestead patents along the Salmon River and its forks to settlers under the Homestead Act of 1862. The government could take years to issue these patents, and Ella stayed at the ranch until she received hers in 1922. She died the following October at 67, Deinhardt said. Ella is buried at the Churchill Ranch, now the Whitewater Ranch, on Little Mallard Creek, overlooking the river. A large rock was placed on the top of her grave, forever marking her final resting place. Born in Oregon, Reho Wolfe moved to Idaho and graduated from Kamiah High School in 1935. A year later, she married musician George Wolfe and moved to Missoula, Montana. When World War II broke out, George refused the draft. “Instead, he and Reho packed their things along with their young son Norman, age four, and headed to the Salmon River,” Deinhardt said. “In 1944, they settled first at the Crofoot Ranch, up Rattlesnake Creek. The following year, they moved to the Allison Ranch, now a wilderness retreat, where their first daughter, Carol, was born. In the spring of 1945, Reho’s father, John Bergman, was too ill to care for himself, so he moved in with the family at the Allison Ranch. George and the couple’s son, Norman, went downriver to transport John’s belongings, and on the way back to the Allison Ranch, Norman fell trying to cross Big Mallard Creek by himself. He was swept into the Salmon River and drowned. The search for Norman’s body lasted four weeks until he was found in an eddy below Campbell’s Ferry. He was buried next to the trail. “Reho was never the same,” Deinhardt said. “She was haunted by the loss of her son. The family had six more children, and Reho and George struggled to provide. But Reho could never forgive George, and eventually they divorced.” According to Deinhardt, Reho felt best on the river and was well known in the community built around it. In 1958, she pulled her seven children from public school and moved them to an abandoned cabin and mining claim at Gaines Bar, according to a Time article published then. The school district filed truancy charges; the Forest Service said she had no rights to the cabin; she fought and won both cases, according to the Lewiston Tribune. Reho homeschooled her children, gave them music lessons every day, and taught them how to survive on the river. She eventually moved back to Lewiston, Idaho, where she received a teaching degree, and then moved the family to Montana. “It was the pattern of her life—constantly on the go, taking odd jobs, doing whatever it took,” Deinhardt said. “But almost every summer she took the kids back to the cabin on Gaines Bar.” In 1998, she set out for one last river trip and died on the night of July 1 at 82, according to the Lewiston Tribune.
