She is buried at Gaines Bar, with a granite headstone that still marks her grave today. Reho spent every possible moment in her wilderness home, and Gaines Bar camp is a testament to this. Today, the river camp is home to historic cabins, and in the early-morning fog, you can feel an otherworldly presence Her son, John Wolfe, wrote Reho’s story in the book Reho Wolf: The End of a Salmon River Era. Buried on the river at the Polly Bemis place. She did not die on the river, but lived on the river for many years. Born near Beijing in 1853, Polly’s father exchanged her for money to buy seed when a famine struck the area in 1869, according to the U.S. Forest Service. Two years later, in 1871, she was sent to San Francisco, later smuggled to Portland, and was eventually sold to a Chinese resident of Warren, Idaho, for $2,500. She arrived in the area by pack train and was given her name there. As with much of the American West at the time, Idaho had a strong Chinese population to support mining. In Warren, she met Charles Bemis, a wealthy jeweler who owned a saloon. In 1887, the couple’s house burned down, and they lost everything but gold dust and a few coins. In 1893, the couple bought a mining claim along Salmon River and married the following year. They became river legends, growing fruit in their riverside orchards and selling their produce in town every summer. Lore holds that Charlie once caught a mountain lion and raised it as a pet. In 1922, their house caught fire once again. Both escaped, but Charlie died shortly after. Polly stayed in the log house for more than a decade, and died in 1933 while recovering from a stroke in Grangeville, Idaho. Deinhardt said that those who knew Polly best understood she wanted to be buried on the river. So they worked with the state and owners of the Polly Bemis Ranch to have her body exhumed and moved to the river. In 1987, historians restored the log cabin and turned it into a museum that paddlers can visit today. Today, Polly Bemis Ranch is a 26-acre estate, and even features the river’s only volleyball net. Whether the mystery woman seen along the Main Salmon is an illusion created by fog and high canyon walls, an elusive backpacker, or something lingering from the past, the sightings speak to the River of No Return’s transcendent nature. In a modern world defined by constant connectivity, the Salmon River remains one of the few places where humans are forced to step away from technology and adjust to the rhythms of the natural world, living like early pioneers. “The river offers something that we don’t have access to anymore in our current everyday lives,” Lewand said. “It’s solitude. Sometimes we forget how to disconnect and just be human with one another, and river trips force us to do that.” As long as river runners push their boats into the swift currents of the Main Salmon, the canyon will keep its secrets—and those who navigate its waters will keep looking closely at the white-sand beaches, wondering who might be watching from the rocks above.

item.title: The 9 Best Women’s Running Shirts and Tanks of October 2026
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy Update October 2026: This fall, we slimmed down our list of best running tank tops and tees to highlight the standout choices. After testing 13 new shirts over the summer and early fall, bringing the total tested this year to 63, we named three new tanks and two new tees to the list of winners. For the most versatile options that transition seamlessly from track to town, consider the Vuori Energy Tank and the Patagonia Capilene Cool Merino Blend Shirt. It’s fall, y’all. Cooler temps are (finally) sweeping the nation, which makes for ideal running weather. Since we still love a running tank or tee for midday outings, layering under long-sleeves, and running on vacation in warm locales through winter, we’re keeping our list of the best running shirts up to date and awarding a few new winners. It may be surprising to find Patagonia in a “Best Value” category, but the versatility and function of this running tank makes the Capillene Cool Daily Tank well worth the just-under-40-bucks price tag. We loved the feel of this workout tank for everything from warm-weather runs in Colorado to high-humidity hikes in the Caribbean. Testers described the recycled polyester Capilene Cool fabric as “extremely lightweight” and said it helped them “maintain comfort while sweating.” The thin fabric dries quickly, whether on the run, during water sports like stand-up paddleboarding, or while traveling. Like most Patagonia apparel, the fit of this running tank runs a little large, but we liked the relaxed shape. It’s one tester’s go-to shirt while wearing compression-style running shorts. “I like the coverage of the longer cut,” she said. We also loved the versatility of the tank’s styling—the only visible branding is a tiny Patagonia tag at the bottom seam, so it doesn’t look overly athletic and out of place off the trail. + Functional and fashionable for a range of activities We love this super-soft, seemingly simple top for hot, dry running in Boulder, Colorado, humid runs in coastal California, and as a do-everything tank on travels around the world. The polyester/elastane blend feels fantastic against the skin. “Vuori nails it with the material,” said a tester. “Is there anything more buttery soft?” While the fabric itself isn’t as breathable as an open mesh, large armholes and a slightly cropped fit allow great airflow. Testers appreciated the wide, flat seams for both their style and their lack of chafing. “I’m in love with this tank,” said a tester, who used it for running, gym workouts, and casual wear. This tank’s honeycomb polyester knit creates a unique mesh (it’s nowhere near see-through) that, combined with the loose cut, allows cooling airflow in the extreme heat of summer and on sultry fall afternoons. The material is soft against the skin but doesn’t cling. “I liked the fabric a lot,” said a Colorado-based tester. “It feels substantial and durable but breathed great and wicked my sweat away from my body.” The one complaint? Some craved a little more length in the hem. “I’d like to be able to wear it to the gym to lift without exposing my midriff,” said one. + Extremely lightweight and quick-drying Unlike tanks with narrow racerback straps, The North Face Summit Series High Trail Tank provides enough coverage to prevent chafing from a hydration pack without compromising its comfort and heat regulation. Testers described the recycled polyester knit pique that makes up the majority of the tank as “super lightweight and breathable” and “extremely soft.” The back and underarms feature an engineered polyester fabric that actively pulls moisture from the skin and dries quickly. We appreciated the lack of sweat build-up, particularly when wearing a pack. Bonded seams at the shoulders and along the sides helped keep us comfortable (no chafing!), and slight notches at the bottom hem enhanced mobility. Testers also praised the tank’s fit and proportions. This $40 running tee works across a range of activity (and inactivity). We loved it for everything from runs in warm temps to a 12-hour car ride, hiking, yardwork, and running errands. The Injinji tee feels soft against the skin, like cotton, but we didn’t find it breathed as well as others we tested. Still, the 95% polyester, 5% spandex tee was comfortable in all but the hottest conditions, and we loved its crossover ability, as well as its price tag. “This is a dependable, easy t-shirt that is super versatile,” said a tester. + Delivers athletic performance and casual style This short-sleeve shirt combines the natural temperature-regulation and odor-control properties of 65 percent wool with the moisture-management capabilities of 35 percent recycled polyester jersey. The blend works great on everything from trail runs to rock climbing to casualwear. And thanks to the wool’s natural insulation and breathability, the Patagonia Capilene Cool Merino Blend Shirt can be worn year-round. We’ve loved it for chilly fall trail runs, and found it thin and breathable enough for high-output road runs on warm days too. Its light weight allows it to also layer well under a second long-sleeve shirt or midlayer. + Antimicrobial finish for odor resistance Testers across the board loved the fit of this tee. The semi-fitted cut is not too loose, nor too tight, drapes nicely while allowing great airflow, and doesn’t ride up. “This shirt has nice coverage, but is also loose enough to feel super light, breathable, and with good movement,” said a tester. The lightweight, stretchy, silky-feeling fabric, made from 86 percent recycled polyester and 14% spandex, wicked moisture fantastically, and dried almost immediately. “This shirt kept me cool in 80-plus degree temps with 70 percent or higher humidity level runs,” said our New Hampshire-based tester. “I never felt that ick wet where the shirt is sticking to me…it always felt loose and breathable, while also having a flattering fit.” + Extremely lightweight, breathable, and quick drying We’ve worn this running t-shirt under a pack over multi-day runs from hut to hut in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, as well as on multiple short runs around the Boulder Foothills and neighborhood suburbs. The shirt performs: Its quick-drying, moisture-wicking, airy—yet durable—polyester jersey material with a “Quick Dry” finish never felt bogged down with sweat. “Loved the material. It’s loose, super ventilated, and fits well throughout,” raved a tester. The Anti-Odor finish also proved effective—did we mention that multi-day, multi-wear hut trip? We got no complaints from our running mates. Flat lock seams, a flat hem, and lack of a tag add to overall comfort, as does this shirt’s ridiculously lightweight feel on the body. The fabric blend (45 percent Merino wool, 45 percent Tencel, and 10 percent nylon) makes this an insanely soft tee that we’ve looked forward to pulling on time and again. The addition of Tencel—a semi-natural fiber made from wood pulp—adds a slightly fuzzy softness that feels great against the skin. But this shirt isn’t all coziness: It breathes exceptionally well and helps regulate body temperature. We’ve worn the Ibex Paradox Shortsleeve Crewneck on mid-day trail runs around Boulder, Colorado, and on high-mountain adventures. In the mountains, the material felt smooth under hydration pack straps and insulated us perfectly when a cool front rolled in. When it comes to summer running shirts and tanks, look for comfort, breathability, moisture-wicking, and a chafe-free fit. Aside from chafe-free seams and a cut that allows full arm movement without restriction, consider how the tank or tee makes you feel. Are you comfortable wearing the top both on a run and stopping for coffee afterward? Are you looking for a tank that makes you feel fast on race day? Do you want a tee that also makes you feel comfortable—both in function and style— in the gym? Breathable, sweat-wicking materials are essential, as is how the material feels against your skin. While some fabric blends prioritize breathability and quick-drying, others provide a more cotton-like feel—the latter sometimes stay wet from sweat longer than the former, but the tradeoff can be worth it. All tops in this round up perform great on the run. The fabric, cut, and seam placement should not restrict your arm movement or your breathing. The best-fitting tops make you forget that you’re wearing them. Some will fit looser or boxier around the middle, while some have a more streamlined fit. Consider what you’re after and shop from there. (Our guide describes the fit of each top.) T-shirts provide more coverage and therefore more sun protection, and they can also deliver more of a cooling effect, depending on the fabric and fit. Tank tops are typically less restricting and more breathable, because of their lack of sleeves. That doesn’t mean all tank tops have freedom of movement. Some fit more streamlined around the midsection than others, while some are looser. The looser ones tend to allow airflow, while the more narrow silhouettes rely on their fabric for breathability. In addition to fit, consider how much skin exposure and coverage you’re comfortable with, and how the tank interacts with your sports bra and running vest, if you’ll be wearing one. And consider all the settings where you’ll want to wear the top, both athletic and casual. With the summer of 2026 being a scorcher nationwide, our test team put the season’s new tees and tanks up to the very difficult task of keeping us cool during high-output running. The best pieces breathed well, didn’t chafe, and kept us heading out on roads and trails under the blazing sun. As the temperatures dropped, we looked for tops that kept the morning chill away but didn’t overheat once we were into the run. We’ve tested 63 tanks and tees since January 2026, with 13 new styles put through their paces since our July update, then compared them to past category winners. Our testers range in age and pace, with one of them an ultrarunning champion, one a six-time Ironman, and all of them with years of experience being hard judges of every top they wear. We evaluated products by comfort first—which includes breathability, drying quickness, chafe-free seams, and fit—followed by style, utility (ability to multitask as casual wear was a big plus), and durability. Lisa Jhung writes, runs, and generally adventures from her homebase in Boulder, Colorado. Raised as a California beach kid, she also makes it back to the coast—any coast, but primarily the Pacific—as often as possible. She’s been testing gear for Outside for a couple of decades and co-manages the road and trail running shoe tests, along with managing the women’s running apparel, sports bras, and running hydration vest tests.

item.title: A Missing Dog Survived 34 Days in Yellowstone National Park. Rescuers Just Saved Her.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Outside associate editor Ella Cobb interviewed the rescuers who are trying to locate and save Luna the Jack Russell Terrier. Cobb also spoke to an expert with the breed to understand how Luna’s innate senses are helping her survive. One of the most improbable survival stories in recent memory has a happy ending. On Wednesday, October 14, officials in Yellowstone National Park successfully rescued a Jack Russell Terrier from California named Luna who had been missing in the park for more than a month. “We got her!” Katie Boucher, president of the Montana-based Norris Ark and Recovery Center, texted Outside. “We are on the way to the vet with her.” Boucher said the team was taking Luna to a veterinarian and that she would share more information later Wednesday. Details about how Luna was captured and her condition were not immediately available. For the last month, Boucher and others have been tracking Luna in the park. The ten-year-old Jack Russell Terrier went missing on September 10 after she bolted from the cabin where her family was staying. According to SFGATE, Luna escaped the cabin after a housekeeper opened the cabin door. Since then, Luna has stayed alive in the park, and multiple people have seen her near lodges and cabins in the park. Boucher told Outside that an eyewitness spotted her on October 13, and that the dog appeared healthy and without any injuries. Luna was found on the morning of October 14 snoozing peacefully inside a small doghouse that rescuers had placed inside an apparatus called a Missy Trap, which humanely captures dogs and other animals by luring them into a cage. Boucher’s team placed the trap near the Canyon Village water treatment center. Prior to a storm hitting the Yellowstone area on October 11-12, Boucher had removed the remote-trigger equipment that allows rescuers to close the trap from a distance, leaving the enclosure open. She then placed a small doghouse filled with grass inside, hoping Luna might use it as shelter while the storm passed. On October 13, a volunteer had spotted Luna circling the trap and lying down nearby. When Boucher returned on October 14 morning, Luna had moved in. “She was sleeping in the doghouse waiting for us,” Boucher told Outside. One of Luna’s owners returned to Yellowstone and accompanied Boucher to the trap that morning. Boucher sent the owner to the trap first. She then approached the trap. “When I walked down there, she was just barely sticking her nose out of the doghouse and just thinking about coming out,” Boucher said.“They had their own private reunification and it’s been absolutely brilliant.” Luna was then driven to a veterinarian in Bozeman. Boucher said she had lost around ten pounds during the 34 days she spent in the wild. Luna’s demeanor was certainly encouraging, Boucher added. “She is in really bright spirits,” Boucher said. “She’s very, very happy to see her mama.” Boucher described Wednesday as “a very emotional day” for Luna’s owners. The recovery was emotional for Boucher, too. She said she cried during the drive from Yellowstone to Bozeman. “This never gets old,” she added. “Being able to successfully reunify a pet with their family that loves them, and this is why I do this work.” Boucher said that her agency’s mission to rescue Luna required more effort than simply leaving out a bowl of kibble and hoping for the best. The National Park Service granted Norris Ark special permission and a trapping permit for its recovery effort, while construction crews working inside Yellowstone have allowed the team into restricted areas that are normally closed to visitors and, in some cases, other workers. Before she became a house dog, Luna spent roughly the first year of her life surviving on the streets of California before she was picked up by the SPCA, according to Boucher. Boucher believes some of the survival skills Luna developed as a stray have resurfaced in Yellowstone. Luna knows how to hide, find food and keep herself away from things she perceives as dangerous. “She does not need people and she knows it,” Boucher said. Luna survived for weeks in a landscape full of cold nights, scarce food and predators, and has repeatedly turned up around buildings and parking lots. Alison Cook Cilliers, a longtime breeder who runs Kimberlite Jack Russell Terriers in California, said that Luna’s survival story is indicative of the breed’s traits. “They work independently of us,” Cilliers told Outside. “They are very tenacious, and they really don’t want to give up.” Jack Russell Terriers were originally bred to hunt underground, chasing animals into dens where handlers couldn’t reach them, Cilliers said. Without a person there to give directions, the dogs had to figure things out on their own. That history left the breed with strong hunting instincts, high persistence and a notable independent streak. Outside previously spoke with Cilliers about Finney, a Jack Russell terrier who in 2024 survived 72 days in the Colorado mountains after his owner died on a hike. But Cilliers sees an important difference between Finney and Luna. Finney remained with his owner after the accident, giving him what Cilliers described as a familiar “cornerstone” in an otherwise dangerous environment. Luna, on the other hand, lost her family almost immediately in a place she did not know. “With this little dog, she is very, very lost,” Cilliers said. This difference might explain why Luna evaded capture for so long, Cilliers said. Early efforts to call to or pursue a frightened dog can push it deeper into a survival response, Cilliers added. Once that happens, an approaching stranger may no longer register as someone offering help. “She’s in that mode of protecting herself and wanting to be safe,” Cilliers said. Norris Ark used a device called a Missy Trap, which is a large enclosure designed for recovering frightened or hard-to-catch animals. Rather than relying on a pressure plate that shuts the door automatically, the version authorized for Luna’s recovery uses a remote trigger, allowing someone watching from a distance to decide exactly when to close it. The National Park Service issued Norris Ark a special trapping permit specifically for the Missy Trap and its remote trigger, Boucher said. The people who developed the trap have also been consulting with the recovery team throughout the effort, sometimes several times a day. Boucher said Yellowstone has required a level of coordination her group does not normally encounter. She described it as an “urban wilderness environment,” where a recovery effort has to contend simultaneously with wildlife, weather, tourists, roads, seasonal closures, contractors and federal rules. Some of those rules also help explain why Luna’s owners are no longer in the park. Luna’s family remained in the Yellowstone area until Sept. 22, Boucher said, but had trouble finding somewhere they could legally stay as lodging filled up and seasonal accommodations began closing. Yellowstone does not allow visitors to simply sleep overnight in a vehicle or camp outside designated areas. Outside reached out to Luna’s owners for this story, but they declined to comment. Boucher said they left reluctantly and contacted her as soon as sightings began coming in after their departure. Norris Ark’s permits for the operation were set to expire on October 31, making the hunt for Luna a race against the clock. Rescuers were also trying to battle Mother Nature. A storm dumped a light dusting of snow on parts of Yellowstone in recent days. And weather was set to become colder in late October. “She’s a California dog. She’s never seen snow before,” Boucher said. But now rescuers no longer have to worry about the chilly temperatures. This is a developing story and Outside will update it with details of the rescue.

item.title: All Your Haunted Attractions Questions, Answered by Someone Who Designed Them for 15 Years
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
A manager overview station at one of the haunts. Systems like this help teams manage guest flow and ensure staff safety. (Kingsville, Ontario). (Photo: Courtesy Angelica Haggert) I’ve never been through a haunted house. The scariest movie I’ve ever watched is The Ring from 2002. I do enjoy a good thriller novel, but I’m quick to scream when someone appears around a corner too quickly. You might think that’s pretty normal—except that every October my friends and family know I disappear into haunt season to run spooky experiences for scare-lovers. I’ve worked in haunts that run through greenhouses, shipping containers, actual corn mazes, forests, and fields. Each one is different, but the goal is always the same: to bring guests into a different world, just for a little while. It’s been a decade (plus) since someone first asked me to manage a haunted experience, and I’m still doing it, having carved a niche out in a small industry full of weirdos like me. I’ve managed hundreds of haunt staff and watched thousands of guests scream and then laugh at themselves. I’ve painted dozens of tombstones, lost too many pairs of pants to fake blood spills to count, and spent a lot of time in strobe lights. Here’s what I’ve learned along the way and the most common questions I get, answered. How do you design the scariest ones? Are there storylines to the haunts, and if so, who writes them? When people ask us this as they enter or exit, my quick answer is that usually I don’t sleep much, or I have a lot of nightmares. While both those things are true, it’s actually from thinking about what’s classically scary—and using that theme to inspire a cohesive story. Yes, the best haunts have storylines! You might not engage with the whole tale, or even catch that parts of it exist, but a more cohesive experience comes from a narrative. From character names (even though they never introduce themselves) to easter eggs in scenes or sets, we use the storyline to pull guests into the peaks and valleys that come with being terrified. I’ve worked at three different outdoor haunts, all with completely different styles of collaboration when it comes to how the stories are written. In my current haunt, we discuss themes and stories as a small group of four, and then the actual characters and scenes are written and designed by our lead storyteller. How does a haunt being outdoors play a role in how it operates? Being outdoors adds a lot of complexity to the behind-the-scenes operations—we have to account for weather (yes, we run rain or shine or snow!), we get to take real fields, trees, and raccoon pals into account, and our actors might need to wear a lot of layers to stay warm. In my current haunt, we also have to handle getting power to our props, lights, and sound systems. We usually do this with car batteries or banked solar power connections. From a guest perspective, being outdoors adds a level of “creep” that I don’t think can be truly replicated indoors. Are those shadows being cast by the real wind through the trees, or is there someone lurking there? Is that noise in the field a raccoon, or a zombie waiting to pop out and scare you? While it’s certainly more challenging, I’ve been “Team Outside” for more than a decade—I wouldn’t want to run an indoor haunt! How long does it take the average performer to get into costume and makeup? The perception that makeup has to be intricate for haunt actors is actually a misconception. Remember, most haunts take place in near-darkness, so fine details on makeup won’t show up well. The best haunt makeup I’ve seen uses dark smudges to portray dirt or dishevelment, or spots of fake blood highlighted to really bring an actor’s features into the story. On average, I’d say it’s maybe a 15-minute job to get makeup-ready. For us, our actors might also need multiple layers to stay warm, rain gear to stay somewhat dry, boots for the dirt and mud paths in the spaces we use, or even hats and gloves! Being outside means the costume doesn’t matter nearly as much as how an actor can make you feel when you interact with them. How scripted is everything? If you’re familiar with theater at all, haunt acting is like performing the same show every 12 minutes for 4 hours, to an entirely new audience every time. Plus, the audience might be cold, obnoxious, scared, intoxicated, and overwhelmed (some of those things are the goal!). Because the interaction with the people in front of you can be different from group to group, or because you’re only interacting with them for anywhere from 30 seconds to 5 minutes, we rely heavily on suggestive scripting rather than set dialogue. Actors might be given key words to share or use, like “They’re coming …” or “Can you see him?” rather than a direct line to include. What are the rules around actor-visitor interaction? Like, can they touch you? This will depend on your region, but where I work in Ontario, Canada, our actors can’t touch the guests. I actually tell my teams to make sure they stay “punching distance away” from the customers—when people are scared, they might react chaotically, and we don’t want anyone to get hurt. There are some haunts that rely on touch scares, but you can do so much more to be scary without actually touching someone. For our guests, we ask visitors not to touch our actors. I’ve been with some haunts that encourage filming, and some that don’t, so cell phone use varies. It’s the same with flashlight use. Wherever you go, follow the instructions given to you before you enter the experience. Where do you manage from while the haunt is in action? One of my favorite set-ups was a haunt made from a series of shipping containers. One container was designed like a master control—night vision security cameras, override triggers for lights and sound—it was a good way to puppeteer the magic that happens. Oftentimes I manage from hidden staff “hallways,” tucked behind hay bales or strategically placed fences, or from corners in the shadows. Guests almost never see me, but the actors know I’m always watching! Do they remove the chains from chainsaws? Always! At least in Ontario, this is a must. Who doesn’t love a good chainsaw scare? You don’t need the actual chains to make the terrifying noise; it’s all about how the actor handles the chainsaw, using it to be threatening and loud while still being safe. The same logic applies to anything you might see like machetes, axes, or pipes: while they might be real, they would typically have dulled blades or be used by well-trained actors who make sure our guests could never come into real harm. Have you ever snuck in a stint as a performer? Heck no! I’m a stage manager and storyteller, not a performer. In ten years, I’ve only been caught “on stage” a handful of times and typically just played dead or pulled all my hair down in front of my face and groaned. Do you have different versions for audiences of different ages? Most haunts are short-term setups, with limited resources. We need dozens of actors to really do a great job, and because of that speed-show mindset (remember, every 12 minutes!), we’re limited in how much we can expect a team to adjust to a younger audience. It would also be next to impossible to change our lighting, sets, or special effects to be less scary. Amusement parks have started to use a “don’t scare me” light-up wand or necklace to give the actors an indication to bring down the intensity level, but this can make it very challenging for mixed groups or for less experienced actors to adjust to in the moment. I have, however, seen some success in operating a few pre-opening time slots, where it might be daylight and without actors, so the scaredy-cats could venture through and enjoy the scenes, lights, and effects. Do you ever have to stop a haunt because someone gets too scared? Is there a protocol to escort people “to safety?” I’ve (knock on wood) never had to stop a haunt outright for safety purposes, but I have had to escort folks out for any number of reasons. Either they got too scared, or they were too unruly and our team asked us to remove them. I’ve also “followed” a lot of groups through haunts, as a sort of warning level before removing them from the experience outright. When people get too scared—we’re talking full panic attacks, meltdowns, or frozen-in-fear reactions—I’ve always trained actors to stop their scare immediately. They know to go from “Zombie One” to “Joe” quickly, remove all indications of threat or fear, and introduce themselves as a real person. This helps the terrified customer know that they’re in a safe place. Teams will typically then radio for assistance, and I get the fun job of calming folks down and making them laugh as I walk them back to the real world. Sometimes this walk back is just as terrifying for the customer, since we’re still outdoors in the haunt environment. Why won’t you visit haunts for fun yourself? I’m too terrified! I love the immersive experience a haunt brings, but I hate being startled or scared. It’s a running joke that my teams know not to spook me when I’m out in the experience checking on them. Happy haunt season, everyone! Go find a spooky spot near you and do what I’m too afraid to do … get scared!

item.title: Can Your Dead-Hang Time Really Tell You How Long You’ll Live? A Longevity Doctor Weighs In.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Somewhere right now, someone hangs from a pull-up bar in their garage, red-faced, breath held, forearms trembling, while a phone propped against a water bottle counts the seconds. When they finally drop to the ground, they post their time on Instagram with a caption implying they just bought themselves another decade of life by completing a dead hang. The dead hang challenge has been circulating on social media, and some people claim the workout is tied to longevity. The dead hang’s popularity skyrocketed after its appearance on an episode of the Mel Robbins Podcast. In the episode, a doctor said the main benefit is better grip strength, which they linked to improved cardiovascular and cognitive health. The goal? Hang for one or two minutes. As a board-certified internal medicine physician who specializes in longevity, I can see the appeal. The challenge costs nothing. You can do it at a playground jungle gym, and it gives you a number you can track. The trouble may be how social media assigns value to that number. The longevity claim borrows credibility from grip strength research, and that evidence is substantial. In a 2015 Lancet study, researchers followed nearly 140,000 adults across 17 countries and found that every 11-pound drop in grip strength was associated with a 16 percent higher risk of death from any cause. In a 2018 British Medical Journal analysis of roughly half a million participants, lower grip strength was linked to higher rates of cardiovascular disease, respiratory disease, and several cancers. Those studies used a handgrip dynamometer, a device you squeeze as hard as you can for a few seconds to register peak force. A dead hang is a far more complex measurement. It tests how long you can hold your body weight, bringing body mass, forearm endurance, shoulder function, technique, and practice into play. “Unlike a maximal strength test, a dead hang requires an individual to maintain force over time,” Prashan Anbalagan, an exercise physiology researcher at the University of Western Australia and the National University of Singapore, told me. Gravity doesn’t grade on effort, apparently. A strong person carrying more mass may drop off the bar before a lighter person with weaker hands. Anbalagan cites a 2025 training study in which hang times improved across all groups, while maximal grip strength improved less consistently. The finding suggests that the dead hang test and maximal strength test track different qualities. In other words, hang time measures sustained upper-body endurance relative to your weight, not grip strength itself. To date, no study has shown that hang time predicts mortality, so applying the grip data to the bar remains an assumption. Even the grip research describes an association. Grip partly stands in for overall strength: a 2018 meta-analysis of roughly 1.9 million adults found that leg strength also predicted lower mortality. Grip and leg tests often flag different people at risk, suggesting grip carries some independent information about muscle health. None of this shows that training your hands alone lowers your risk of disease or prolongs your life. Anbalagan cautions that a longer dead hang shouldn’t be read as better cardiorespiratory fitness, metabolic health, lower body strength, or balance. “These qualities require their own appropriate training stimuli,” he said. That doesn’t make dead hangs useless. Climbers have used hangboards for decades to build the forearm endurance and shoulder strength that hard routes demand. For the rest of us, sustained grip is a capacity that matters more with age: holding a railing on a slick staircase, catching yourself during a stumble, carrying a heavy bag up a flight of steps. As for a reasonable time, targets of one to two minutes circulate widely online, and they can serve as useful training goals, but no measurement of length has been validated as a longevity threshold. Anbalagan advised against testing yourself against a universal benchmark, since age, sex, body mass, and training history all shift results. To measure your grip strength, the number worth watching is your own. The key is to measure it the same way each time. Use the same bar, the same grip width, chalk or no chalk, and a fixed rule on whether regripping counts. If that number rises over a few months, you’ve improved your grip, which is a real and worthwhile result. I tell my patients to treat the dead hang bar as one tool among many, and to build it into a program that also includes aerobic work, leg strength, mobility, and balance training. According to Anbalagan, “The goal should be to develop physical capacities that support long-term health and everyday function, rather than relying on a single exercise to predict longevity.”

item.title: On this South Pacific island, there are no chains, no high-rises, and no McDonalds. And the locals want to keep it that way
item.description:
Source: Adventure
With no building higher than the tallest coconut tree, the Cook Islands’ ‘Mana Tiaki’ spirit has made its people natural guardians of culture, land and sea. But can it stay true to its values while balancing tourism and hungry developers? Eating ika mata, the national dish of raw fish marinated in citrus and fresh coconut cream, at the Barefoot Bar of the Pacific Resort on Muri beach, I look out over the luminous, jewel-bright lagoon. It’s clear now why my sub-four-hour flight from Auckland to Rarotonga was full of returning New Zealanders. “We come every year,” the woman seated next to me said. “It’s like a second home to us.” With a mix of 15 volcanic islands and reef-fringed atolls, the idyllic South Pacific archipelago is the kind of paradise luxury developers fight to get a slice of—so how have they resisted overdevelopment? “It’s a mix of government policy and people power,” Cook Islands tourism trade manager Rachel Harris-Best tells me. “Nobody wants it.” We’re sitting at Trader Jacks, a popular Rarotongan beachside café in Avarua, the northerly capital of the archipelago. The neutral-colored waterfront Vaka Bar is so low-rise it blends in with the harbor, and its open-terraced restaurant offers panoramic ocean views. My attention shifts to a group of canoeists carrying their outrigger crafts onto the shimmering water. Hopping down onto the warm sand for a closer look, I wonder: How could such a pristine location be the commercial capital of the archipelago? The islands are grouped into low-lying coral atolls in the north and volcanic isles in the south. Roughly 1,864 miles (3,000 kilometers) from Auckland, Aotearoa/New Zealand, ‘Raro’ is just 20 miles (32 kilometers) in circumference, with one ring road circling its agricultural interior. With no traffic lights, and motorcycles the preferred form of transport, I don’t witness a single blaring horn or impatient tailgater—even when newly arrived tourists drive at a snail’s pace. And public transport is even more genteel—a simple roadside wave will halt one of the two buses that loop the island in opposite directions. It’s the notion of hereditary bloodlines, written into the 1965 Constitution, that’s the fundamental bedrock of Cook Island society. It’s the reason no foreigner can own anything outright—which has largely kept chains and franchises at bay. I start to grasp the essence of island life at the Arataki Organic Garden, a short drive from Trader Jacks, where I meet owner Mirella Mairi. It’s rooted in Mana Tiaki. Made up of tiaki (keeper or guardian) and mana (influence or power), this philosophy of sacred guardianship runs through everything, from cultural preservation to taking care of the environment. And that’s exactly what Mirella and her husband Katoa are doing. During the pandemic, the islands were largely cut off, with no tourism and widespread disruption of freight delivery. Islanders leant on their age-old practice of Tapora Kai Enua—sharing produce within the community. “It was then we thought we should make our own food cupboard,” Mirella tells me. From cuttings and planting free seedlings provided by the government, they’ve since created something extraordinary—a garden of Polynesian staples, including taro (root vegetable), ginger and coconut, where visitors can book a botanical walk to learn about biodiversity and regenerative farming. Tours start at the compost section. By breaking down specially grown nutrient-rich plants, Mirella and Katoa have no need for chemical fertilizers. “What’s important is feeding the soil, not the plant,” says Katoa. Bugs are sprayed with chili, fermented overnight in dishwashing liquid, as a homemade natural pesticide. Even mosquitoes aren’t blitzed by DEET. “In the past, we used to light small fires under trees to keep mosquitoes away,” recalls Mirella. I’m reminded of an earlier conversation with a young, island-born woman returning for the first time, whose most vivid childhood memory is the odor of burning leaves: “I knew I was home!” she’d said. It had struck me as strange to think fondly of smoke, but Mairi enlightens me. Burning fires is a wider part of maintaining the land that’s at the beating heart of Mana Tiaki— that you leave a place better than you found it. The Cook Islands have, like many Pacific islands, a complex history. Settled by Polynesians who navigated by sea and stars in vaka, (double-hulled canoes) around 800-1000 AD, the islands became a British protectorate about a century after Captain James Cook’s initial colonialist explorations in 1773. It wasn’t until 1965 that they became a self-governing island nation in free association with New Zealand—meaning islanders have New Zealand citizenship and assistance with education, health and finance. But the House of Ariki, a parliamentary council of hereditary Indigenous High Chiefs, continues to advise on matters surrounding customs, culture and land ownership. And it’s the notion of hereditary bloodlines, written into the 1965 Constitution, that’s the fundamental bedrock of Cook Island society. It’s the reason no foreigner can own anything outright—which has largely kept chains and franchises at bay. Elders insisted that generational succession be written into law—land is inherited by direct descendants—while non-islanders can only buy property on a 60-year lease. By popular demand, Airbnb is one global platform that has broken through. A lucrative way to rent out properties, many say it’s worth the small amount of profit leaked overseas, especially given all accommodation is islander-owned. Even the new five-star Grand Resort Rarotonga, on Arorangi Sunset Coast Beach on the westerly sunset coast, is a local business. I meet its CEO Brett Baudinet at the building site as they prepare to open in March 2027—Baudinet is a Davis Cup tennis player and a doubles record-holder, but that’s another story. Currently a hive of activity, we carefully make our way up the unfinished stairwell to see some of the show suites. There’s little doubt this is going to be the archipelago’s most luxurious offering. On my site tour though, it’s hard not to be skeptical about the ‘no building higher than a coconut tree’ assertion. “Well, let’s have a look, shall we?” says a smiling Baudinet. “You can see for yourself.” We head up to the fifth-floor rooftop. He’s right. Even here, we’re surrounded by taller palms, with the tree-clad hillside behind us and ‘Golden Mile beach’ out front. It’s impressive. Back down on the sand, looking up at the new structure, it strangely seems to fit into the environment. The government acknowledges that this includes balancing “economic growth interests, such as tourism, fishing and deep-sea mining, with conserving core biodiversity and natural assets.” And there are tensions. Baudinet explains that there are building height restrictions, but the tree measurement, for him, is more of a guiding philosophy “than a hard and fast rule”. Measuring trees is never going to be an exact science, of course. Similarly, the ‘no chain’ maxim isn’t strictly true either—luxury hotel brands have been wooing him with partnership and investment offers, but he made the decision to decline them and retain control. I also hear later of an infamous 1980s derelict government-sanctioned Sheraton resort in Vaimaanga, that despite being almost complete, never managed to open. Beset by political and financial obstacles, people whisper of mafia involvement and the archipelago’s near bankruptcy over the debt. Island Elder and knowledge holder, the renowned artist and master carver Mike Tavioni, adds to what I’ve heard elsewhere, with talk of “the curse”. Dating back to last century, it’s said that a long-held dispute over land rights had culminated in the murder of an islander by a European settler in 1911. A powerful hex, or makutu, was put on the land by the dead man’s daughter—and reignited by her descendant on the day the Sheraton developers broke ground. With 70 percent of the islands’ GDP tied up in tourism, it’s clear there’s a fine line to tread between the economy and conservation. In 2017, the Cook Islands announced the world’s largest marine park—Marae Moana—spread over 734,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) and designed to protect and conserve biodiversity and the ocean environment. But the government acknowledges that this includes balancing “economic growth interests, such as tourism, fishing and deep-sea mining, with conserving core biodiversity and natural assets.” And there are tensions. Like elsewhere in the the world, deals with US corporations to begin explorations into deep-sea-mining for fossil fuels and rare earth minerals have been met with local condemnation. Environmentalist and upcycle artist Sabine Janneck is one of those voices. Originally from Germany, she moved to the Cook Islands with her tourism dive business, but it was concerns about ethical practices on the reef that drew her into conservation. Now making items from plastic waste (think burst inflatables and car tyres), her CIRCLE Cook Islands luxury handbags are highly prized, with prices to match. As the Vice President of the Te Ipukarea Society, which translates as ‘our heritage’ and is the only non-government environmental group on the archipelago, she’s the very embodiment of Mana Tiaki, upholding island values as a papa’a, or foreigner. It’s clear that marine conservation is key to this South Pacific island nation—marae moana means sacred ocean, and it’s a fundamental principle of life on the archipelago. During the trip, I’d flown to the nearby island of Aitutaki to observe and swim with humpback whales where ‘Bubbles Below’ dive company owner and skipper Onu Hewett unpicks the dichotomy around the pressure to increase visitor numbers. “We have to be careful what we wish for.” As he watches his clients following whale-swim guide Chanaya Aukaha-Larsen in her Olympic-level pursuit of another humpback, he says he’d prefer year-round tourism, rather than even bigger numbers during the Australasian winter, from June to August. Back at the Grand Resort site, I ask Baudinet one last question before leaving. “Do you think there’ll ever be a McDonalds here?” He hesitates before replying. “Probably.” It’s not the answer I was expecting, especially when the thick-cut, purple taro and cassava ‘island fries’ here are the best chips I’ve ever eaten. Maybe he’s just being pragmatic—it’s a worldwide battle to hold back the tide of capitalism, after all. But this is one Eden nobody’s going to give up without a fight. The writer’s travels were supported by The Cook Islands Tourism Corporation—Te Mato Manava Turoto (CIT) Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Award-winning photographer and travel writer Nori Jemil lives between London and Perth, Australia. She writes for numerous publications including Rough Guides and National Geographic Traveller UK, teaches travel photography courses, and is the author of 'The Travel Photographer's Way', published by Bradt in 2021. item.title: Want to help Nepal recover from its deadly floods? Here’s what tourists need to know
item.description:
Source: Adventure
Our research following Cyclone Marcia in Queensland similarly found that trust and consistent communication between tourism organizations were critical to effective recovery. The objective is to manage the return of tourism in a way that supports affected communities, without putting visitors or residents at greater risk. People visiting friends and relatives in Nepal, or other tourists who have visited the country before, are the most likely to return earlier once Nepal is ready, due to their stronger personal ties and better knowledge of local conditions. The challenge for Nepal is not simply deciding when the country is âopenâ again. It is being clear about which specific places are ready for visitors to return, and when tourism will support Nepalese communitiesânot complicate their recovery. Travelers should also check their own governmentâs official travel advice, such as Australiaâs Smart Traveller, New Zealandâs Smart Travel and the United Statesâ State Department websites. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

item.title: Wisconsin’s Longest Trail Might Be the Midwest’s Best Fall Thru-Hike
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Out-of-state visitors travel to Wisconsin for many things—the cheese, beer, football, fishing—but rarely for hiking. And yet, winding through the Badger State is one of the Midwest’s longest hiking routes: a nearly 1,200-mile National Scenic Trail that crawls along glacial terrain, skirts peaceful lakes, and showcases some of the state’s most spectacular landscapes. It’s not the kind of trail that’s going to destroy your legs with vertical climbs or challenge you to cross inhospitable areas, but for hikers who want to cruise, crush miles, and get lost in the flow state of forest hiking, the Ice Age Trail (IAT) should be at the top of your list. In September, Backpacker’s editorial team traveled to Wisconsin to see for ourselves what all the IAT was about. We’d covered this trail previously.:Earlier this year, we interviewed Jamieson Hatt, who set the record for the longest unsupported hike ever on the IAT, covering 1,160 miles in 30 days. In 2025, writer Grayson Haver Currin wrote about everything he wished he’d known before thru-hiking it (tip: prepare for roadwalks), and fellow Triple Crowner Barney “Scout” Mann reported on how it stands out from the Big Three. However, none of our editors had ever set foot on the IAT. So we decided to change that. Backpacker couldn’t have hiked it at a better time. Not just because the deciduous forests were exploding with gold and vermillion fall colors, but because the temperatures were perfect, there were almost no bugs to contend with, and we saw very few other hikers along the way. The trail was all ours, and it had a lot to show us about Wisconsin. The IAT’s eastern terminus is in Potawatomi State Park in Sturgeon Bay. From there, it squiggles down the eastern side of the state into southern Wisconsin before turning north, skirting around Madison, and finally hooking west to the other terminus on the Minnesota border. While Wisconsin is just about 260 miles wide, the IAT covers nearly 1,200 miles. Twelve thousand years ago, this area looked very different. In fact, you wouldn’t have seen much of it because it was buried under massive sheets of glacial ice. Mammoths roamed the area, and the climate was more like Alaska’s is today. As the Earth warmed over the next several thousand years, the glaciers retreated, revealing the sculpted landscape that exists today. Those glaciogenic features are a hallmark of the IAT. We hiked along multiple eskers—long ridges that elevated us above the forest floor. We camped beside ancient glacial lakes, walked along moraines, explored dells (narrow river gorges with steep rock walls), and more. If you’re into glaciology, this trail is a kick. As Backpacker cruised along, it was fun to identify the features and talk about them as we went. Unfortunately, the Backpacker team only had time for a taste (for a full, detailed trip report, check out the story Mann wrote in 2025). Instead, we backpacked about 25 miles between Jerry Lake and Mondeaux Flowage. The forests were thick, and tree roots crisscrossed the loamy trail beneath our feet. Boardwalks traversed muddy areas and small creeks, and occasionally we’d pop out of the trees onto a dirt county road, offering a brief glimpse of uncanopied sky, before plunging back into the woods on the other side. We put down about 10 miles of hiking a day, with plenty of time for casual mornings and nights around a campfire. With its frequent road crossings, this trail is very accessible for day and section hikers, making it easy to plan sections based on how much time you have or the distance you want to cover. Some of the most popular sections are the Baraboo Segment (which is actually an urban path through the quaint town of Baraboo, WI), Mondeaux Esker Segment (which we hiked), Eagle Segment (which passes through prairies, over limestone outcroppings, and through thick oak forests), and the St. Croix Falls Segment (the western terminus of the trail, which offers views of the St. Croix River). Explore each individual section with the IAT Alliance’s Segment by Segment Tour page. Thru-hikers should expect the trail to take between seven and 12 weeks to complete. There are nearly 30 official “IAT communities” (recognized trail towns) along the way, which make resupplies and hotel breaks relatively easy to line up. Those communities are also opportunities to experience Wisconsin’s culture, taste its flavors, and meet its people. The IAT Alliance even has a story map detailing itineraries, local highlights, and places to explore for each community along the route. If you’re thru-hiking the IAT, be warned: The trail is still unfinished, and many sections follow roads for significant distances. Currently, about 700 miles are marked with the distinctive IAT yellow blazes. The remaining 500 miles linking those segments are unmarked, although IAT Alliance volunteers blaze 10 to 15 miles of new trail every year. It’s a good idea to download your maps or bring a hard copy. As we learned while hiking the IAT, it is easy to branch off in the wrong direction if you aren’t paying close attention. Check the IAT Trail Reports page for up-to-date information on closures, reroutes, and more. The IAT is open year-round. In the winter, it’s popular for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. For hiking, the optimal months are May to October. However, the best time for hiking is in the fall (September and October). The colors we witnessed as the maples, oaks, birches, and hardwoods settled into their fall palettes were mesmerizing. We caught the color change early, so the bright greens of summer were still mixed with the vibrant yellows, oranges, and reds of fall. There are also very few bugs on the trail this time of year. Everyone in our group exercised tick caution, but we didn’t have to worry about mosquitoes, horse flies, or wasps. September and October temperatures are also ideal. In the winter, Wisconsin gets cold, and unless you’re prepared for winter camping, overnight hiking trips are off the table. In the summer, temperatures rise into the 80s, and sometimes 90s, and the humidity can be brutal. The easy answer is Midwesterners who want to experience the region on foot, get closer to the landscape they live in and around, and dive deep into Wisconsin’s trail town culture. If you love the Midwest, this is one of the best trails to experience its natural beauty. The IAT is also a great long trail for beginner backpackers. The terrain is manageable, following clear, mostly level singletrack. Rolling hills and features like the eskers provide some elevation change. The access to IAT Communities along the way also makes this a good trail for beginner backpackers. Resupplies are easy; you can access wifi and download maps, get a hotel room, meet other humans, and generally break up the hike. Logistically, that makes planning a backpacking trip simple. By that same token, I think experienced thru-hikers and even FKT seekers could find that the IAT has a lot to offer. If you really want to crush miles and cruise through days, this is a great trail for that, assuming that the idea of a few hundred miles on roads isn’t enough to scare you off. The IAT might not be for everyone, but it has something for every type of hiker. I’m really glad I got to experience even a piece of it, and I know there’s much more to explore. Next time I travel to the Badger State, I’ll be bringing my backpack again.

item.title: The Vampire Trail
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
The wolf tracks cross the trail and disappear straight over the edge of the precipice. It makes no sense. We’re descending from the summit of Mt. Moldoveanu, at 8,346 feet, the highest peak in Romania. The trail, a stony, knife-edge arête with thousand-foot drops on both sides, runs along the spine of the Transylvanian Alps. Steep, grassy slopes with wooded ravines drop away to the south. To the north, just 3 feet from the muddy trail, sheer black cliffs plunge down into the mist. The wolf tracks—huge prints with claw marks dug deeply into the mud—come up from the south and go right over the edge, as if the wolf had simply leapt into the abyss, transforming itself into some kind of flying beast. Two hours earlier, at 3 p.m., we’d reached the Refugiul Vistea Mare, our original destination for the day. The hut was a tiny, red-and-white striped stone building. Other than a wall-to-wall sleeping platform and anti-communist graffiti, it was empty. At least it appeared cozier than the first trail shelter we’d stayed in—a corrugated metal hut that clanged in the wind all night long—but Martha, my hiking partner, wasn’t ready to stop. “It’s too early. We still have two hours of daylight.” It was mid-October, but the weather looked wintry. Bulbous clouds had rolled in over us, and it looked like it might snow. “We won’t make it to the next hut,” I said. “Then we’ll bivouac,” she responded brightly. “Could be uncomfortable.” “No, it will be fun!” “When was the last time you bivied high in the mountains, Martha?” She flashed me a big grin. “Never!” And that’s how we came to be standing on the rocky summit of Moldoveanu so late in the day. It was almost dusk, and the serrated crest of the Transylvanian Alps ripped the world in two distinct halves: light and dark. The southern flanks were bathed in gold, the northern walls shaded in Stygian black. The trail wove along the serpentine edge between the two. We signed the log book beneath the blue, yellow, and red striped flag of Romania and descended into a purpling haze. It’s twilight when I spot the wolf tracks. At first I think they must be dog tracks, but upon closer examination, I realize they couldn’t have been made by any animal other than a wolf. The tracks are too big, bigger than my fist, and single-tracked—the rear paws landing squarely in the prints of the front paws (dog tracks meander). For a few minutes, I stare down into the darkness of the north side, looking for movement. Nothing. We’re using our headlamps by the time we find a low stone windbreak. “Somebody bivied here,” I say, surprised to find a semi-flat space along the ridgecrest. “Perfect!” says Martha, too enthusiastically. We had gone light on this hut-to-hut, 62-mile traverse of the Transylvanian Alps, so we have neither tent nor stove. My sleeping bag, rated 35°F, is not much better than a blanket. Martha had wisely packed her 0°F bag. Nevertheless, we curl up on the ground and read Bram Stoker’s Dracula together, as we’ll do every night of the trip. Of course we do. How often does a world-class trek dovetail with the most successful horror novel ever written? It’s day two, and we’re still near the beginning of the book. Three of Dracula’s witches have already kidnapped a peasant infant for a blood feast. When we resume, the hysterical mother has come to Dracula’s castle and is tearing out her hair and beating her breasts. “‘Monster, give me my child!’” Count Dracula doesn’t answer. Instead, in his “harsh, metallic whisper,” he summons the wolves. “His call seemed to be answered from far and wide by the howling of wolves. Before many minutes had passed a pack of them poured, like a pent-up dam when liberated, through the wide entrance into the courtyard.” From the very beginning of Dracula, wolves are harbingers of evil. Every time they appear, we know something bad is about to happen. “There was no cry from the woman, and the howling of the wolves was but short. Before long they streamed away singly, licking their lips.” Originally published in 1897, Dracula capitalized on vampire mythology that pervaded Eastern Europe. It’s a sinister story told through the diaries of English men and women who hunt down “the Count,” a bloodthirsty, sun-fearing vampire hundreds of years old. Stoker’s book made such a cultural impact that it seems every adult in the Western hemisphere knows who Dracula is. The Transylvanian Alps traverse—unlike Dracula—is hardly known except among serious hikers in Eastern Europe. Nevertheless, the trail is well-marked with signs and painted boulders along the crest of the Făgăraş Mountains in the southern Carpathians. Doing research for the trip, we’d been warned repeatedly that the hike was difficult, with dangerous terrain and fast-changing alpine weather. Ill-prepared hikers can and do die in the Făgăraş. This admonition resurfaces during our bivy, when, at 4 a.m., it starts to snow. Graupel popcorns on our sleeping bags, and I leap to my feet. “We gotta go!” I shout. Martha, deeply ensconced in her fat sleeping bag with only a lock of hair showing, is fast asleep. I’m about to wake her when the storm abruptly passes. Feeling foolish, I reinsert myself into my damp, paper-thin bag and wait for daylight. In the morning, the trail is slippery, and we step cautiously along the cliff edge. In places it’s like walking atop the parapet of a castle, the stone walls dropping away beneath our feet. We glimpse Cabana Podragu far below us on the north side of the ridge. A dark stone hut beside a black lake, it looks to be a place that the sun never reaches. We had contacted the caretakers and been told that they were entirely booked for the night we would arrive. But peering down through the shadows, we can see there is no smoke from the chimney, no light inside, no sign of life. It is like a giant, rain-stained mausoleum. “Maybe that’s where the wolf was going,” I say in mock solemnity. “Looks like Dracula’s vacation home,” quips Martha. A couple hours farther along the trail—steep up and steep down, from one col to the next—we spot a less mythical Carpathian animal: chamois, a herd of five on the rock buttresses below us. They graze on the tall tufts of grass atop the stone towers. Carpathian chamois are distinctive, with a flicker of white on the hindquarters of their black bodies, a face half-white and half-black, and two narrow, curled black horns. Something spooks them, and they scatter instantly, leaping off the towers in different directions, bouncing off ledges and leaping again into space. If wildlife is a sign of wildness, Transylvania is home to one of Europe’s best-preserved ecosystems. The wolves are the most potent symbol: There could be as many as 2,500 of them in Romania—15 percent of Europe’s entire population, excluding Russia. The country is also home to the largest population of Eurasian brown bears—perhaps as many as 5,000—and the Eurasian lynx, of which there might be 2,000. Large numbers of three ungulate species—roe deer, red deer, and wild boar—can also be found here, and are the primary prey for wolves. Wolves also occasionally kill livestock, especially lost sheep. Not surprisingly, just like in the Western U.S., local ranchers and farmers have an intense antipathy toward the wolf. (Since 1996, wolves have been protected here, with limited hunting.) The Eurasian wolf, Canis lupus lupus, is of moderate size, 75 to 130 pounds, and once ranged over millions of square miles. Wolves were commonplace in Europe from antiquity through the Middle Ages and into the 19th century. To this day, the ensign of Transylvania is a wolf’s head, the snapping jaws wide open, with the body of a dragon. Stories of wolf attacks are part of the facts and folklore of Europe. Little Red Riding Hood, an ancient oral tale, was first published in France more than three centuries ago. Although healthy wolves rarely attack humans, rabid wolves were the horrific beasts of every hearthside story, with good reason. In France in 1739, a rabid wolf bit 70 people, 50 of whom died. In 1766, a rabid wolf bit 23 people in the forests around Warsaw, and all died of rabies. In 1852, a rabid wolf bit 135 people in Turkey and killed 85 sheep. There’s no definitive proof that vampire mythology originated with rabid wolves, but the links are hard to ignore. Dracula, per Stoker’s description, has hair on his palms, long, claw-like fingernails, and sharp fangs. Humans infected with rabies display monster-like behavior—snarling, biting, hyperactive sexual appetites, delirium, and an aversion to light and water. Throughout Europe, as late as the 15th century, people who contracted rabies were put to death by strangulation, bloodletting, or suffocation. Rabies isn’t the only disease with a plausible connection to the vampire myth. Pellagra, a niacin and tryptophan deficiency attributed to a diet based exclusively on corn—the most common medieval crop—causes hypersensitivity to sunlight and a wasting and bleeding of the gums, which make the front teeth appear grotesquely prominent. Such scientific explanations offer a rational counterweight to the spooky factor—which is palpable here, even if you don’t get unnerved by ghost stories. Of course, reading Dracula every night doesn’t help. On the third night, in a lodge at Bâlea Lac, we’re at the part where Jonathan Harker, the book’s protagonist, is a prisoner in Dracula’s castle. One night, peering down from his cell in the tower, he witnesses the Count creeping out a window below him: “. . . I saw the whole man slowly emerge from the window and begin to crawl down the castle wall over the dreadful abyss, face down with his cloak spreading out around him like great wings . . . just as a lizard moves along a wall.” Back on the trail, we hike in heavy fog all day, reaching the summit of 8,317-foot Negoiu, the second-highest peak in Romania, around 3 p.m. Thunder booms all around us and lightning zigzags through black clouds. We have to get off the summit immediately. The trail sign says the next hut is five hours away, long past sunset if we were to go the standard pace. Thus far, we’ve been cavalier in our approach to stated distances and times because nothing has been as challenging as we’d been told. But now, if we can’t cut the posted time in half, we are setting ourselves up for another bivy—this time in cold rain. We march down the trail with intention. Within 10 minutes, thick mist has dropped our visibility to 10 feet, and the trail transforms into a Transylvanian via ferrata. Sharp rock towers with chains and cables bolted to their sheer walls loom out of the mist. Our progress recalls Dracula lizarding over his castle walls, as we move up and over one gendarme after another. The granite is wet and slippery. The heavy chains drip with ice water. Had we not both been rock climbers, the route would have been impossible in these slick conditions. As it is, we make it to Refugiul Scara—barely finding it in the fog—in two hours flat. Refugiul Scara is mostly an empty shack that feels as if it were abandoned years ago. However, we do find a half-full bottle of Cava D’Oro tequila and help ourselves while reading Dracula out loud. We’re at the end of the book now. Dr. Van Helsing, in order to save the soul of vampire-bitten Madam Mina—“so radiantly beautiful”—must pound a wooden stake through her heart. In this detail, Stoker’s book also echoes historical fact. Between 1448 and 1476, Vladislav Dracula reigned over Transylvania. Often fighting enemies with much larger armies than his, Dracula resorted to terror: All prisoners, as well as the peasants in conquered villages, were impaled on stakes. According to one account, Vlad the Impaler, as he was known, “invented frightening, terrible, unheard-of tortures.” A 1499 German woodcut shows Dracula dining al fresco, surrounded by a forest of impaled corpses. Neither of us takes the threat of vampires seriously, of course, but Martha still makes me stack stones against the rattling metal door. The next morning, the mountains are still socked in. It’s so misty we feel lucky for the trail markers painted on the rocks under our feet. We quickly cross up and over two small cols, and start dropping north, down out of the alpine. Just above treeline we find black bear scat on the trail—large chunks filled with undigested berries. “I wish we’d seen a bear,” I say, “or a wolf.” “Or a vampire,” says Martha with a smirk. We’ve both enjoyed the way fiction and history have combined to enhance our walk. There’s always an element of the unknown in the wild, and the mythology heightens that feeling here. We plunge back down into the pines, then further down into deciduous forests, brown and yellow maple leaves carpeting the trail. In just a few hours, we reach Cabana Suru, tucked into the deep green woods like a cottage for elves. It’s the last hut on our hike and the only one that has a host. Before the trip, we had called the proprietress, Ioana Popa, who told us that they were planning to close for the winter, but would stay open one more weekend just for us. Cabana Suru is the kind of quaint hut you might find in the Italian Alps—thick walls to withstand heavy snows, slippers at the front door, wooden benches along wooden tables, a wood stove at one end of the room, and bunk beds on the second floor. We arrive soaked to the bone, and Popa ushers us directly to two stools beside the black stove and puts cups of tea into our rigid hands. When we finally warm up, we hang up our wet clothes and trade hot tea for cold Ursus beer. That evening four Romanian hikers—one of only two parties we meet on the trail—arrive for the night and share their homemade cherry liqueur. We pass around the plastic bottle and swap stories. They were just out for the day, hoping to spot a wolf or bear, but the rain shut them down. For dinner, we feast on steaming bowls of Romanian goulash. The bunkrooms are so warm we have to open all the windows. We fall asleep to the sound of soft rain on the metal roof. In the morning, the Romanians are already gone. Ioana is in high spirits and serves us plate-sized omelettes that we cannot finish. Her English is perfect, so we ask her about Dracula and vampires. She laughs. “That stuff is all for the American tourists. Dracula means nothing to Romanians. Real hikers come here for the mountains, not the myth.” She tells us that the tourist board has now even designated a random castle as Dracula’s castle, just to trap visitors. I’m not disappointed. Reading Dracula added a fun dimension to the hike, but the big payoff here is hiking an alpine ridgeline for days, with views in all directions. Plus Europe’s wildest wildlife, as Ioana reminds me. “We have bears and wolves here,” she says proudly. “I’ve seen them with my own eyes! Who needs vampires?” World Explorer Mark Jenkins wrote about trekking the Ifugao Rice Terraces in the Philippines in January 2018 TRIP PLANNER Season June to October Maps Fagaras 135,000 and 175,000 Guidebook The Mountains of Romania: A Guide to the Carpathians, by James Roberts, Cicerone Press Huts None of the rustic huts have caretakers or food except Cabana Suru; Bâlea Lac’s lodge requires a detour and is more luxe. Water In autumn, water can be difficult to obtain and often requires dropping down off the crest. Route The traverse can be done east to west or vice versa, but either way, getting to the trailheads on either end requires hiring a car or hitchhiking with local loggers for about 10 miles. Guide Florin-George Bana Outdoor Shop ProAlpin in Brasov

item.title: The Enchantments Hike Guide (For First-Timers)
item.description:
Source: HikingGuy.com
The Enchantments Traverse is 19 miles of jaw-dropping beauty that feels like you are hiking through a postcard. But between climbing Aasgard Pass, the focus needed to navigate, and over 7,000 feet of knee-crushing descent, it’s much tougher than the stats let on. I’ve done the Enchantments 10 times over the years, both as a day hike and as an overnight trip with a nearly impossible-to-get permit. If it’s your first time doing the hike, here’s everything you need to know, including what I wish I’d known before my first trip. Here’s a video I made showing you exactly what the hike looks like and what to expect along the way. While you can technically just show up and do this as a day hike, you’re going to want to do some planning beforehand to not only get the most out of the hike, but also to stay safe. Which Direction? There are a few ways you can do the Enchantments, but the most popular route for first-timers is from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the Snow Lakes Trailhead (West to East). Here’s why: - There is about 2,000 feet less climbing when going in this direction. - Going up Aasgard Pass is tough, but going downhill on the loose slippery dirt there is worse. - It’s easy to get a hiker shuttle in this direction. - Even though it’s long, it’s doable as an all-day hike. So for this guide, we’ll be assuming West to East. Day Hike or Overnight? This is a popular hike. Permits limit the number of campers, but the trail can have hundreds of day hikers. Weekends, as you’d expect, are the worst times if you want solitude. On my last mid-September hike on a Tuesday, I counted 35 other people on the whole route. For 19 miles I don’t think that’s a big deal. When you cross paths with other hikers, remember that these are public lands. Every visitor has an equal right to be there, regardless of their experience level or whether they were inspired by social media. If you meet someone with less trail knowledge, choose to treat them with kindness and respect. Is It Worth It? If you research the route online or browse Reddit, you’ll inevitably stumble into debates about whether the Enchantments has been “ruined” by crowds, whether social media is destroying the outdoors, or if there are nicer, quieter alternatives. Tune that crap out. You can find these exact same arguments about any beautiful, popular natural space. If you haven’t done the Enchantments and it looks fun to you, do it. I think it’s worth the expense and hassle of doing at least once, especially if you can land an overnight permit. I have a non-hiker buddy who I drag around on various backpacking trips, the Olympics, Sierras, Mojave, all over the place. I took him here to do the day hike and he still refers to it as his favorite trip we’ve ever done. An AllTrails review I read perfectly sums up why: This hike is the most beautiful, incredible thing I have ever done. This hike is also the hardest thing I have ever done. AllTrails Reviewer The heart of this hike is exposed above 7,000 feet, through an alpine basin in the Cascades. It’s cold and holds the snow longer than the surrounding area. That makes the ideal season for doing your first hike here snow-free relatively short. Even if you have winter hiking experience, this is not the place to show up without local knowledge. Do it first without the snow, then find someone local to take you on the winter/snow routes. There have been multiple deaths here in icy shoulder seasons. A permit zone is an area where you camp. All permit zones have many dispersed backcountry camping sites and usually a toilet nearby. - Core Enchantment is the most beautiful area. It’s full of alpine lakes that feel like you’re camping in a postcard. - Colchuck is just below Aasgard Pass, offering beautiful lakeside camping. - Snow offers camping along lower altitude lakes and is still picturesque. - Stuart has camping along the first 2 miles of trail, alongside Mountaineer Creek. - Eightmile/Caroline isn’t on the Enchantments Traverse hike route. My favorite Core Zone areas to camp at are around Inspiration and Perfection Lakes. Later in the guide you’ll see what camping and the different areas look like, but here are my ideal itineraries based on how much time you can/want to spend in the Enchantments. - Figure out how much time you have to spend in the Enchantments. - Apply for the overnight permit lottery with your ideal timing. For me that’s 2-5 days in late August / early September. - If you get your overnight permit, you’re all set. - If you don’t get a permit, train for the day hike and do that. Try for an overnight next year. Overnight permits are some of the hardest to get in the USA, but day hike permits are free and just a formality. - You need a permit for overnights between May 15 and October 31. - Unlike the day hike permit, “demand for overnight permits far exceeds the number available” according to Recreation.gov. Based on public lottery data from the Forest Service, your chances of landing an overnight permit range between 1% and 12%. - You are only allowed one permit per season. - A Core Zone permit allows you to camp in any zone, but other zones only allow for camping in the respective zone. Obviously there are many factors, including luck, in deciding who wins or not, but based on an analysis of recent official Forest Service permit data, here are some tips on nabbing a spot, ranked from best odds to worst: For me the months are non-negotiable because it’s not a route you want to be slipping and sliding on, so I always go for late August and early September. But I’ll often try the days with better odds. I’ve only scored an overnight permit 3 times in 15 years of trying. Once you have your dates, figure out lodging and trailhead logistics. Leavenworth, WA is a cute Bavarian-styled tourist town. It’s got the basics like grocery stores, restaurants, and smaller shops. There are two small sporting goods stores in town if you need to pick up a last-minute piece of gear. It’s popular with tourists and can get busy during times like Oktoberfest. I’ve stayed in a different hotel every time I’ve visited, and they’ve all been decent. You can also find campsites and dispersed camping in the area. Have a dog? Dogs aren’t allowed on the Enchantments Traverse because they disturb the native ptarmigan. Let your dog live it up while you’re away at the pet lodge. The easiest way to do the point-to-point is to park at Snow Lakes Trailhead, hop on the regularly scheduled shuttles to Stuart Lake Trailhead, and then finish your hike back at your car. The shuttles can book out in advance, so I recommend booking the shuttle once you lock your permit and lodging in. Make sure you use the “Snow Lakes Trailhead” in Leavenworth, WA. There’s another “Snow Lake Trailhead” about 2 hours away. - If you can hike 15 miles with 4,000 feet of climbing, you should be ready for the Enchantments. - If you’re not at the level yet, start where you are and gradually build your climbing and mileage up every week until you get there. - Over the years I’ve found that my knees hurt way less on the descent when I do leg strength training. Work in squats and lunges to build up your leg muscles and descents aren’t so bad. If your fitness and preparedness levels do not meet the trail conditions, seek an alternate trail to recreate on. Chelan County Sheriff’s Office So what are appropriate “fitness and preparedness levels” in ideal conditions? A common sentiment I hear from day hikers is “the Enchantments is tougher than Mt. Whitney, but without the altitude,” and I agree.
