Plan on the Enchantments Traverse requiring more focus and energy than a standard hike or backpacking trip. - Even with a well-groomed and graded trail that you can cruise on, 19 miles and 5,000 feet of climbing is a tough day. - The Enchantments generally doesn’t have well-groomed and graded trails, stacking 10+ hours of intense focus onto those already daunting stats. - Much of the surface is covered in rocks, roots, and uneven ground, requiring care for every step. - About 15% of the trail is extremely steep climbing or descending, requiring a much slower pace, and sometimes butt sliding or hands on the ground. The steep downhills often take a toll on people’s knees. - There are many social trails, and finding the official trail requires a slower pace, checking for upcoming cairns (rock piles used for navigation), and sometimes cross-referencing with a GPS. - Some people with a fear of heights can find sections of the descent from Lake Viviane to Snow Lakes scary and emotionally draining, especially when slick. When you add up all the effort, it’s easy to be tired and make a mistake. For example, a misstep on the steep descent to Snow Lakes at mile 10 could mean a sprained ankle, and now the remaining 9 miles will take longer. Having an overnight permit means you can do shorter days and get more rest, but you also have to carry a heavier pack. I’ve canceled trips to Leavenworth when the conditions weren’t ideal. For me, if there is a solid chance of rain forecasted, I give this a skip. Temperate rain in Leavenworth usually means cold rain, sleet, or snow at higher altitudes, adding another challenge onto an already challenging day. And descending wet granite slabs isn’t a fun time for me. Aside from gauging the effort correctly, there are some other things to watch out for. - If you are going early in the season, expect snow. I strongly recommend waiting until August to do this as a first-timer. Snow on Aasgard and the Core Zone can hide weak snow bridges and avalanche zones that can result in death. - Don’t assume people ahead of you are in the right place on the trail. Rely on your GPS and the cairns before cross-referencing where the other group is. - Thunderstorms happen, and in the Core Zone there isn’t really any shelter. Luckily the basin is surrounded by high peaks, which are more probable targets for lightning. But it can really hit anywhere, so it’s just part of the deal. - September and October can bring big swings in temperature and early winter conditions. - This isn’t a high-altitude hike, but if you’re coming from sea level you may find yourself short of breath, especially on the Aasgard climb which gets close to 8,000 feet. Hard to say if it’s the altitude or effort though. - Be careful swimming in the (cold) lakes. In 2025 a hiker died in Colchuck Lake. For a day hike, give swimming a skip and focus on finishing. - Nearby fires can affect the air quality. Check conditions on WatchDuty.org and Firesmoke before heading out. If you’re in the area and can’t or don’t want to do the full Enchantments Traverse, use this guide to do the out-and-back hike to Colchuck Lake. That section of the trail is your standard PNW rocky and rooty trail under tree cover, but Colchuck Lake gives you a magical alpine experience. At Colchuck hang out for a bit, enjoy the amazing views, and then simply hike back down to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. Having the right gear can help keep you safe, but it’s not a substitute for good judgement. Here’s what I bring and why. - Headlamp - You’ll likely start before sunrise, and you may finish after sunset, so a headlamp with a battery backup is a must. Don’t rely on the flashlight on your phone. - Extra Layers - It’s often much cooler in the Core Zone than at the trailhead. I bring a long-sleeve top, convertible pants where I can hike in shorts and put the bottoms on as needed, a rain jacket and pants, gloves, and a beanie. If conditions change, you need to be prepared. - Water Filter - I use a 1L bottle and a 2L bag and filter that I can scoop water up with and filter right into the bottle. When I stop to filter I’ll usually drink 0.5 liters right away (camel up), then just carry 1L with me. There are lots of water refill spots along the route. - Food & Gels - I usually have trouble eating when I’m doing longer days at altitude, and gels and bars are easier to get down. I’ll try to eat breakfast before the start, then fuel up at Colchuck, the top of Aasgard, and again at Lake Viviane before the descent. Gels give me the extra boost in places like Aasgard. - Long Pants - It’s easy to scrape your legs on the granite scrambles, and pants give you some protection. - Multiple Navigation Tools - I find the best system is to have your track loaded onto a GPS watch that you can glance at as you go. If you don’t have a watch, make sure you have the route on a phone (with a battery backup). I carry both just in case. I also have a paper map from National Geographic that has trail segment distances on it. - Trekking Poles - Because there’s lots of loose dirt when climbing and descending, poles are crucial on this hike. If you don’t have poles, plan on more butt sliding and crawling with your hands. - Trail Runners - I use trail runners with good grip for the granite. Trail runners are the most comfortable option for this long day. - Satellite Communicator - Don’t rely on cell phone coverage. I bring a dedicated satellite communicator (Garmin inReach), which has a battery that lasts days and can be used for SOS and non-emergency messages. The last time I did this hike I was running late and simply messaged my family so they didn’t have to worry about me. - Gallon Ziploc Bag - This is key for carrying out my trash like sticky energy gel and food wrappers, and maybe picking up trash you may see along the way. - Full Hiking Essentials - I carry the things needed to not only stay comfortable but also light emergency gear to stay overnight if things don’t go as planned. Overall it may seem like a lot, but it should be under 10 lbs if you pack light. The less weight you carry the happier you will be. If I’m hiking earlier than August, there’s generally more moisture on the lower slopes and lingering snow in the Core Zone. - Bug Spray & Headnet - Mosquitoes and flies can be intense on the lower-altitude portions of the hike. - Microspikes - Snow can linger late into the season, but I’m usually safe leaving these home in August. Earlier in the season I carry them just in case. You may also need to scoop and melt snow to filter and drink, but there’s usually water flowing somewhere, even if the lakes are frozen. You can see all the overnight gear that I recommend here, but these are some specifics for the Enchantments. - Bathroom Kit - Bring toilet paper and hand sanitizer, and pack it out in the Ziploc bag that I mentioned earlier. - Camping Stove - There are no campfires in the Enchantments, so bring a stove and canister. If you are flying and can’t bring fuel, you can get canisters in town. - Bear Canister - While it’s not required to use a bear canister, I use one anyway because it does the job. Rodents are probably the biggest hassle with food. Seeing bears is rare on this hike, but they are here, and I’ve seen a tent site pillaged by a black bear at Nada Lake. If you have an Ursack and want to save weight, I think that works well too. - Warm Sleeping Bag - Check the conditions for your trip (see below) but usually a 20°F to 30°F sleeping bag does the trick for an in-season overnight. - Tent Stakes - It can get very windy in the Core Zone, so make sure your tent is sturdy and staked out properly. 18, 19, or 20+ Miles? I’ve seen reported distances from 18 miles to well over 20. After looking at all my tracks over the years, the actual route clocks out to approximately 19 miles. But doing things like visiting a viewpoint or lake, or maybe taking the wrong trail and then backtracking, etc. will nudge the mileage up toward 20. It’s important to get an idea of where you should be, and when, for this long hike. This table takes your pace and builds a timetable with gut-check points and directions along the way. If you’re running late, there aren’t bailout points, so it just means you’ll likely finish later than planned, maybe in the dark. - Pace - Pick your average total pace for hilly hikes, complete with ascent, descent, and the normal breaks you take. The chart will adjust your average pace based on the terrain. - Aasgard Pass - Can be a wildcard because it’s steep and challenging to navigate. Most people take 1.5-2.5 hours to climb it, but it can take longer, especially with a full backpacking kit. - Aasgard Break - It’s fairly normal to stop at the top, have a snack, refill your water, and regroup. Don’t linger too long or you could start getting stiff. - Turnaround Check - If you get to Colchuck Lake way behind schedule, the full Enchantments Traverse is probably not a smart move this time. Since going down Aasgard can be sketchy, make Colchuck Lake your gut check turnaround point. If you shuttled up to Stuart Lake, it shouldn’t be hard to hitch a ride from the trailhead back to Snow Lakes. - Daylight - Check the sunrise and sunset times against your timetable. You’ll want to see as much as possible during the day, but doing the first stretch to Colchuck Lake in the dark isn’t a big deal, you won’t miss much. Summer days are plenty long at this higher latitude. Colchuck means “Cold Lake” in a language called Chinook Jargon, a mashup dating back to 1790 of several Indigenous PNW languages, English, and French, used by Indigenous peoples and Europeans to communicate. The Chinook didn’t actually live here; the local tribe was the Wenatchi. Fuel up at the viewpoint for the next couple of miles over the boulders and up Aasgard. Here is the navigation workflow I find easiest. - Know your general direction of travel from the map above. - Look ahead to the next cairn. - Look down to find the most trodden path to the next cairn. - If you can’t see the path or next cairn, consult your GPS and see where the track goes. You’ll use that same method of navigation for the next several miles, until you reach the lower slopes closer to Snow Lakes. For Aasgard specifically: - Expect this to take between 1.5-2.5 hours for most people. - The dirt can be loose on the steep slopes; anchor your foot into solid rocks lodged in the ground. - Trekking poles are very helpful here. - It’s a north-facing gully, so it can be shaded when hot but also hold snow and ice longer than usual. - If you knock a rock loose and it starts to tumble down, yell “rock!” to warn anyone below. - After going left of the larch grove, there are a few false summits. I have a waypoint in my GPX called “climb over” letting you know when the pass is truly done. - I wouldn’t call the climb scary, but it is steep. If you have a problem with heights, stay focused forward until you reach a spot with a flat rock where you can rest and enjoy the views. Aasgard or Colchuck Pass? The official name here is the Colchuck Pass, and you’ll see that on USGS maps. Aasgard is a term from Norse mythology loosely meaning “the place where the gods live,” and was given this name (unofficially) by local climbers Bill and Peggy Stark in the 1950s. At the top of Aasgard Pass you’re not halfway, but rather about a third of the way through the entire hike. This is a good place to fuel up for the rest of the Core Zone. If there’s still snow in this section, be extra careful when crossing snow patches, which could be snow bridges across lake outlets. Are There Fish in the Lakes? Yes! The lakes have been stocked for roughly the last 100 years with trout. I’ve seen golden and cutthroat trout in the clear waters many times. If you want to fish, you’ll need to pick up a license. Now we start a stretch which has some of the sketchiest sections of trail. Please be advised: the trail between the Core Enchantments and Upper Snow Lake is a primitive route marked with rock cairns. It’s hard to navigate, challenging, and is recommended only for experienced hikers. Wenatchee River Ranger District What's the Deal With the Water? In the 1930s the Bureau of Reclamation dammed Nada and Snow Lakes to supply water to the fish hatchery in Leavenworth. As part of that they built a tunnel from Upper Snow Lake to the cliffs above Nada Lake to release the water. Every summer they turn the valve on creating the plume you see today. The Bureau of Reclamation also built the trail that you’ll use to get back to the start. Make sure you have enough water for the descent by filling here. There are some spots to fill from Snow Creek on the descent, but this is the easiest option. The last 5.5 miles or so aren’t tricky, but really for most people just a formality to wrap up. It’s a long 3,600 feet of descending on numerous switchbacks and straight trails. There are two small talus fields to cross, but other than that you should be able to just grind out the miles here. Was this helpful? If so, please do me a solid and send this guide to anyone you know who’s planning the Enchantments. And if you see someone asking about the hike on Reddit or social media, share it there too. I appreciate it and I’m sure it will help keep others safe.

item.title: The Next ‘It’ Apple Might Be 300 Years Old
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine
Esopus Spitzenburg, Cornish Gilliflower, Hubbardston Nonesuch: Antique varieties, with names recalling Dickensian villains, are packed with fresh flavor and texture. Honeycrisps get a lot of hype. But have you ever sunk your teeth into a coconutty Roxbury Russet? Or a champagne-tart Ashmead’s Kernel? Snow White’s apple may have been crimson and comely, but these days some of the most exciting varieties in American orchards are old, odd and decidedly unpolished. Their names have the ring of Dickensian villains — Esopus Spitzenburg, Cornish Gilliflower, Fearns Pippin, Hubbardston Nonesuch — and their flavors vary from honeyed sweetness to dark clove spice. Recipes: Slow-Cooker Applesauce | Apple Amaro Spritz For history buffs, heirloom apples represent a link to centuries of human lore. For curious cooks, they’re worth seeking out during their fleeting seasons for textures, subtle flavors and creative uses that far outmatch the usual options you encounter at the grocery store. At the turn of the 20th century, the United States Department of Agriculture cataloged an estimated 14,000 apple varieties grown domestically in the previous 100 years. Nowadays, according to the industry group USApple, just five — Gala, Red Delicious, Honeycrisp, Granny Smith and Fuji — typically account for more than 60 percent of U.S. production. Buzzy “brand name” apples, like Cosmic Crisp and Pink Lady, are strictly licensed, patented and trademarked, making them inaccessible to many growers. Heirloom apples, on the other hand, remain open source — and thanks to the work of a network of fruit detectives and pomologists, many once-forgotten varieties have begun making their way back into fields, markets and the public consciousness. For more than 50 years, pioneers like Tom Burford of Virginia, John Bunker in Maine and, more recently, David Benscoter in Washington State, have surveyed old property maps, aerial photos, deserted farms, vintage nursery catalogs, county fair records and more to ferret out and identify antique apples, and prevent them from disappearing. James Wargo, founder of Hidden Gem Orchard in Southbury, Conn., considers himself the beneficiary of that community’s efforts. “Because of the way apple trees are propagated, the connection to history with this fruit isn’t just a metaphor, it’s actually tangible,” he said. “You have to take a twig or bud and graft it onto a rootstock — so, in a real physical way, the trees we’re growing today trace back to the originals.” Founded in 2017 on a once-abandoned plot in western Connecticut, Hidden Gem opened for its first pick-your-own season in 2023. Among the antique apples currently on offer in its seven-acre orchard and farm stand are the Ashmead’s Kernel, a firm, golden 18th-century English variety with an outsize crunch and electric fizzy flavor, and the juicy Ribston Pippin, which does appear in a Dickens work (“The Pickwick Papers”) and was reputedly the foundation of one of the author’s favorite desserts, a Victorian baked confection of apples, marmalade and cream sherry called Apples à la Princesse. Next year, Mr. Wargo plans to have more heirlooms ready for harvest, including the Kandil Sinap, a petite, egg-shaped variety discovered near the Black Sea around 1800, and the Black Oxford, a 1700s specimen from Maine that stores well and whose deep purple skin lends homemade applesauce a striking tint. Customer enthusiasm has been strong, Mr. Wargo said: “Opening weekend, we did double the business as last year. I can’t tell you how many people come back and say, ‘I can’t eat grocery store apples anymore.’” For those who can’t make it to the farm stand before it closes in late November, he also offers limited-edition shipments of Hidden Gem’s heirlooms in partnership with White Flower Farm, a mail-order nursery. Genevieve Weston’s ancestors started growing apples in Waukesha County, Wis., nearly a century ago, when her great-grandfather planted his first 200 trees with the help of the Civilian Conservation Corps. Convinced that older varieties were generally of higher quality and had more taste and aroma than modern hybrids, the family decided early on to establish themselves as specialists in antique and heirloom fruit instead. She says that she and her brother, Bill Weston, now fourth-generation growers, see themselves largely as apple educators. Under the banner of Weston’s Antique Apples, Ms. Weston brings their fruit to farmers’ markets around the Milwaukee area each weekend in fall, starting with around 30 varieties in September and climbing to as many as 75 in October, with late-season stalwarts like Calville Blanc d’Hiver (the classic apple for tarte Tatin) closing out the harvest in November. To simplify shopping, they offer samples and arrange crates according to profiles like “sweet,” “tart for eating” and “tart for baking.” Still, Ms. Weston is quick to add, even within those categories, people are shocked by the diversity. “If there’s one thing I hear over and over,” she said, “it’s, ‘I didn’t realize apples had so many flavors to them.’” Unfortunately, though many antique apples ace the taste test, getting customers who’ve been reared on pristine red orbs past their homely looks sometimes takes more convincing. To the uninitiated, naturally mottled skin and russeted textures can be mistaken for blemish or blight, said Erin Robinson, orchard manager of Scott Farm Orchard, which grows more than 130 varieties of heirloom apples outside Brattleboro, Vt., and ships gift boxes throughout the country. Consider the Knobbed Russet, a rare British heirloom. “My son says it tastes like banana bread,” Ms. Robinson noted. “But it looks like a shrunken head.” Events like Heirloom Apple Day, which brings together hundreds of amateur and professional apple lovers at the farm for talks and tastings each October, are one way to widen perspectives, Ms. Robinson said. But, she added, the quirks of the fruit are also what makes them so beautiful. She’s currently smitten with the Blue Pearmain, a crisp eating variety whose “blooming cheek” Henry David Thoreau immortalized in his 1862 essay “Wild Apples.” “That’s the thing about apples — they’re both totally ubiquitous and really personal,” she said. “When you see a variety that has been around since the 1500s, you have to remember that it’s because someone cared enough to keep it going.”

item.title: Why I Can’t Stop Making Eggplant Omelets, Filipino-Style
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine
Easy and delicious tortang talong is a staple of Filipino home cooking. It’s also a canvas, ready to be topped to your liking. Tortang talong, a comforting eggplant omelet, was one of the first dishes that Tita Becky, a content creator focused on Filipino cooking, learned to make when she was little. Back in Santa Rosa, in the Filipino province of Laguna, her family had a chicken coop, which meant fresh eggs all week. Plus eggplants were cheap, sometimes free, because neighbors grew them in the yard. These eggplants weren’t like the stout, drop-shaped Italian ones, nor were they like the giant, dark-purple globes sold ubiquitously in the United States. They were Asian eggplants — often labeled as “Chinese eggplants” or “Japanese eggplants” — long and slender, a vivid, sugarplum purple and much, much sweeter. In a Filipino household, where there’s eggplant, there’s also egg. It feels almost poetic to coat a grilled, peeled and flattened aubergine in a little seasoned beaten egg and then pan-fry it in oil until crisp, browned and delicious. A staple of Filipino home cooking, tortang talong (pronounced TORE-tahng tuh-LONG) is an exceedingly resourceful, ingenious egg dish. It’s also a canvas for the cook. For Amelia Rampe, a chef and recipe creator, tortang talong tastes best when the eggplant is charcoal-grilled whole until absolutely custardy. During this cooking process, she said, “the skin acts as a protective sheath” while the moisture inside turns into steam and collapses the spongy flesh. “There’s beauty in the structural breakdown,” said Ms. Rampe, who has contributed recipes to New York Times Cooking. After interviewing dozens of Filipino and Filipino American cooks for this column, it became clear that for many smoke is a main ingredient. Whenever Ian Rivero smells charred eggplant wafting from the kitchen, he knows that tortang talong isn’t far away. Charring an eggplant — truly blackening its skin — he said, “has this really specific smell, a little sweet-leaning.” Mr. Rivero, whose debut cookbook, “Filipino Style,” comes out in February, has recently been broiling his talongs “for a more hands-off approach.” Whether you broil the eggplants (which takes about 20 minutes) or roast them over an open flame (which takes about five), you can get enough blackened skin for that quintessential flavor, the kind that makes dishes like baba ghanouj so hauntingly delicious. With so few ingredients in tortang talong, that smokiness is key. If you live in New York and want to taste an expertly calibrated iteration, down to the smokiness, head to Leland Eating and Drinking House in Prospect Heights, Brooklyn, where the chef, Delfin Jaranilla, increases the egg count from one per eggplant (the Filipino home cook’s standard) to four. At first, he made his version of the classic for dinner, until his business partner and the restaurant’s owner, Randi Lee, asked him: This is more of a brunch dish, don’t you think? Upping the eggs wasn’t just a brunch move. The eggs are more seasoned than the dish’s center — that perfectly charred, peeled, flattened, battered and pan-fried eggplant — which means you bounce from one extreme to the next: from smoky and sweet, to salty and savory, to fresh and green with local cherry tomatoes, arugula and a lemon aioli. A shower of pecorino makes the dish feel slightly Italian, but it’s decidedly Filipino at heart. Though the eggplant omelet is lovely on its own, its tablemates — a bowl of rice, a squirt of banana ketchup and some kind of relish or salad, usually — turn the singular dish into an everyday luxury. That’s what Filipino food is: celebrating the ordinary, making use of the ingredients you have. My friend and colleague Amber Spry, who regularly cooks and eats the dish, says what you pair it with is up to the house. For some, that may be ketchup or a spiced vinegar with chile and garlic; for others, a cane vinegar-doused relish of tomato and onion. Mr. Rivero prefers his with mango. Ms. Rampe likes to add aromatic lamb crumbles. For Ms. Spry, it’s some form of salad made with fresh ingredients like chile and scallions, a foil to the rich yet somehow still light eggplant. For anyone who finds banana ketchup too sweet, you could stir a little Sriracha into plain ketchup, as the chef and journalist Wilma Consul does. I love tortang talong with a really good soy sauce and a cheek of lemon for spritzing all over. If tortang talong is a canvas for the home cook, it’s also a love letter to the diner. Tita Becky makes the dish several times a week for her husband and son. When cooking for others, it’s the everyday that feels the most special.

item.title: These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Eater
American resorts are once again having a moment — and it’s not pickleball partisans driving the trend. A new generation of travelers, beset with decision fatigue in their daily lives, are embracing the all-inclusive stay where activities, amenities, and dining are all on the menu and usually just a short walk from their rooms. These Resorts Offer a Real Taste of American Regional Cuisine No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience. Fortunately, stress-free no longer needs to mean bland or generic when it comes to cuisine and culture. Resorts have begun forging deep culinary connections to their surroundings, far beyond merely offering a few regionally specific cocktails or themed burger toppings. Onsite farms, creameries, and distilleries provide fresh ingredients with true terroir, as well as a new category of resort activity: food-and-drink-focused tours and workshops to fill the time between morning yoga and an afternoon poolside nap. Some resort restaurants, like Clay at Wildflower Farms in New York’s Hudson Valley and Sierra Mar at the Post Ranch Inn in Big Sur, California, have become destinations in themselves, where star chefs take diners deep into a region’s foodways. These resorts leave visitors not just relaxed but also satisfied, having truly experienced — and tasted — a particular place. Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more. By the time you get to Hawks Cay Resort in the middle of the Florida Keys, the blue vistas of the Overseas Highway will have made mainland worries seem very far away. The 60-acre resort on Duck Key offers a spa, five pools (including a saltwater lagoon), and soon a full water park. Also making a splash is Salt + Ash, the resort’s flagship live-fire restaurant from Florida native, Top Chef winner, and former Eater Miami Chef of the Year Jeremy Ford. Of course, fish and seafood from the surrounding waters feature prominently. But Florida flavors shine through in other ways too: Much of the produce on the menu comes from Ford’s Farm, strategically located between Miami Beach and the Keys. That might mean homegrown lychees in a uniquely local take on conch salad, or heirloom tomatoes just hours off the vine accompanying crisp-fried spear-caught fish. Many resorts lay claim to a signature dish or cocktail. But the Tides Inn, situated on a quiet tributary of the Chesapeake Bay about 3 hours’ drive from Washington, D.C., has something few resorts, if any, can boast: its own oyster. Cultivated near the property by resident ecologist Will Smiley and served exclusively at the resort’s Salt & Meadow restaurant, the Widgeon oyster provides guests with an intimate connection to the estuary it calls home. To taste it is to taste the tides and the weather. “Our oyster changes salinity as the season changes, and as the weather changes,” says executive chef Kyle Perkins. He further notes that the freshwater influx with a heavy rainfall can quickly, if temporarily, change how much of a salty punch a Widgeon possesses. Beyond bivalves, Perkins sources everything from beef to blackberries from the region. Along with activities from lawn games and pickleball to kayaking, guests can even help themselves to the harvest: Those blackberries, a thornless variety, grow in abundance on the property, giving many children a first foraging experience. Though it’s only about a 90-minute drive from the concrete canyons of Manhattan, Auberge Collection’s Wildflower Farms feels a world away. The Hudson Valley property’s 65 cabins, cottages, and suites feature floor-to-ceiling windows framing arcadian views. Thistle, an Auberge Spa, makes use of local botanicals and blooms in its treatments, while the on-site farm provides more than 14,000 pounds of produce annually for the restaurant, Clay. “The Hudson Valley is unique in the array of locally grown ingredients available,” says farm director Will Conway, noting that the resort’s culinary reach extends beyond its 140 acres. The menu is resolutely seasonal; even a dish like ricotta meatballs provides a changing taste of what is coming from nearby producers, with the protein shifting from pork to lamb depending on the time of year. The Kohler name is, for most people, synonymous with kitchen and bath fixtures. But the company is also a serious player in hospitality, most notably with Kohler, Wisconsin, its sprawling resort in the town where the company is headquartered, two and a half hours from Chicago. Along with golf, a legendary spa, and outdoor activities like canoeing, hiking, hunting, and fishing, Kohler, Wisconsin, puts a strong emphasis on dining with Midwestern ingredients and hospitality. Among the on-site options is River Wildlife, a log cabin restaurant offering regional specialties like walleye, pheasant, and duck. The Wisconsin Room, meanwhile, combines steakhouse fare with Wisconsin supper club favorites like a “Not So Lazy” Susan, which includes deviled eggs, chicken liver mousse, and pickled vegetables in a nod to the classic relish tray. Regional cocktails like a brandy Old Fashioned and a grasshopper (de rigeur after dinner) leave no doubt where you are. This resort three and a half hours northwest of Denver is big — about twice the size of Manhattan big. That leaves plenty of room for culinary operations that include a distillery, a bakery, and a greenhouse. Brush Creek Ranch’s herd of American wagyu cattle is raised using Japanese methods, which minimize stress in the name of producing superior marbling for added tenderness. You may not run into a steer getting a facial in one of the resort’s two spas, but rest assured, these animals are living their best lives. The ranch’s goats, meanwhile, don’t just assist with yoga classes: Some provide milk for the property’s Medicine Bow Creamery and its range of excellent cheeses. It all comes together at the Cheyenne Club restaurant, where meals and most beverages — like many of the resort’s activities, ranging from horseback riding and hiking to fly-fishing and standup paddleboard yoga — are included in the room rate. At Castle Hot Springs, everything comes back to the water. The 130-year-old resort in the Bradshaw Mountains, about an hour north of Phoenix, was Arizona’s first spa retreat; families like the Rockefellers and Astors would come to soak in the spring-fed pools first discovered by Native American people thousands of years before. Along with a full roster of wellness and outdoor activities, the resort grows 35 types of citrus and features a 3-acre farm, irrigated by the same mineral-rich water that fills the pools. “Everything tastes a little bit better because it’s already pre-seasoned for me,” said executive chef Chris Knouse. To get a taste of “the farm on a plate,” Knouse recommends the lunchtime “farmer’s hummus,” which comes with that day’s harvest as a crudités assortment. At dinner, Harvest restaurant offers a tasting menu where dishes like cavatelli with corn, zucchini, tatsoi, and cherry tomatoes offer a deeper dive into what the Sonoran Desert can produce. Arguably the only thing more beautiful than Post Ranch Inn is the drive there. It is, after all, located along what might be the most picturesque stretch of road in the entire country: Highway 1 in Big Sur. On a cliff overlooking the Pacific Ocean, the resort offers guests access to a spa and three pools, as well as activities like forest meditation and stargazing. Of Post Ranch Inn’s 100 acres, 90 are kept wild, and just over one is dedicated to a chef’s garden, which supplies the resort’s restaurant Sierra Mar. On this patch of land, chef Reylon Agustin and his team grow everything from apples and tomatoes to herbs and specialty ingredients like celtuce. From the surrounding forests come wild mushrooms, while nearby waters provide treasured ingredients like abalone for Sierra Mar, which is housed in a glass and wood pavilion that feels like it’s hovering over the cliff’s edge. Augustin knows well enough not to try to compete with the view. Instead, dishes like abalone congee and Grimaud Farms guinea hen with sunchokes and stone fruit highlight local ingredients to “complement the experience” of being in such a singular place.

item.title: Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts
item.description:
Source: Eater
Plenty of resorts across the country have excellent restaurants, but travelers seeking more should explore the hands-on side of culinary resort experiences. From New York’s Hudson Valley to the South Texas Coast, adventurous food lovers can partake in workshops and experiences that get them out of the dining room and into the kitchen, garden, farm, or ocean. Whether you’re looking to forage or fish, these excursions will introduce you to local people, ingredients, and techniques, and ultimately offer a true taste of the destination. Enjoy Fishing, Foraging, and Focaccia-Making at These U.S. Resorts Guests today expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field. At these properties, it’s less about what’s on your plate and more about how it got there. Big Sur is the perfect place to forage for edible botanicals and aromatics, and on Chesapeake Bay, harvesting and shucking oysters is woven into the community’s cultural fabric. Those wanting to escape the hustle and bustle of New York City can head up to the Hudson Valley for focaccia-making, while a desert oasis on the outskirts of Scottsdale, Arizona, teaches you how to craft pasta like a pro. No matter your level of expertise, these resort experiences are designed to connect curious travelers with an impressive network of chefs, farmers, ecologists, mixologists, and bakers. For a vacation that will also quench your thirst for knowledge, head to these exciting culinary resorts. Acura has always done things its own way. We believe the best experiences are created through intentional choices, thoughtful craftsmanship, and the confidence to pursue a different approach. This spirit is reflected in our philosophy of Precision Crafted Performance. Learn more. Head down to the South Texas Coast for a true catch-to-table culinary experience. Local guides at La Pesca Lodge take guests to prime spots throughout Baffin Bay, offering everything from fly-fishing and wading to drifting and sight casting. Though you’re welcome to bring your own gear, the lodge provides spinning rods, lures, and live bait if needed. Expect to reel in an array of speckled trout, redfish, flounder, and black drum. Your catch will be cleaned and bagged for you to take back to the lodge, where chefs transform your bounty into ceviche, grilled fillets, and more. Just remember that you’ll need to purchase your own Texas fishing license in advance. Those more interested in old-fashioned hunting can partake in dove, duck, or nilgai shoots. The Andaz Scottsdale Resort & Bungalows is a retro, palm-tree-lined oasis with a premier spa, unique art collection, and the on-site restaurant Weft & Warp. Every Thursday, guests can beat the desert heat with a hands-on pasta class in the restaurant for $65. You’ll learn a variety of techniques while crafting a few different pasta shapes. You might make agnolotti filled with a chive and shrimp paste; and you will also learn simpler pastas, like classic linguine or fettuccine. Once you’re done, enjoy your finished product with an optional wine pairing on the patio. If you’ve got dessert on the brain, book the Sweet Escape truffle-making workshop (hosted every Friday) and elevate your pastry skills by learning the basics of chocolate tempering. Virginia’s Tides Inn gives travelers the chance to live like a Chesapeake waterman for the day. This signature activity pairs guests with a resident ecologist who takes you out to oyster cages via boat for an educational experience that’s all about shellfish. You’ll haul up your own oyster cages and sort through the very best bivalves, all while learning about the region’s longstanding history with oystering and the positive impact it has on the local ecosystem. Oysters harvested during the excursion need to be refrigerated for at least 24 hours, so when you return to the inn, enjoy a shucking how-to with the previous day’s haul while sipping on local wine and beer. The Chesapeake Gold experience is a similar outing, but includes a visit to one of the inn’s very own oyster farms, meaning you get to consume the same ones you collect. Once back at the inn, enjoy them both raw, grilled, and topped with your favorite seasonings. Located in the foothills of Tennessee’s Great Smoky Mountains, Blackberry Farm is a working estate that maintains a strong connection to Appalachian agriculture. A twice-daily farmstead tour is available all year long, giving guests an in-depth look at the heirloom gardens, heritage livestock pasture, and dairy barn. These manicured, bright green gardens create a scenic backdrop to your itinerary, which includes sampling of farmstead cheeses, cured meats, preserves, and a rotating seasonal beverage. Those wanting a more formal culinary experience can book a three-hour artisan cooking demo with a three-course educational lunch and a glass of wine to pair. Located about an hour and 20 minutes away from Phoenix, Castle Hot Springs is a picturesque desert resort with a thriving agricultural operation. The 3-acre garden yields more than 150 seasonal fruits, veggies, herbs, and flowers, supporting a dynamic farm-to-table ethos across the resort’s Relais & Châteaux-approved restaurant, Harvest. Start your day with a one-hour farm tour, tasting your way through a variety of crops as you learn about the fertile soils supported by the area’s natural geothermal hot springs. In the afternoon, test your skills with a hands-on mixology class using produce and botanicals straight from the property grounds. The Osthoff Resort & Spa is about 150 miles north of Chicago, right along the shores of Wisconsin’s Elkhart Lake. It doubles as a professional cooking school, hosting a plethora of gourmet classes fit for any season or holiday. The culinary curriculum is overseen by chef Rodney Schulz, with courses changing week to week. October’s schedule features everything from paella- and pasta-making to creepy themed cocktails for Halloween. November sees hearty soup demos and holiday pies, while December embraces a festive spirit with Christmas libations and cookies. There is plenty of hands-on instruction, and you’ll be returning home with a new set of skills that are far more useful than any souvenir. Ready to hard-launch your sourdough baking era? Learn the basics with Ashley Napoli, also known as the Focaccia Flourist, at the Hudson Valley’s Wildflower Farms. This Auberge Collection property is about 90 miles away from New York City, which makes it an easy escape for city dwellers needing to touch some grass. The focaccia workshop costs $168 per person and starts by teaching you how to care for and maintain a living sourdough starter. You then knead, arrange, and shape your loaf, topping it with herbs, onions, florals, olives, and anything you’d like before baking. This particular workshop is being offered every Sunday and Tuesday through the end of October, but the resort typically hosts some version of a focaccia class throughout the year. In Big Sur, towering redwood forest meets dramatic, bluff-lined coast, creating a diverse ecosystem brimming with unique plant life. The serene 54-room Alila Ventana Big Sur is a wellness-focused resort that spans 160 acres of lush, open meadows, tree-lined trails, and shaded ravines, creating the ideal conditions for a plethora of fungi and botanicals. Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, the hotel hosts a complimentary foragers hike for guests, who will learn all about wild-food harvesting and spotting secret ingredients hidden within the local terrain. There’s also a year-round Foragers Cocktail class ($99), a more in-depth experience that begins with an outdoor search for various herbs and aromatics, and culminates in a mixology lesson where you craft small-batch bitters for a custom cocktail.

item.title: Steal my Food Itinerary: A SoCal Beach Dive Bar Crawl
item.description:
Source: Eater
Do birthdays matter? Not really. But they are, at the very least, an excuse to do something you might not usually do as a middle-aged father of two. On this most recent occasion, my birthday was a reason to drag an assortment of friendship flotsam across the Los Angeles coastline, working our way down through a selection of Southern California beach dive bars. (It also marks the second time I’ve used my assignments for Eater and Punch to rationalize, or maybe subsidize, a birthday bar crawl.) I truly believe that these old, salt-crusted pubs are an essential, last-remaining stronghold of our regional culture, and that they demand both our respect and our money. Steal my Food Itinerary: A SoCal Beach Dive Bar Crawl In my opinion, this is the best way to celebrate your birthday. If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. This crawl took place on a Saturday in September, filled with drinks and snacks (but mostly bites of bar burgers), working our way from Santa Monica to Manhattan Beach before wandering inland for dinner in Torrance, home to some of the best Japanese food in the United States. The plan was to start relatively early, enjoying as much sunlit ocean breeze as we could, while also allowing me to get a normal amount of sleep at the end of the night before waking up at traditional dad hours. The great thing about a bar crawl is that it allows people to jump on and off as they see fit. I’m also a sucker for a brisk itinerary, moving quickly from place to place: the key is to not care who shows up when and where, simply telling someone to add the necessary ETAs to the group chat as applicable. Stop 1: Chez Jay — Santa Monica — 3:25pm Opened in 1959, and a roughly 8-minute walk from the beach, Chez Jay has remained a staple and a refuge in a city that has been rapidly pricing out old neighborhood bars and restaurants. It is a place to drink a martini or a beer, where the only rules are that you “take no pictures, and throw your peanut shells on the floor.” (I broke one of the rules.) The kitchen was not open yet, but the peanuts were plentiful and the pours were heavy. The red booths and red checkerboard tablecloths evoke an old Italian restaurant, though it is certainly more of a steak-and-seafood kind of place to have dinner. It started strong, with six people showing up, including my dad and stepmom. Stop 2: Hinano Cafe — Venice Beach — 4:38 p.m. Hinano Cafe has been operating on a busy stretch of Venice Beach since 1962. This perpetually packed place has become an iconic surfer hang serving beer and burgers (no full liquor license here) — and like a true surfer bar, it serves breakfast from 8 a.m. until noon. Our group swelled with more friends at our second location, where pitchers of beer were poured in a standing-room-only setting, alongside board-short-wearing day drinkers who were far too young and attractive for us to stay any longer than it took for this gaggle of graying dads to order and split a hamburger. At $12.50, this perfectly acceptable bar burger on a sesame seed bun was a pleasant enough edible intermezzo. I’d prefer to come back again at another time, like maybe 1975. Stop 3: Prince O’ Whales — Playa del Rey — 5:30 p.m. We had now crossed to the other side of the marina — something of a traffic dividing line in Los Angeles County — and settled into a perfect little three-bar-crawl that exists on a 0.2-mile stretch of this hidden, working-class LA beach community. The sun was starting to drop and the ocean breeze was relaxing our shoulders (although that also may have just been the drinks). We sauntered into Prince O’ Whales, which has been serving drinks under this name for over five decades, with another 18 years before under a different one (“The Bowsprit”). There are two indoor bars, though one was closed for the afternoon. Our bartender was the kind of grumpy you look for in a sailor’s saloon, and the room was crowded with some rather loud folks watching college football. (It turns out I’m getting old.) We took our drinks to the back patio, a serene little patch of cement, brick, faded paint and sun-withered wood. There was also a ping-pong table, and this round was highlighted by exactly the kind of late-summer weather that makes people live by the beach in Southern California. Stop 4: The Harbor Room — Playa del Rey — 6:01 p.m. After walking for about 90 seconds, we made it to a place known as “the smallest dive bar in Los Angeles.” It would feel like a California-themed yokocho in Tokyo if it weren’t so perfectly lived in, lined with old wood that feels like you’re drinking in the bowels of a turn-of-the-century vessel crossing the Atlantic. A drunk, nonthreatening stranger joined our group and asked a lot of questions. I ordered a vodka-soda and they gave me a gin and tonic, so I ordered a gin martini. It came with a “sidecar” that was, incredibly, just a rocks glass with a splash of rapidly warming gin in it. I curiously wandered into the adjoining Italian restaurant and was convinced by some very friendly women to order some food. I told them to pick their favorite dish and near the end of my martini, a foil container of steaming hot ravioli was dropped at our table. If my wife divorces me, I could see myself paying rent on one of these barstools, living out my twilight years and wondering where it all went wrong. Stop 5: The Shack — Playa del Rey — 6:27 p.m. Looking back at my iPhone photo timestamps, I am incredibly impressed that we were able to have a round of martinis and a plate of ravioli in 26 minutes. We soldiered on, with an even shorter walk to our next location: the classic old surf bar and restaurant, The Shack. It feels almost set-decorated, with the perfect amount of wear and tear. This place was significantly more spacious and we found room at the bar, where we ordered the Shack Burger for all to try, as well as some wings. The signature burger comes, miraculously, with a butterflied Louisiana hot link on it, operating like juicier, snappier, spicier bacon. I, meanwhile, remained impressed with my ability to have five drinks (or was it six?) — a skill that rarely gets tested anymore. Stop 6: Ercole’s — Manhattan Beach — 7:23 p.m. Nearing its 100th year of operation (though not always as a bar — it opened during Prohibition), this could easily have been the last stop of the tour, the flagship bar you build a crawl around. Known among my friends as “the best dive bar burger in LA County,” this proud, defiant establishment has stood the test of time, surviving rapidly escalating real estate prices to remain the great neighborhood dive it has always been. It feels like a sacred escape from the rest of this wealthy beach community. The whole place seems to be made of wood and beer signs; there is one line for ordering and another for the bathroom; and every single patron — whether gray-haired in Hawaiian shirts or tatted-up bikers — seems to know how lucky they are to be there. There is a small grill behind the bar in the corner, under a yellow sign proudly proclaiming “no fries.” The cheeseburger is an exercise in simple chargrilled perfection, its meat sourced from the butcher shop next door, all served in a basket with a bag of potato chips. The menu also claims to have a teriyaki chicken sandwich, though I’ve never seen one there. I wished we could have stayed longer, or to have eaten a whole burger instead of just two bites, but such is the nature of a crawl. We quickly made our way out, calling our next restaurant to let them know we were running about 20 minutes late for our reservation. Stop 7: Torihei — Torrance – sometime not long after 8 p.m. We did a decent job of snacking rather than eating on our beach dive crawl, so after we settled into a long table adorned with sake and beer, there was perhaps no more comforting bite of food in the world than Torihei’s simmered slab of daikon radish, served in dashi and blanketed in katsuobushi (smoked, dried skipjack tuna flakes). It warmed my chest. This classic standby izakaya specializes in yakitori (grilled chicken skewers) and oden (simmered ingredients in broth). We sipped beers and crunched tender chicken cartilage alongside grilled chicken meatballs before finishing the night with some soborodon (a ground chicken and rice bowl). I was home, showered, and in bed before 11:15. I think we nailed it.

item.title: Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes
item.description:
Source: Eater
Chicago’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Is Cooking From 900-Year-Old Recipes An interview with the chef behind Muhājir This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings. Zubair Mohajir is one of Chicago’s most prolific new chefs and restaurateurs, behind such openings as Lilac Tiger, Mariela, Mirra, Sarima, and most recently, Muhājir, a restaurant that traces historical spice routes to tell the story of global migration. I talked to Mohajir about how the opening is going, how he thinks about collaboration across his different projects, and why Muhājir is finally the restaurant that feels like home. Pre Shift: What did you want to explore with Muhājir that you hadn’t been able to do yet with your previous restaurants? Zubair Mohajir: Muhājir is such a personal story for me, because my last name is Mohajir, and the meaning of “muhājir” in Arabic and Urdu is “one who migrates.” When the partition [of India and Pakistan] happened, the Muslims that were moved from India to Pakistan were named Muhājirs because they were migrated. In my family, we always wondered why that was our last name. When I started cooking [after working in finance], it really started to settle in. Our late maternal grandfather was obsessed with mapping where this family name came from. It comes from Southern Basra, Iraq, and that was so mind-blowing for me because it’s one of the biggest spice roads. At Coach House for the past five years, I’ve been exploring ancient recipes in southern Spain and southern Portugal. [They] bring in pre-Crusade Muslim, Christian, Jewish [influences] that are also affected by the Southeast Asian traders coming on the spice road that shoots through the Mediterranean and hits North Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. I’m just obsessed with history and it started to become very evident for me that I really wanted to feed people, but with the context of where the food came from. At Muhājir, it’s all about riding the spice road that runs from Portugal through the Mediterranean, through the Levantine [region], and then hits out of Basra, Iraq, into the Persian Gulf, and the first landmass it comes across is southern India, where I’m from. We’re all muhājirs — you know, all of our families came from somewhere, and that really has been the driving force for me. Why did you decide to build the restaurant around live fire? I’d never cooked on live fire, but we’re cooks, and it was going back to core things. I remember growing up in my grandmother’s house back home in India, and it’s not like there were gas stoves everywhere. When I decided that I was going to do Muhājir, it became so obvious to me that it couldn’t just be a sauté pan on a stove. The story that we wanted to tell had to be told through wood fire. Is there a dish that feels especially representative of Muhājir? We do a duck that is inspired by a 927-year-old recipe we found from southern Spain that is influenced by Roman garums, Muslim origins, and Jewish origins. We do this duck “experience,” where we take a whole duck, butcher it, and have the crown dry-aging for seven days. We take the wings and make a jus [and] take the legs and make a confit. We blast that duck crown over the fire when we start service every day, and then it gets finished in the brasa. If you’re sitting in the restaurant, you can see the ducks hanging over the fire. When we present it, we have this beautiful ornate Turkish platter. There’s black raspberry achaar, the duck jus in a saucier, the duck rice next to it, the duck skin cut in these beautiful medallions on top almost like duck chicharrón, and then we’re also presenting the duck breast itself that has a very crispy skin. The top of that duck breast is the spice mix from that exact recipe that’s more than 900 years old, with cumin, coriander, cardamom, toasted pine nuts, red wine vinegar, and fish sauce. It’s a story of cross-cultural collaboration. You have a bar called Bobo behind the restaurant. How do the two spaces complement each other? Bobo’s really inspired by Jacob Dela Cruz, who’s my partner here. We built Sarima together, and it became very important to me to highlight his upbringing and his background as well. He was one who said, “You should name the restaurant Muhājir.” His point was that we’re all immigrants. I was like, “That’s such a simple statement, but such a profound statement.” It was kind of vice versa when we were talking about the bar: Jacob’s father is an amazing person and his name is Bho, and “bobo” in Tagalog means “silly” or “stupid,” as a term of endearment. We always say that as Spice Road-driven and transformative the food experience at Muhājir is, we still like to have fun. If people are early for their reservation, we take them back to Bobo, or they stop by after dinner. You can’t get to Bobo without walking through the restaurant, so the spaces contribute to each other. If you came to Bobo, you might be like, “I want to eat there.” And if you come straight to Muhājir and see people walking back constantly, you might be like, “What’s happening back there?” I wouldn’t say it’s easier [than my other restaurants], but now I don’t freak out. I’ve created a methodical way of approaching issues or problems head-on and figuring it out as a group or with the people that support us. We don’t have investors who are private equity firms; our investors are our guests. When it comes to managing expectations and navigating obstacles, you get better with repetition. I’m living a dream. Sometimes, when you’re building restaurants with others, you’re not necessarily in the kitchen. [At Mirra, I] was like, “I’m helping create and build this concept, but that’s [chef Rishi Kumar’s] kitchen to run.” Here, it’s the home that I’ve been yearning for and working toward my whole career. I plan to be old in this place. Things have been so crazy and wild and amazing, but slowly, every day, I sit more and more in that moment where I’m like, “This is home.” This interview has been edited and condensed. See More:

item.title: The Fine Dining Flip
item.description:
Source: Eater
When Chateau Royale opened in New York City last year, it embodied the city’s rising “swankstaurant” moment, in which the saturation of the steakhouse gave rise to “a new age of gloss,” per Grub Street’s Matthew Schneier. At Chateau Royale, a single-bite beggar’s purse of caviar and crème fraîche went for $39. A $72 lobster thermidor and $90 Dover sole anchored the entrees. The $24 martinis were made tableside on a trolley. At its opening, co-owner Cody Pruitt described the restaurant as “familiarity, just with a little bit more of a tuxedo on it.” Across the country, some owners are doing the unimaginable: replacing their high-end restaurants with ones where diners can spend less That restaurant is no longer, though, replaced in August by Floradora, a drastically different concept from the same ownership. This reincarnation is more like jeans-and-a-T-shirt familiar: mozzarella sticks, $17; pull-apart garlic bread, $7; vodka sauce pasta, $25. Here, the steak frites au poivre run $49, significantly less than Chateau’s $69 rendition. At Floradora, it uses bavette as opposed to the latter’s filet mignon, but the argument is that filet is for an occasion, and Floradora is meant to be not just for any night, but many nights. It’s “everyday luxury,” Pruitt says, which, to him, is about “generosity, ease, and feeling welcome.” There are still tableside martinis — the custom cart was an investment, after all — but the prices have dropped, since each table’s server now pours the martini, as opposed to an attendant who manned only the cart. Over the past few months, Pruitt and his business partner Jacob Cohen have done two shake-ups like this, in an almost too-on-the-nose manifestation of the current economic climate. In June, they replaced their French bistro Libertine, where duck for two clocked in at $72 in 2023, with Capitaine, where — excluding the caviar and seafood towers — the highest-priced item on the menu is the $52 steak frites. Most dishes are under $30, with more snacks on the menu to allow diners lower-key ways of stopping in — there are only so many special occasion spots a city can sustain. “At a certain point, the world around both [restaurants] began to change,” Pruitt says. “We were increasingly conscious of what a restaurant costs people and how often they could use it.” There is a difference, he notes, between a restaurant that belongs to a neighborhood and one that merely takes up space in it. The accepted logic across these years of rampant inflation has been, however bleak, that once prices hit a certain point, they won’t go back down again. Receipts from 2021 inspire shock at how much further money went just a few years ago. A $30 burger at a nice restaurant has gone from spectacle to surprisingly common. The $20 cocktail paved the way for the $24 one, and given this escape velocity, the $30+ drinks now on menus were simply inevitable. Every month brings some new absurdity — $60 bread, $40 half-chickens — that makes people wonder: Who is even buying this? Prices can only go so high before diners start to drop out of the whole endeavor, and restaurants, however counterintuitively, begin to price themselves out of existence. For the owners of some high-end restaurants, the current economic landscape has led to an existential pondering. Does everyone really want near-$100 shareable mains, especially on the average weeknight? What’s the point of the luxurious, glitzy restaurant to which many diners might go only once or twice? In a reassessment similar to Pruitt and Cohen’s, some operators across the country have been taking the same action: flipping their higher-end restaurants to more affordable models that they hope will be more sustainable — that’s both for diners and for themselves. If the steakhouses and swankstaurants of 2025 represented, at best, a display of status aspirations (and, at worst, the growing economic stratification of American society), the flipped restaurants of 2026 represent a necessary reckoning with reality, in which our collective foundations feel more unstable than ever. Some high-end restaurants in Los Angeles — where even bars are now lowering prices — have come to the same conclusion. When Anthony Wang’s Firstborn and Mei Lin’s 88 Club opened in short succession in the spring of 2025, the two restaurants represented an exciting moment for upscale and innovative diasporic Chinese food in the city. At Firstborn, Wang took cues from twice-cooked pork with a barbecued cabbage that took two days to make, slow-roasting cabbage until its leaves turned tender, then pressing them terrine-like with confit leeks and serving it in broiled slices with a sauce of burnt alliums and black vinegar. It went for $22. At 88 Club, Lin served a fancy shrimp toast, sliced into three teatime-esque pieces, dolloped with hot mustard on one side and sweet-and-sour sauce on the other. Its going rate: $38. At the time of 88 Club’s opening, Lin cited some concern about the viability of a high-end restaurant amid the economic climate. The combination of wildfires, immigration raids, and the writers strike (and its ripple effects across the entertainment industry) in recent years have pummeled the city’s restaurant industry, leading to constant, heartbreaking closures. Perhaps for this reason, the two restaurants remain oddly synchronized: This year, both flipped into pointedly more accessible formats. In February, Firstborn announced that it would be scrapping its a la carte menu in favor of a four-course prix fixe, priced at $68 per person. In the original model, check averages were dwindling and becoming unpredictable. While the previous menu of shareable dishes sometimes left diners unsure of how to structure a meal, the restaurant’s current goal is to “get a full meal in front of you and just tell you what it costs,” says Wang. Given that the $100-ish tasting menu is now considered a deal in many cities, $68 per person felt like a “manageable” number that communicated that “this is a value-driven restaurant,” Wang says. Operationally, there have been some benefits to the flip at Firstborn. With just three options available for each course, the restaurant can put more unconventional products such as sweetbreads or lamb neck on the menu with some certainty that they’ll sell. (The restaurant’s popular fried chicken and mapo tofu with sweetbreads remain available as supplements.) In the kitchen, prep can be more focused since cooks are doing fewer things, though more of each. Turn times have also become more predictable. 88 Club has seen slightly more upheaval. In April, Lin stepped away from the restaurant, leaving it to former business partner Francis Miranda. Last month, Miranda flipped the concept into Tiger Tiger, where under the direction of chef Michael Chih, $36 black pepper filet mignon and $30 char siu take the place of $125 black pepper strip steak featuring Westholme wagyu and $88 char siu using Ibérico pork. With its small menu and its no-substitutions approach, 88 Club was “honestly just way too expensive,” Miranda says. The check average for two people without alcohol was $250 on the low end; add drinks, and it was closer to $400. “It really became a place where you would come to say you’ve come once, and then you wouldn’t come again,” Miranda says. At Tiger Tiger, the goal is for the check average to be in the range of $60 to $80 per person. Right now, diners care less about buzzwords signifying high-end ingredients and more about whether the portion sizes will allow for leftovers. 88 Club’s approach was “chef-driven,” Miranda says. “Now, it’s really guest-driven.” If Tail Up Goat, the Michelin-starred restaurant in Washington, D.C., had continued as it was, “we would have limped to the end of our lease,” says Jill Tyler, who opened it in 2016 with her husband, chef Jon Sybert. That’s not to say that the restaurant — which alternated its format between a la carte and tasting menu, the latter priced at $135 per person by the end — didn’t have its wins. 2019 and the start of 2020 were its busiest years ever. But after the pandemic, “the pieces never fit back together,” Tyler says. By the time Tail Up Goat closed in late 2025, they’d “essentially been running a nonprofit for five years.” While cutting benefits might have made the restaurant profitable, that wasn’t the business Tyler and Sybert wanted to run. At the suggestion of Arjav Ezekiel, who runs Birdie’s in Austin, Texas, the couple considered a different model: counter service. Tyler was initially skeptical of the concept, having only seen it employed in D.C. at restaurants much more casual than the one she wanted to run, but the math made sense. The couple flipped the space into Rye Bunny, which opened in April. It offers dishes as thoughtful as at Tail Up Goat — ricotta cavatelli with grilled cabbage and smoked onion cream; arctic char a la plancha paired with mustard beurre blanc — but in a different format. Without table service, Tyler and Sybert have cut their staffing needs by 22 percent and their labor costs by 30 percent, while still providing the benefits they found essential, such as healthcare and a week of PTO for all full-timers. Over half the workers previously worked at Tail Up Goat. The price of the food at Rye Bunny might still run counter to some diners’ expectations. Pasta is $28 and large proteins hover between $30 and $50, though Tyler’s goal is for all of its pricing to come with an “impressive” amount of food. “[We want people to think], Wow, that felt like a value,” she says. Unlike the structure of Tail Up Goat, the looser Rye Bunny, which doesn’t take reservations, gives diners more control over how much they might spend. “By no means are we an inexpensive night out,” Tyler says. “But we’re trying to responsibly occupy the middle [of the dining spectrum].” While the challenges of running a restaurant remain, some of the pressure has eased over Rye Bunny’s short time in business. They’re making their loan payments without worries about what payroll looks like in six weeks. “I can’t imagine having done anything else now that we’re in it,” Tyler says. Towards the end of Tail Up Goat, even staying in restaurants felt tenuous. Right now, Tyler says, the main feeling is fun: “It’s been freeing to totally reset.” To her, Sybert’s cooking feels imbued with new energy; Rye Bunny’s format allows him to still put dishes he’s excited about on the menu on a whim, like a beef rib special of which only six might be available in a given night. That freedom of approach is not necessarily a universal feeling. For 88 Club, the trade-off of the flip into Tiger Tiger has been, most notably, a loss of ambition. The menu is made up of familiar favorites available at most Chinese restaurants: chow mein, dan dan noodles, salt and pepper shrimp; their execution isn’t intended to push the envelope. It’s comfort, and comfort food is common. “To me, that is the formula for what actually survives these crazy times that we’re in,” Miranda says. He’s seen many peers close, either unwilling to change their highbrow concepts or unable to modify their pricing by virtue of their expensive buildouts. Dialing back ambition can have some silver linings. Lowering expectations via dishes that sound run-of-the-mill creates the opportunity for chefs to over-deliver in their execution. And when the dishes on a menu seem affordable and not immediately like the restaurant is trying to take diners for a ride, diners might be inclined to order an extra dish they might not have tried otherwise, or to get a glass of wine when they might have previously written drinks off as a needless expense. A sense of generosity on the restaurant’s end can beget a similar generosity from guests. Now, value feels like the utmost form of hospitality. With a somewhat wistful nature, Miranda mentions Nightshade, the creative and universally beloved restaurant that he and Mei Lin opened in 2018. It became a pandemic casualty, its premature closure prompting people who’d dined there to still speak with reverence of its mapo tofu lasagna, tom yum bloomin’ onion, and playful cocktails. “We’re living in different culinary times and different political times,” Miranda says. Running a restaurant, especially at this moment, requires shaking off some sentimentality in favor of clear-eyed practicality. “Right now, it’s not a matter of any feelings,” he says. “It’s adapt or you will close.”

item.title: Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesnât overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, whatâs not to love? A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Donât be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that weâve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Donât be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cookingâthatâs to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Donât forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauceâs success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you donât accidentally drain away that liquid gold). Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Step 2Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced Â¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2â3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6â8 minutes. Step 3Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1â2 minutes. Pour in Â¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in Â½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2â3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed. Step 4Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding Â½â1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes. Step 5Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about Â½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed. Step 6Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

item.title: Can You Make Stuffing Ahead of Time? Yes—Here’s How
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
The key to a breezy Thanksgiving is the same as for any dinner party: Do absolutely everything you can ahead of time. I donât just mean getting a jump on cranberry sauce, pie dough, or overnight-brining the birdâyou should cross every single item, big and small, off your to-do list as far in advance as possible, to free up the big day for last-minute mishaps and (this is going to sound crazy) to enjoy yourself. Can you make stuffing ahead of time? Absolutely. Many Thanksgiving stuffing recipes can be prepared at least partially in advance. Our make-ahead stuffing recipe uses a two-stage baking process: cook the stuffing through the day before Thanksgiving, then refrigerate it overnight. The next day, all thatâs left is to reheat it and crisp up the top while your turkey rests. If youâre used to throwing together a dish of stuffing from a store-bought mix, this make-ahead stuffing recipe is a very easy, very delicious upgrade. Instead of coating a bag of brittle dried bread cubes with unidentified poultry seasoning, this homemade stuffing recipe builds big flavor with hearty torn sourdough bread, hot Italian sausage, fresh herbs, and a boatload of caramelized onions. It requires minimal day-of labor (without sacrificing taste) by relying on the prep time youâll carve out on Thanksgiving Eve. The result is a stuffing thatâs ready when you areâand plenty of time on T-Day to focus on your turkey recipe and all those other Thanksgiving side dishes. If you want to make stuffing ahead of time, the type of bread matters. Some classic stuffing recipes call for plain white bread, which will likely absorb too much moisture and disintegrate. A sturdier loaf, like sourdough bread, is more likely to retain its structure as it soaks in the chicken broth, making it the ideal choice for this make-ahead stuffing recipe. Drying the bread on two baking sheets gives you room to spread the bread cubes into a single layer for even toasting. Youâll dry them in an oven on low heat (250Â°). Donât skip this part, even if youâre using a stale loaf (since stale bread isnât actually dried out), as it helps the sourdough maintain its integrity once submerged into its custardy bath. Transfer the dried bread chunks to a large bowl and prep the rest of the mixture. True caramelized onions take a long time to break down and become the melty, sweet-savory magic you want them to be. On Thanksgiving dinners past, you would not find a caramelized onion within 100 feet of my table because I absolutely did not have that kind of time. But if Iâm assembling the entire stuffing the day before, I can cook spicy sausage, caramelize onions, and create a sage-scented base for torn bread without worrying about the clock. Build layers of flavor by sautÃ©ing the onions in the same skillet you used to render the sausage fat. Season the onions with kosher salt, add a little extra olive oil, and cook over medium heat until theyâre a deep golden brown. If anything starts to stick, add a little water and scrape up the bottom of the pan. Donât stop cooking the onions until they are certified jammy. Then add in the rest of the aromatics: celery, garlic, and black pepper, plus finely chopped herbs and unsalted butter. Deglaze the pan with white wine and let it simmer before adding it to the bowl with the bread; add the eggs and chicken stock or broth, then transfer the whole mixture to a casserole dish. (Donât have one? Use a large skillet insteadâovensafe, please.) Bake the stuffing through its first stage a day or two before Thanksgiving, then let it cool briefly before refrigerating it within two hours of cooking. On Thanksgiving Day, when your roast turkey is resting, remove the foil and return the stuffing to the oven for its second bake. The recipe calls for another 10 to 15 minutes to warm through and crisp up the top, but go by temperature, not just the clock: The center should reach 165Â°F before serving. Can you freeze stuffing? Yes. Many stuffing recipes can be frozen ahead of Thanksgiving. Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing, for example, can be baked through its first stage, then frozen for up to six months before the final bake. Let the stuffing cool briefly, wrap tightly, and freeze. Thaw it in the refrigerator before reheating, allowing at least 24 hours for a large dish. Reheat until the center reaches 165Â°F, uncovering toward the end to crisp up the top. How do you reheat stuffing without drying it out? If your stuffing seems dry, add a splash of chicken or vegetable broth before reheating. Cover the baking dish with foil to help retain moisture, then reheat in an oven set to at least 325Â°F until the center reaches 165Â°F. Remove the foil toward the end to crisp up the top. How long can you keep stuffing in the refrigerator? According to the USDA, stuffing can be refrigerated for 3â4 days, as long as itâs cooked through and refrigerated promptly. Store it in a covered container, ideally shallow enough to cool quickly, and reheat it thoroughly before serving. Additional reporting contributed by Zoe Denenberg.

item.title: Caroline Chambers on Why Cooking Can Feel Like ‘An Absolute Hellscape’
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
What does Caroline Chambers cook when she doesnât feel like cooking? Thatâs what I wanted to ask her after reading her brutally honest and heartwarming essay from our series The Fourth Trimester, all about postpartum meals. In it, Caroline writes about finding herself as a cook after giving birth to her first son. Now she has added three more kids to the mix and is navigating a wild blend of family, work, and life, yet showing up with incredible authenticity and humor. Read our conversation belowâand make it to the end for the cover recipe from Carolineâs latest book. Chris Morocco: Our team loved your first book (for readers who donât know, we named it one of our favorites of 2024) and eagerly awaited your second. How did you decide on time as the theme for your next title, Make It Fast? Caroline Chambers: I think that a huge, huge part of why cooking dinner can feel like such an absolute hellscape is that we simply do not have the time. Weâre overbooked, overworked, weâre trying to make time to be good parents and good friends and somehow get in a few minutes of exercise in. At the end of the day, cooking yet another meal usually feels like the absolute last thing on earth that you want to do. So knowing exactly how much of a time investment you are going to have to make feels really good. Being able to flip through the 15-minute chapter and think, Okay, I can freaking do this! Or the âwalk awayâ chapter and know that, with under 30 minutes of prep time, you can throw something in a pot to simmer away, or in the oven to slow roast, while you go about your day. You made the bold choice to incorporate all ingredient prep in your recipe instructions, so your active times actually include how long it takes to chop every onion and shred every carrot. Very few recipes do this! How did you arrive at this practice? Like Bon AppÃ©tit, I have years of hearing directly from my readers via my Substack, What to Cook When You Donât Feel Like Cooking. When something takes longer to chop than I thought it would take them, I hear about it. And this is a wonderful thing!
