I can adjust, learn what their pain points are, and help educate them about ways to do it with more ease the next time. But Iâve definitely learned that people do not like to be bamboozled by the prep step being included in the ingredient list. They want to be told exactly when to do it. Plus, when I lay out exactly when they should prep each ingredient, I can help maximize their efficiency in the oven. Mince the garlic while the chicken sears. Chop the herbs while the pasta cooks. Without spelling it out for them in this way, a novice home cook might mise-en-place it all out at the beginning, and that adds a lot of time. And time is of the essence with this book, we ainât got time to spare! What are the ingredients you canât live without that save you time in the kitchen? I freaking love a bagged salad. I had this series on Instagram once all about how to make bagged salads taste better. I need to bring that back. Taylor Farms Caesar is a regular staple in my householdâitâs just an honest-to-God delightful Caesar salad. Weâll have that and steaks for dinner at least a couple of times a month. I know that isnât really an ingredient, but it sort of is? Other staples: lemons, rice (I cook a huge batch and freeze it in individual portions), those frozen garlic and ginger cubes, Better Than Bouillon (Iâm a low-sodium chicken gal but I dabble in the fun ones, too, like âsofritoâ and âsautÃ©ed onionâ). I always have a jar of Trader Joeâs salsa verde (poach chicken thighs in it, shred, dinner is served). I love many types of chili crisp for instant flavor, but Red Clayâs southern chili crisp with peanuts and shallots is king. During my time in food media, I have seen a trend of the most popular recipes in the zeitgeist getting simpler and easier. Is there any hope for people wanting to roast a chicken again, or has the prevalence of rotisserie chickens in supermarkets made such recipes obsolete? I have a theory that cooking is really hard for everyone right now, not only because none of us have the time to do it, but also because none of us were taught how to do it. Our mothers and fathers were the first generation of parents where it was really widespread for both parents to be in the workforce. Mom wasnât home cooking and teaching her daughters how to cook. She was at work! So a lot of people simply never were taught fundamental cooking skills. Like how to cut an onion! If you donât know how to cut an onion, or mince a garlic clove, youâre instantly pissed. The second you start cooking a recipe, and it tells you to cut an onion, you instantly feel like you suck at cooking and it takes forever. Soâ¦I donât know, Chris! The irony of my entire brand, What to Cook When You Donât Feel Like Cooking, is, of course, that my readers do feel like cooking. Instead of ordering DoorDash, theyâre willing to give my newsletter and cookbooks a try. They want to want to cook! I know, and you know, that people feel so proud of themselves when they cook a delicious meal. So I do think that the more people can nail really simple, easy recipes, and learn to cook from those simpler recipes, the more incentivized they are to try things that intimidate themâlike roasting a whole bird. On that noteâ¦favorite thing to do with a rotisserie bird? I have an entire section in What to Cook about what to do with a rotisserie chicken, but the honest answer is that I mostly just eat it straight up! Chop it up for the kids, throw a leg to the baby in his high chair, slice up the breasts and serve them with a salad. I had some leftover rotisserie tonight, in fact, and fed it to the boys with baby broccoli, and made a version of the kale and quinoa salad for my husband and brother and his girlfriend (they live with us!). Itâs so goodâfrom the new book! My other favorite thing to do with a rotisserie chicken is to keep it in the front seat for the drive home from the store and tear it apart with my hands like an absolute animal. If anyone ever sees me eating a chicken leg while cruising on the 1, no you didnât. I have two kids with such different tastes in food. Sometimes I think they exaggerate their preferences just to show the world how different they are, which is fine when it comes to hairstyles and shoes, but a bummer with dinner. Is it challenging for you to find meals that all your kids will eat? Chris. Yes. These kids kill me. I have four boysâ7, 6, 4, and 14 months. Those little turds will tell me ribs are their favorite meal, that they dreamed about ribs (!), and then Iâll make the exact same ribs recipe I cooked the last time, and half of them will tell me theyâre too spicy. Iâm with youâI think kids use food preferences as power. It allows them to have their own opinions and their own say. It absolutely kills me. I recently instigated a very strict and probably absolutely not child-therapist-approved two-bite rule. They have to try at least two bites of dinner, and if they truly do not like it, Iâll make them a PB&J or hummus and veggies. Most of the time, my 7- and 4-year-olds wind up eating the entire thing. My 6-year-old very, very rarely does. That guy is eating a lot of PB&Js right now. And just FYI, the PB&J is: Daveâs Killer Bread 21 Whole Grains, Ground Up Honey Sea Salt peanut butter, Bonne Maman Strawberry Jam. I canât really blame him, itâs delicious. After a day working on recipe development, when you have been elbow-deep in pasta and dishes since 9 a.m., do you ever think to yourself when dinner time rolls around, Oh heck no! Is that just me? What do you cook when you donât feel like cooking? And whatâs your go-to takeout? HELL YES. The cobblerâs kids get no shoes, as they say!!! We live kinda in the country, so our take-out options absolutely suck. My take-out option is steaming frozen dumplings and broccoli florets at the same time in a steamer basket and making a peanut sauce while theyâre steaming. Everyone absolutely devours this meal. Except for my six-year-old, of course. But the good news is that the peanut butter is already out for his dinner. You have two pieces of advice in Make It Fast that I absolutely adore: âLay corn flat on its side to cut it,â and âsalt and pepper are not married.â I guess that isnât really a question, just wanted to say thank you! And if you have any other sage advice like this, I want to hear it. Oh my gosh, thanks for noticing those! Iâm a self-taught cook, meaning that Americaâs Test Kitchen and the Bon AppÃ©tit Test Kitchen are responsible for so much of my early learning. So that means a lot to hear from you. I read this book called Eight Flavors about the eight major flavors in American cuisine many, many years ago. One of the chapters is about black pepper and to absolutely butcher her beautifully done research and writingâthe common use of salt and pepper together, in every single freaking recipe, basically boils down to really good marketing when spice traders first introduced black pepper to America. Salt and pepper are not married! A few other pieces of advice from the book, for people who do not feel like cooking: - Cook once, eat twice. Always cook more than youâre going to eat. If you donât need leftovers the next day, freeze it! Make extra roasted sweet potatoes, and freeze a little bag of them! In two weeks or two months, you can thaw them and throw them on a bagged salad to make it more interesting. Always cook an extra pound of meat for lunch the next day or dinner later in the week. Donât think of them as leftovers, think of them as prepped ingredients. - You donât need to buy a huge fancy knife block full of knives. Youâre never going to use them. All you really need is a chefâs knife, a paring knife, and a serrated knife. And youâll use the chefâs knife 95% of the time. - Have a stack of compostable plates for the nights when you absolutely cannot. Being able to just throw away the plates at the end of the meal is bliss.

item.title: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Itâs That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious youâll text home about them. Thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint. No matter how expertly you time the meal, the sides are rarely eaten straight from the oven. They linger on the table while guests graze, refill their drinks, and share every detail about cousin Charlotteâs dating life. Thatâs why I gravitate toward easygoing dishes that thrive at room temp. This year, try my brussels sprouts with a crispy, cheesy skirt. Known as frico in Italian, itâs what happens when you bake grated cheese until it morphs into a golden savory cracker. The texture is lacy and light like a potato chip, shattering at the tap of a spoon or chomp of your teeth. And even with only one ingredient, itâs enough to turn a brussels sprouts skeptic into a full-blown convert. After removing the brussels from the oven, you might worry you didnât nail the frico. The cheese will look soft and pliable. Just give it time while you baste the turkey, check those rolls, or take a sip of wine. After a few minutes itâll harden into a brittle shell. If the stars align and youâre feeling adventurous, peel the entire sheetâcheese, sprouts, and allâoff of the parchment paper or mat in one swift go like a sticker and hold it up as a golden trophy, enticing admirers who want a taste. I mean, just look at it. How could anyone resist?

item.title: Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. Itâs a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you. Itâs That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious youâll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt. Need to make a substitution? - Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400Â°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1Â½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and Â½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a Â½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20â28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, itâs done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

item.title: Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
These brutti-ma-buoni-inspired hazelnut blondies take inspiration from the namesake Italian meringue cookie, which translates to âugly but good.â While I donât think the original cookies are ugly, Iâve translated their combination of toasted hazelnuts and caramelized meringue into a slightly more visual format: a chewy and fudgy brown butter blondie baked with a layer of crunchy hazelnuts on top and finished with swoops of torched meringue. The meringue is really a bonusâthe blondies are excellent even without it. For a little extra something in the flavor department, add the finely grated zest of a large orange to the warm brown butter. Need to make a substitution? - BlondieStep 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325Â°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15â18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside. Step 2Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7â9 minutes. Remove from heat. Step 3Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1Â¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, Â¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and Â¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6â9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl). Step 4Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1Â½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts). Step 5Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35â45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack. - Meringue and AssemblyStep 6Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170Â°. Step 7Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8â10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and Â½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Â¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed Step 8Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares. Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.
